________________ 
 
No. 3D25 -1051  
Lower Tribunal No. 22-5310- CA-01 
________________ 
 
 
Miurel Del Carmen Menuez , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Westport Recovery Corporation , 
Appellee.  
 
  An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, Charles 
Johnson, Judge.  
  Dorothy G. Negrin, P. A., and Dorothy G. Negrin , for appellant.  
  Friedman & Greenberg, P.A., and Robert D. Friedman (Sunrise) , for 
appellee.  
  Before  SCALES, C.J., and LOGUE and LINDSEY , JJ.  
 
 LOGUE, J.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2  Miurel del Carmen Menuez appeals the trial court’s final summary 
judgment entered in favor of Westport Recovery Corporation in her action to 
quiet title to real property, vacate a Sheriff’s Levy, Sale, and Deed, and for 
declaratory relief. The challenged final summary judgment determined that, 
by virtue of a n unelaborated order in a county court case to which Menuez 
was not a party, the doctrine of res judicata served as an absolute bar to  
Menuez’s  circuit court claims. We reverse.  
BACKGROUND  
In December 1998, the county court entered a judgment against Kenan 
L. Paicely and Tammy P. Paicely.  In September 2018, almost twenty years 
later, Westport, as successor -in-interest of the original judgment creditor, 
obtained title to a property previously owned by one of the judgment debtors, 
Kenan L. Paicely (hereinafter, the “Property”) , through a sheriff’s levy and 
sale. Five years prior, however, Menuez had acquired title to the  Property 
via a warranty deed. Westport did not seek to amend the county court’s final 
judgment to add Menuez as a party.  
Menuez, in turn, sought to intervene in the county court action to 
reopen the matter and vacate the sheriff’s sale. The county court conducted a hearing on Menuez’s Second Amended Motion to Reopen, Intervene, 
Vacate Sale, and Set Aside Sheriff’s Deed, but no transcript of this hearing

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 has been provided. The county court subsequently entered an unelaborated 
written order stating: “ORDERED AND ADJUDGED that third party, Miurel 
Del Carmen Menuez’s, Second Amended Motion to Reopen, Intervene, 
Vacate Sale and Set Aside Sheriff’s Deed is deni ed.” 
Menuez did not appeal the county court’s order but  rather brought the 
underlying  action in the circuit court seeking to quiet title to the Property and 
to set aside the sheriff’s sale. In addition to raising several arguments she 
would have asserted in the county court action had she been granted leave to intervene and the matter had been reopened, Menuez also asserted in the 
circuit court action that the Property was her homestead .  
The parties ultimately  filed competing summary judgment motions. 
Westport argued it was entitled to summary judgment because Menuez’s 
claims were precluded by the doctrine of res judicata. Specifically, Westport 
contended the county court’s order denying Menuez’s Second Amended 
Motion to Reopen, Intervene, Vacate Sale and Set Aside Sheriff’s Deed 
constituted a decision on the me rits of the same claims Menuez now brought 
in the circuit court.  
Menuez, in turn, argued in her own summary judgment motion that the 
county court’s order denying her Second Amended Motion to Reopen, 
Intervene, Vacate Sale and Set Aside Sheriff’s Deed did not rule on the

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 merits of her claims, but rather simply denied her request to re-open the case 
and intervene. As such, Menuez contended , the order did not adjudicate the 
issues presented in her circuit court action and therefore did not have 
preclusive effect.  
The trial court conducted hearings on the parties’ summary judgment 
motions and thereafter entered the challenged judgment , granting final 
summary judgment in favor of Westport and denying Menuez’s summary judgment motion. The trial court determined Menuez was entitled to no relief because Westport’s res judicata defense constituted a complete bar to 
Menuez’s claims. Menuez timely appealed the final summary judgment . 
ANALYSIS  
We review, de novo, a trial court’s summary judgment. Volusia Cnty.  
v. Aberdeen at Orm ond Beach, L.P. , 760 So.  2d 126, 130 (Fla. 2000). 
Whether a cause of action is barred by res judicata is a question of law that we also review de novo. Fernandez v. Cruz , 341 So.  3d 410, 412 -13 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2022) . 
A party claiming the benefit of res judicata has the burden of 
establishing, with sufficient certainty by the record or by extrinsic evidence, 
that the prior order adjudicated the merits of the matter. State St. Bank & Tr. 
Co. v. Badra, 765 So. 2d 251, 253 (Fla. 4th DCA 2000) . “For res judicata or

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 collateral estoppel to apply, there must [ ] exist in the prior litigation a ‘ clear -
cut former adjudication’ on the merits. ” Suniland Assoc s., Ltd. v. Wilbenka, 
Inc., 656 So. 2d 1356, 1358 (Fla. 3d DCA 1995)  (quoting State, Dep’t  of 
Health & Rehab. S ervs. v. LaPlante , 470 So.  2d 832, 834 (Fla. 2d DCA 
1985) ).  
We conclude that Westport  failed to meet its burden at summary 
judgment to establish with “sufficient certainty” that the county court’s  order 
actually adjudicated the merits of the same claims Menuez  now brings in her 
circuit court action . 
First, Menuez’s claim that the Property was protected homestead falls 
outside the ambit of any res judicata stemming from the county court order 
because it could not have properly been raised or adjudicated in the county 
court as such claim s are  within the exclusive jurisdiction of the circuit court . 
Sepulveda v. Westport Recovery Corp. , 145 So. 3d 162, 169 (Fla. 3d DCA 
2014) (holding section 222.10, Florida Statutes, grants circuit courts exclusive jurisdiction to determine a claimed homestead exemption).  
More broadly, without a transcript of the county court hearing, we do 
not know whether the county court reached, much less adjudicated, the merits of Menuez’s  Second Amended Motion to Reopen, Intervene, Vacate 
Sale, and Set Aside Sheriff’s Deed. And, the county court’s unelaborated

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 order, merely denying Menuez’s motion, provides no guidance. An 
unelaborated order is generally not deemed a decision on the merits unless 
there is a citation to authority or other statement that clearly shows the issue 
was considered and adjudicated by the court. Topps v. State , 865 So.  2d 
1253, 125 8 (Fla. 2004).  
Finally, res judicata does not apply when, as here, the prior judgment 
might have rested on either of two grounds, only one of which goes to the 
merits. deCancino v. E. Airlines, Inc. , 283 So.  2d 97, 98 (Fla. 1973).  See also  
Kent v. Sutker , 40 So. 2d 145, 147 (Fla. 1949)  (“Where there are two issues 
in a case, upon either of which a judgment may rest, one going to the merits 
and the other not, its disposition is generally considered as resting upon the latter, so that the merits remain unadjudicated, unless the judgment appears 
to have been upon the merits. ”). Here, the county court certainly could have 
denied Menuez’s  intervention motion without reaching the merits, thus res 
judicata is inapplicable.  
Westport urges us to read Pensacola Beach , L.L.C v. American Fidelity 
Life Insurance  Co., 294 So.  3d 976 , 981 -82 (Fla. 1st  DCA 2020) , for the 
proposition that denial of a party’s motion to intervene in all cases, ipso facto , 
constitutes a merits adjudication of the claims that would have been brought 
had intervention been granted. We do not read Pensacola Beach so broadly

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 and, in any event, find Pensacola Beach  dispositively distinguishable. Unlike 
the instant case, Pensacola Beach  does not involve a party seeking —almost  
two decades post -judgment —intervention  into a case in which it was never 
a party, nor does it involve a situation in which the basis for the denial of 
intervention is wholly unknown.  
In sum, our de novo review of the summary judgment record  leads us 
to conclude that Westport  did not meet its burden to establish that the county 
court’s order  constituted an adjudication on the merits. Thus, the doctrine of 
res judicata is not applicable to bar Menuez’s claims in the instant circuit 
court action. And because, in our view, the trial court’s determination that res 
judicata barred Menuez’s claims permeated its conclusions throughout the 
challenged judgment , we reverse both the trial court’s grant of Westport’s 
motion for summary judgment and its denial of Menuez’s motion for summary judgment and remand for further proceedings not inconsistent with this 
opinion.  
Reversed  and remanded.

items.summary:
Holding: The judgment creditor did not establish that an unexplained county-court denial of a nonparty’s motion to reopen, intervene and vacate a sheriff’s sale adjudicated the merits. Res judicata therefore did not bar the later circuit-court claims. The claimed homestead exemption also lay within the circuit court’s exclusive jurisdiction. The court distinguished, rather than rejected, Pensacola Beach.
Disposition: Reversed the grant of Westport’s summary judgment and denial of Menuez’s motion; remanded for further proceedings, without directing judgment for Menuez.

SIXTH DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
Case No. 6D 2026-0149  
Lower Tribunal No. 2021 -CA-003430- O 
_____________________________  
 
LITTLE ROBERT ROBERTSON , 
Appellant ,  
v. 
ORANGE COUNTY , 
Appellee.  
_____________________________  
 
Appeal  pursuant to Fla. R. App. P. 9.130 from the Circuit Court for Orange  County.  
Heather Pinder Rodriguez , Judge.  
 
October 9, 2026  
 
PRATT, J.  
Appellant has filed an appeal from an order granting summary judgment. 
However, the summary judgment order at issue in this appeal is neither an appealable 
final order under Florida Rule of Appellate Procedure 9.110 nor an appealable 
nonfinal order under Florida Rule of Appellate Procedure 9.130. See, e.g. , Atrium 
Med. Corp. v. MSP Recovery Claims, Series, LLC , 367 So. 3d 573, 575 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2023) (“[I]t is well -established that an order which merely grants summary 
judgment, without more, is only appealable as a final order when no judicial labor

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 remains to be done by the trial court.” (citation omitted)); Dixon v. Allstate Ins. Co. , 
609 So. 2d 71, 71 (Fla. 1st DCA 1992) (“Clearly, [the order granting summary 
judgment at issue in this case] is not an appealable non -final order pursuant to Rule 
9.130(a)(3) because it does not fit within any of the limited categories of appealable 
non-final orders set out there.”). See generally S.L.T. Warehouse Co. v. Webb, 304 
So. 2d 97, 99 (Fla. 1974) (“Generally, the test employed by the appellate court to 
determine finality of an order, judgment or decree is whether the order in question 
constitutes an end to the judicial labor in the cause, and nothing further remains to 
be done by the court to effectuate a termination of the cause as between the parties directly affected.”); Timmons v. Lake City Golf, LLC , 293 So. 3d 596, 599 (Fla. 1st 
DCA 2020) (“[A] judgment is final when it puts an end to judicial labor, with only execution and enforcement of the judgment remaining.” (citation omitted)); Fla. R. 
App. P. 9.020(f) (defining “order” as “[a] decision, order, judgment, decree, or rule 
of a lower tribunal”); Fla. R. App. P. 9.130(a)(3) (listing the types of nonfinal orders that are appealable). Accordingly, we dismiss this appeal as premature. See Fla. R. 
App. P. 9.110(l ). 
DISMISSED.  
STARGEL and WOZNIAK, JJ., concur.  
 
 
Little Robert Robertson, Orlando, pro se.

 Bobby G. Palmer, Jr. and Damon S. Starrett, of Hilyard, Bogan & Palmer, P.A., 
Orlando, for Appellee.   
  
NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF TIMELY FILED

citations.quote:
SIXTH  DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
Case No. 6D2025-0045 
Lower Tribunal No. 2023 -CA-009103  
_____________________________  
 
LONNE LETTERI , 
Appellant ,  
v. 
SAFEPOINT INSURANCE COMPANY , 
Appellee.  
_____________________________  
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for Lee  County.  
Michael T. McHugh , Judge.  
 
October 2, 2026  
 
TRAVER, C.J.  
  Lonne Letteri appeals the trial court’s final summary judgment for Safepoint 
Insurance Company.  We have jurisdiction.  See Fla. R. App. P. 9.030(b)(1)(A).  
Letteri raced to the courthouse to file a breach of contract lawsuit against his insurer 
before the claims process broke down.  Accordingly, Safepoint’s post -filing payment 
of policy limits following an appraisal process that complied  with the insurance 
policy’s terms did not constitute a “confession of judgment” entitling Letteri to recover his attorney’s fees  under section 627.428(1), Florida Statutes (2022).  
Letteri’s notice of intent to sue under section 627.70152, Florida Statutes (2022),

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 does not change this conclusion.  While this statute allowed Letteri to file his lawsuit, 
it did not require it.  Finally, the statute neither imposed an  extra -contractual 
appraisal deadline nor entitled L etteri to recover his attorney’s fees  automatically .  
We affirm.1 
I. 
Letteri’s home suffered damage from Hurricane Ian, and he promptly filed a 
claim.  Safepoint inspected the property, accepted coverage, and issued payments 
totaling about $200,000.  A month later, Letteri submitted a  notice under section 
627.70152 .  This statute require s insureds to notify the Department of Financial 
Services of their intent to sue.  § 627.70152(3)(a).  The notice must contain, among 
other information, an explanation of “[t]he alleged acts or omissions of the insurer 
giving rise to the suit” and a presuit settlement demand.  § 627.70152(3)(a)2. , 5.a.  
The Department then notifies the insurer.  § 627.70152(3)(a) .  The insured must give 
notice at least ten business days before suing, but only after the insurer has made a coverage determination.  Id.   
 
1 We separately affirm the trial court’s denial of prejudgment interest without 
further discussion.  See § 627.70131(7)(a), Fla. Stat. (2022) (“However, failure to 
comply with this subsection does not form the sole basis for a private cause of 
action .”); see also Riley v. Heritage Prop. & Cas. Ins ., No. 23 -11678, 2025 WL 
574244, at *3  (11th Cir. Feb. 21, 2025) (rejecting appellants’ breach of contract 
claims for insurance company’s failure to pay interest because claims were “thinly 
disguised claims for statutory breach of Subsection [(7)](a)” which were “precluded by Subsection [(7)](a)’s private action bar”).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 
 Within ten business days of receiving notice, the insurer must respond to the 
insured.  § 627.70152(4).  If the insurer does not deny coverage, it “ must respond by 
making a settlement offer or  requiring the claimant to participate in appraisal or 
another method of alternative dispute resolution.”   § 627.70152(4)(b) (emphasis 
added).  If the insurer elects appraisal, and that process is incomplete within  ninety  
days after the expiration of the ten- day notice period, the insured “may immediately 
file suit without providing the insurer additional notice.”  Id.    
When Letteri served his notice, section 627.70152 contained an attorney’s 
fees provision.  § 627.70152(8).  That provision, since repealed,2 grounded an 
insured’s fee recovery, if any, under section 627.428(1).3  § 627.70152(8)(a).  It first 
required determination of the difference between  the “amount obtained” by the 
insured and the insurer’s “ presuit settlement offer ,” and then a calculation of a  
percentage based on that figure and the “ disputed amount .”  § 627.70152(2), (8)(a).    
In his notice of intent to sue, Letteri sought more than $200,000 in additional 
damages and $10,000 in attorney’s fees.  In response, Safepoint required him to 
participate in appraisal.  See  NCI, LLC v. Progressive Select Ins. , 350 So. 3d 801, 
806 (Fla. 5th DCA 2022) (“Appraisals are creatures of contract and the subject or 
 
2 Ch. 2022- 271, § 17, Laws of Fla. (eff. Dec. 16, 2022).   
 
3 This statute has also since been repealed.  Ch. 2023- 15, § 11, Laws of Fla. 
(eff. Mar. 24, 2023).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 
 scope of appraisal depends on the contract provision.” (quoting Fla. Ins. Guar. Ass’ n 
v. Branco , 148 So. 3d 488, 491 (Fla. 5th DCA 2014) )).  The policy outlined the 
parties’ appraisal rights and procedure for it.  “ The goal of appraisal provisions is to 
settle disputes without litigation. ”  Id. (citing SafePoint Ins. v. Hallet , 322 So. 3d 
204, 207 (Fla. 5th DCA 2021)).   
The policy required each party to choose a competent appraiser within twenty 
days.  The appraisers would each set the amount of loss, and if they could not agree, 
select  a competent and impartial umpire.  The policy did not contain a deadline for 
the parties to complete appraisal, but if an appraisal award was filed, Safepoint had 
to pay Letteri that amount within sixty days.    
The appraisal process proceeded uneventfully.  Both parties timely chose 
appraisers, and those appraisers agreed on an umpire.  But when the process did not 
conclude within ninety days, Letteri sued Safepoint for breach of contract.  He alleged that Safepoint had breached the policy by refusing to pay him for his benefits owed.  Safepoint immediately moved to abate the lawsuit to allow for completion of 
the appraisal process, and Letteri agreed.  The umpire later issued an appraisal aw ard 
for policy limits, and Safepoint paid the award within the sixty days the policy 
required.  Below, Letteri conceded that any delay in finalizing the appraisal award 
was nobody’s fault, and his appraiser attested that the umpire’s inability to complete 
the process sooner stemmed from her post-hurricane workload.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 
 Both parties moved for summary judgment.  Letteri moved first, claiming the 
appraisal award was a confession of judgment entitling  him to recover his attorney’s 
fees and prejudgment interest.  Safepoint moved next, claiming it did not breach the 
policy when it timely paid the appraisal award, and insisting  it would have paid the 
appraisal award whether Letteri sued or not.   
The trial court granted Safepoint’s motion and denied Letteri’s.  It concluded 
the claims process had not broken down, and just because section 627.70152 allowed 
Letteri to sue, it did not mean that an attorney’s fees award was appropriate or 
authorized.  It determined that the ninety- day deadline in section 627.70152(4)(b) 
was not a deadline for appraisal’s completion, and that because Safepoint had elected 
appraisal rather than make  a settlement offer, section 627.70152(8)’s fee recovery 
formula did not apply.  Lastly, it observed that if an insurer unreasonably delayed the appraisal process or payout, a confession of judgment allowing for fee 
entitlement may occur.  But it concluded that this had not  occurred.  
II. 
We review de novo the trial court’s summary judgment .  Pial Holdings, LTD 
v. Riverfront Plaza, LLC , 379 So. 3d 547, 550 (Fla. 6th DCA 2024) (citing Volusia 
Cnty. v. Aberdeen at Ormond Beach, L.P. , 760 So. 2d 126, 130 (Fla. 2000)). We 
likewise review statutory interpretation issues de novo.  See Marlin Constr. Grp., 
LLC v. Bollinger, 412 So. 3d 812, 815 (Fla. 6th DCA 2024).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 
 III. 
On this record, no confession of judgment occurred.  We decline to apply this 
judicially created doctrine when  the parties’ claim process has not broken down, and 
the insured races to the courthouse to seek his attorney’s fees  under section 
627.428(1).  Nothing about section 627.70152 alters this conclusion .   
A. 
Section 627.70152 has never  provide d an independent right to attorney’s fees ; 
our inquiry is driven by section 627.428(1)’s applicability .  See Citizens Prop. Ins. 
v. Vazquez , 368 So. 3d 456, 460 (Fla. 4th DCA 2023).  As the Fourth District 
explained, section 627.70152(8)’s plain language recognizes section 627.428(1) as 
the source of the insured’s fee claim.  See id. (citing § 627.70152(8) ).  And we agree 
with our sister court that “a dispute over attorney’s fees alone cannot be the trigger 
for a lawsuit or a fee award” under section 627.70152.   See id.   
B. 
Section 627.428(1) is inapplicable  to Letteri’s case , and it does not compel  his 
fee recovery.  Before its repeal, this statute provided that an insured could recover 
his attorney’s fees  “[u]pon the rendition of a judgment or decree by any of the courts 
of this state against an insurer and in favor of any named or omnibus insured or the 
named beneficiary under a policy or contract executed by the insurer.”  § 627.428(1).  
Of course, no such judgment occurred when Safepoint paid the appraisal award.  But

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 
 the Florida Supreme Court broadened section 627.428(1)’s applicability to include 
situations where an insurer settle d a case before a judgment’s entry.  See Wollard v. 
Lloyd’s & Cos. of Lloyd’s , 439 So. 2d 217, 218 (Fla. 1983).  In Wollard , an insured 
suffered a loss, and the insurer denied coverage.  Id. at 217– 18.  The insured hired 
an attorney and sued.  Id.  at 218 .  On the eve of trial, the parties settled.  Id.   The 
trial court awarded the insured his attorney’s fees, but the district court reversed, relying on section 627.428 ’s plain language requiring a judgment’s entry.  Id.   The 
Wollard  Court disagreed, reasoning that the statute’s “literal requirement . . . exalts 
form over substance to the detriment of public policy.”  Id.   It observed that 
“[r]equiring the plaintiff to continue litigation in spite of an acceptable offer of 
settlement . . . puts an unnecessary burden on the judicial system, fails to protect any interest—the insured’s, the insurer’s or the public’s —and discourages any attempt 
at settlemen t.”  Id.   This “confession of judgment doctrine” thus addressed policy 
considerations; the Wollard  Court concluded it was unfair to require  an insured to 
continue litigating a lawsuit that the insurer forced him to file based on its belated 
acceptance of its contractual  breach .  Id.  
Untethered to the statute’s plain language, the confession of judgment 
doctrine led to predictable questions .  Relevant here, whether an insured is entitled 
to fees when an insurer did not breach the policy,  but the parties’ resolution occurred 
after the insured had filed suit .  Our sister courts have all said no. See, e.g. , Allstate

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8 
 Fire & Cas. Ins. v. Castro , 351 So.  3d 127, 133 (Fla. 1st DCA 2022); Progressive 
Select Ins. v. Hilchey, 396 So. 3d 775, 783 (Fla. 2d DCA 2024); Valdivieso v. 
Citizens Prop. Ins. , 388 So. 3d 1004, 100 7 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024); People’s Tr. Ins. v. 
Farinato , 315 So. 3d 724, 728 (Fla. 4th DCA 2021); State Farm Ins. Co. v. Lorenzo , 
969 So. 2d 393, 397 (Fla. 5th DCA  2007) .  The Lorenzo court, for example, declined 
to apply the confession of judgment doctrine “where the insureds were not forced to 
sue to receive benefits; applying the doctrine would encourage unnecessary litigation 
by rewarding a race to the courthouse for attorney’ s fees even where the insurer was 
complying with its obligations under the policy.”  969 So. 2d at 398 .  The Farinato  
court asked whether  the insured’s lawsuit  “was filed for a legitimate purpose, and 
whether the filing acted as a necessary catalyst to resolve the dispute and force the 
insurer to satisfy its obligations under the insurance contract .”  315 So. 3d at 728 
(quoting State Farm Fla. Ins. v. Lime Bay Condo., Inc. , 187 So. 3d 932, 935 (Fla. 
4th DCA 2016)) .  If it was not, the confession of judgment doctrine did not apply.   
Id. 
While we are bound by Wollard ’s holding and must apply the confession of 
judgment doctrine, we need not expand it to include situations to which the holding does not pertain.  See Pedroza v. State , 291 So. 3d 541, 547 (Fla. 2020) .  We thus 
agree with our sister courts that the doctrine does not apply to a “race to the courthouse” situation.  And t his is what L etteri did here .  Safepoint accepted

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 9
citations.quote:
9 
 coverage and elected its right to appraisal.  This process led to a policy- limits payout 
that Safepoint timely paid  under the policy.  Letteri did not have to sue Safepoint to 
obtain this recovery.  Safepoint did not, for example, avoid or delay appraisal or 
payment following appraisal.  See, e.g. , Travelers Indem. Ins. of Ill. v. Meadows 
MRI, LLP , 900 So. 2d 676, 678 –79 (Fla. 4th DCA 2005) (concluding confession of 
judgment occurred post -appraisal when insured had to hire counsel to compel  insurer 
to accept coverage and seek declaratory relief on “an expensive and drawn out” 
appraisal procedure); Goff v. State Farm Fla. Ins. , 999 So. 2d 684, 688 (Fla. 2d DCA 
2008) (awarding fees under confession of judgment theory because “lawsuit forced 
[insurer] to request an appraisal and to pay significant additional amounts”).   
Nobody forced L etteri to sue  to receive his benefits, and his lawsuit did not act as a 
necessary catalyst to resolve the dispute.  The confession of judgment doctrine does 
not apply.  
IV. 
Section 627.70152 does not alter this conclusion .  It permitted  Letteri to sue 
Safepoint when appraisal had not concluded within ninety days.  See § 
627.70152(4)(b); Burzee v. Am. Traditions  Ins., 425 So. 3d 1161, 1163 (Fla. 6th 
DCA 2025).  But the statute’s permissiveness did not compel his actions .  See § 
627.70152(4)(b) (“ If the appraisal or alternative dispute resolution has not been 
concluded within 90 days after the expiration of the 10- day notice of intent to initiate

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 10
citations.quote:
10 
 litigation specified in subsection (3), the claimant or claimant’ s attorney may  
immediately file suit without providing the insurer additional notice. ” (emphasis 
added)) .   
Nor does this ninety- day deadline to sue constitute a deadline for an 
appraisal’s completion.  The statute does not reference such a deadline .  Neither  does 
the policy .  Concluding a deadline existed  would require us to add something to the 
statute that is not there , and we decline this invitation .  See Dep’t of Child . & Fams. 
v. J.H. , 418 So. 3d 765, 775 (Fla. 6th DCA 2025) (citing Iselin v. United States, 270 
U.S. 245, 251 (1926)) .   
Finally , we reject  Letteri’s invitation to award fees based on section 
627.70152 (8)’s formula, which turned , in part,  on the insurer’s presuit settlement 
offer.  L etteri insists that because Safepoint did not make a settlement offer, we 
should assess its “presuit settlement offer ” at $0.  See id . § 627.70152(2), (8)(a).  To 
Letteri, a zero -dollar presuit offer justifies his fee recovery  under the statute .  But he 
again  misreads section 627.70152 to include words that are not there.  The statute  
did not require an insurer to make a settlement offer if it did  not deny coverage and 
instead elect ed to force an insured to participate in appraisal.   See § 627.70152(4 )(b) 
(“If an insurer is responding to a notice provided to the insurer alleging an act or 
omission by the insurer other than a denial of coverage, the insurer must respond by 
making a settlement offer or  requiring the claimant to participate in appraisal or

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 11
citations.quote:
11 
 another method of alternative dispute resolution. ” (emphasis added)) .  Because 
Safepoint  accepted coverage of Letteri’s loss and invoked appraisal , it need  not have 
made  a presuit settlement offer.  See id . § 627.70152(4)(b); Telophase Soc. of Fla., 
Inc. v. State Bd. of Funeral Dirs.  & Embalmers , 334 So. 2d 563, 566  (Fla. 1976) 
(“‘Or’ when used in a statute is generally to be construed in the disjunctive.”  (citation 
omitted) ).   
V. 
On this record, the confession of judgment doctrine does not apply, and L etteri 
has no basis to recover his attorney’s fees.  We thus affirm.  
AFFIRMED.  
 
STARGEL  and BROWNLEE, JJ., concur.  
 
 
Michael A. Cassel, of Cassel  Law, P.A., Hollywood, and Mark A. Boyle  and 
Thomas E. Shepard, of Boyle, Leonard & Anderson, P.A., Fort Myers, for 
Appellant.  
 Patrick M. Chidnese and Frieda C. Lindroth, of Bickford & Chidnese, LLP, Tampa , 
for Appellee.   
 
 
NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF  TIMELY FILED

items.summary:
Holding: Under the 2022 insurance statutes applicable to the claim, timely payment of an appraisal award after suit was not a confession of judgment where the claims process had not broken down and litigation was not a necessary catalyst. Permission to sue after the statutory period neither imposed an appraisal-completion deadline nor independently entitled the insured to fees. The opinion expressly notes subsequent repeal of the fee provisions; this is not a statement that they remain generally operative.
Disposition: Summary judgment for insurer affirmed; denial of prejudgment interest also affirmed.
Author: Chief Judge Traver. Stargel and Brownlee concur.

citations.quote:
SIXTH DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
Case No. 6D2025-2413  
Lower Tribunal No. 2024 -CA-002218  
_____________________________  
 
PROGRESSIVE MICHIGAN INSURANCE COMPANY , 
Appellant,  
v. 
ALEAH A. HOLMS , 
Appellee.  
_____________________________  
 
Appeal  pursuant to Fla. R. App. P. 9.130 from the Circuit Court for Collier  County.  
Lauren L. Brodie , Judge . 
 
October 2, 2026  
 
KAMOUTSAS, J.  
 
Progressive Michigan Insurance Company appeals a nonfinal Order Denying 
Exceptions and Approving the General Magistrate’s Status Report and 
Recommended Order pursuant to Florida Rule of Appellate Procedure 
9.130(a)(3)(C)(i). However, as explained below , we dismiss this appeal for lack of 
jurisdiction because the order on appeal  does not determine personal jurisdiction.  
The relevant  procedural history is as follows. Aleah Holms filed a complaint  
and i n response, Progressive filed an answer and affirmative defenses, which  
concededly did not raise the affirmative defense of lack of personal jurisdiction.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 Progressive  then moved for leave to amend its a nswer  to include this affirmative 
defense  and filed a proposed amended answer raising lack of personal jurisdiction . 
Progressive also moved  to dismiss count II of Holms’s c omplaint for lack of p ersonal 
jurisdiction . The trial court granted Progressive’s motion for leave to amend and 
accepted its proposed amended answer and affirmative defens es as filed. Holms  
moved to strike portions of Progressive ’s amended pleading with respect to  the lack 
of personal jurisdiction as an a ffirmative defense . The trial court referred 
Progressive ’s still-pending motion to dismiss and Holms ’s motion to strike  to a 
general m agistrate  under rule 1.490.  
After a hearing, the magistrate entered a r ecommended order, which stated :  
Defendant had the option to raise a lack of personal jurisdiction defense 
either in a pre -answer motion or the answer. See Gannon v. Cuckler, 281 
So. 3d 587 , 593 (Fla. 2d DCA 2019). If the defense is not joined in the 
pre-answer motion it may not be asserted in a subsequent motion . . . any 
defense not asserted in a pre -answer motion or the answer is waived. Id.   
 
Defendant, Progressive Michigan Insurance Company failed to assert a 
Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.140(b)( 2) motion to dismiss at the outset of the action 
and instead elected to raise personal jurisdiction as an affirmative defense in its amended answer which superseded its original answer. The current motion to dismiss was filed after the filing of the initial 
answer and the amended answer, and therefore, the defense of personal 
jurisdiction cannot be raised in the current motion.  
 
The recommended order concluded that “ Plaintiff’s Motion to Strike Portions of 
Progressive Michigan Insurance Company’ s Lack of Personal Jurisdiction as an 
Affirmative Defense is DENIED [and] Progressive Michigan’ s Motion to Dismiss 
Count II of Complaint for L ack o f Personal Jurisdiction is DENIED. ” After a hearing

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 
 on Progressive’s exceptions to the r ecommended order, the trial court entered the 
order on review  denying Progressive’s  exceptions and approv ing the recommended 
order.  
Jurisdiction is a threshold matter. Progressive Marathon Ins.  v. Rivera , 430 
So. 3d 367, 368 (Fla. 6th  DCA 2026);  Art. V, § 4 (b)(1), Fla. Const. ( “District courts 
of appeal . . . may review interlocutory orders in such cases to the extent provided 
by rules adopted by the supreme court .”); Fla. R. App. P. 9.030(b)(1)(B) (“District 
courts of appeal shall review, by appeal . . . nonfinal orders as prescribed by rule 9.130.”).  Appellant asserts  appellate jurisdiction based on rule  9.130(a)(3)(C)(i ), 
which  authorizes this Court’s review of non- final orders , but such review is “limited 
to those that  . . . determine . . . the jurisdiction of the person .” We have recently 
recognized that “ [t]he rule requires that an interlocutory order on appeal must 
actually adjudicate and determine the personal jurisdiction issue. ” Rivera , 430 So. 
3d at 368 (quoting Torres v. SBE Hotel Grp., LLC, 403 So. 3d 883, 885 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2023)) .  
The Florida Supreme Court has said,  “Webster ’s Third New International 
Dictionary, Unabridged, defines ‘ determine’  as, among other things, ‘ to fix 
conclusively or authoritatively, ’ ‘to settle a question or controversy about, ’ and to 
‘decide by judicial sentence. ’”  Doctor's Hosp. of Hollywood, Inc. v. Madison, 411 
So. 2d 190, 191 (Fla. 1982).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 
 Substantively, the order on appeal, which approves the findings of the 
recommended order, does not settle a questio n and does not fix conclusively or 
authoritatively  or decide by judicial sentence  as to the issue of personal jurisdiction 
with respect to Progressive, nor does it find that Progressive waived the defense. 
Appellant seek s to convince this Court  that the order has by operation  determined 
the issue of personal jurisdiction , and therefore , the appeal falls within the orbit of 
our jurisdiction. B ut on its face , that is not what the order did, nor are we allowed to 
expand the scope of our jurisdiction. See Art. V, § 4 (b)(1), Fla. Const. ; Dexx Med. 
Indus., CA v. Fitesa Naotecidos S.A.,  346 So. 3d 1215, 1217 (Fla. 3d DCA  2022)  
(“A plain reading of rule 9.130(a)(3)(C)(i) demonstrates ‘ the requirement that we 
are to construe narrowly the categories of non- final orders subject to interlocutory 
appeal. ’” (quoting Citizens Prop. Ins. v. Calonge , 246 So. 3d 447, 450 (Fla. 3d DCA 
2018)) ). It follows  that this Court lacks jurisdiction over this appeal.  
DISMISSED . 
 
NARDELLA and GANNAM , JJ., concur.  
 
 
Joye B. Walford, Michael C. Clarke and Paz A. Garcia  Griego , of Kubicki Draper, 
P.A., Tampa , for Appellant . 
 
Stephen G. Edlund, of Sawgrass Law, PLLC, Bradenton, for Appellee.  
 
 
NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISP OSITION THEREOF IF TIMELY FILED

items.summary:
Holding: The order denying a motion to dismiss while leaving the personal-jurisdiction defense in the amended answer neither actually decided personal jurisdiction nor found the defense waived. Rule 9.130(a)(3)(C)(i) therefore did not authorize interlocutory review.
Disposition: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Author: Judge Kamoutsas. Nardella and Gannam concur.

JOHN J. LAWRENCE ,

v.

Responde nt. 
_____________________________  
 
Petition for Writ of Certiorari to the County Court for Polk County.  
Bob Grode  and Jordan Wells , Judge s. 
 
October 2, 2026 
   
PER CURIAM.  
 
John Lawrence petitions for a writ of certiorari to quash a final default 
judgment of foreclosure. This Court lacks jurisdiction over the petition for writ of 
certiorari for two reasons. First, Lawrence seeks review of  a final order from the 
circuit court which  was not sitting in its review capacity . But certiorari is reserved 
for nonfinal orders that are not appealable under Florida Rule of Appellate Procedure 
9.130 or final orders of circuit courts acting in their review capacity. See  Fla. R. App. 
P. 9.030(b)(2)(A), (B). Second, the petition is untimely because  it was filed more

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 than thirty days after the judgment was rendered.  See Fla. R. App. P. 9.100(c)(1) (A 
petition for writ of certiorari “must be filed within 30 days of rendition of the order 
to be reviewed.”). Accordingly, we dismiss the petition for writ of certiorari.  
Lawrence also petitions for a writ of prohibition to prevent the clerk of the 
lower tribunal from issuing a Certificate of Title while his objections to the sale of the subject property are pending. As it appears from the record that his fear is unfounded,  we deny his petition. The sale occurred nearly two months ago, and the 
record contains no evidence that the clerk intends to issue the certificate while objections are pending, or that the lower court is likely to order its issuance before 
resolving those  objections.  
PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI DISMISSED. PETITION FOR 
WRIT OF PROHIBITION DENIED.  
NARDELLA, WHITE  and KAMOUTSAS , JJ., concur.  
 
 John J. Lawrence, Lakeland, pro se.  
 No Appearance for Respondent.  
  
NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF TIMELY FILED

items.summary:
Holding: The court dismissed certiorari review of a final foreclosure judgment both because the order was not within the stated certiorari categories and because the petition was filed beyond thirty days. It denied prohibition where the record did not substantiate the anticipated issuance of a title certificate before sale objections were resolved.
Disposition: Certiorari petition dismissed; prohibition petition denied.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 1
citations.quote:
FIFTH DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
Case No. 5 D2025-1458 
LT Case No. 2021 -CA-000558  
_____________________________  
         
SECU RITY FIRST INSURANCE 
COMPANY D/B/A SECURITY FIRST 
FLORIDA , 
 
Appellant,  
 
v. 
 
MARK ANNON AND AMY ANNON , 
 
Appellee s. 
_____________________________  
 
 On appeal from the Circuit Court for Flagler County.  
Andrea K. Totten, Judge.  
 
Michael Fox Orr and Loreyn P. Raab, of Orr Cook, Jacksonville, 
for Appellant.  
 
Michael Ciocchetti, of Michael Ciocchetti, PLLC, Daytona Beach, 
for Appellee.  
 
October 9, 2026  
 
 
L
AMBERT , J.  
 
Security First Insurance Company (“Security First”), which 
was the defendant below in a first- party property dispute that was 
resolved without a trial , timely appeals the trial court’s 
subsequent final judgment that awarded attorney’s fees against it

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 under section 627.428, Florida Statutes (2021),1 in favor of the 
appellees/insureds, Mark Annon and Amy Annon.  Consistent with 
Florida Patient’s Compensation Fund v. Rowe, 472 So. 2d 1145 
(Fla. 1985), the trial court first computed and then awarded to 
Appellees in its final judgment the  lodestar amount of $125,080.00 
for attorney’s fees, which Security First has not challenged  in this 
appeal.  T he court then applied a 2.0 contingency fee multiplier to 
this lodestar figure, resulting in an attorney’s fees award  to 
Appellees totaling $250,160.00 , with which Security First does 
take issue.  
 
Security First primarily argues that the 2.0 multiplier award 
should be reversed because it is not supported by competent 
substantial evidence.  Concluding that Security First is correct, we 
reverse the final judgment and remand with instructions to the 
trial court to enter an amended final judgment that  awards the 
lodestar attorney’s fees sum of $125, 080.00  to Appellees,  without 
a multiplier.  
I 
In Standard Guaranty Insurance v. Quanstrom, 555 So. 2d 
828 (Fla. 1990), the Florida Supreme Court set forth the following 
three factors to be utilized by courts when determining whether a 
multiplier is necessary in the instant type of case:  
 
(1) whether the relevant market requires a 
contingency fee multiplier to obtain competent counsel; (2) whether the attorney was able to mitigate 
the risk of nonpayment in any way; and (3) whether 
any of the factors set forth in Rowe are applicable, 
especially, the amount involved, the results obtained, 
and the type of fee arrangement between the attorney 
and [the] client.  
Id. at 834.  
 
 
1 Section 627.428, Florida Statutes, which permitted an award 
of attorney’s fees in this type of case, was repealed in 2023.  The 
claim in this case pre-dates the repeal.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3  As the party seeking attorney’s fees,  Appellees had the 
burden to establish each of these factors to justify the contingency 
fee multiplier.  See Foot & Ankle Ctr. of Fla., LLC, v. Vargas, 412 
So. 3d 825, 828 (Fla. 6 th DCA 2024) (citing Quanstrom, 555 So. 2d 
at 834).   And “[w]hile the tria l court’s determination to apply a 
multiplier to the lodestar amount is reviewed for an abuse of 
discretion, the trial court’s findings as to the multiplier must be 
supported by competent, substantial evidence.” Universal Prop. & 
Cas. Ins. v. Deshp ande, 314 So. 3d 416, 420 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020)  
(citation omitted).  
 
II 
 
 In arguing that the trial court’s application of the 2.0 
contingency fee multiplier was not supported by competent substantial evidence, Security First contends that Appellees failed 
to meet their burden of presenting evidence sufficient to prove that 
the relevant market required a contingency fee multiplier to obtain 
competent counsel  in this case.  See SafePoint Ins. v. Castellanos, 
394 So. 3d 731, 735 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024) (“If there is no evidence 
that the relevant market required a contingency fee multiplier to 
obtain competent counsel, then a multiplier should not be awarded.” (citation omitted)) .  
 
Security First also contends that the trial court’s finding on 
the second prong or factor in Quanstrom, that Appellees’ counsel 
was unable to mitigate the risk of nonpayment in any way,  lacks 
record evidentiary support.   
 
 To establish the first factor under Quanstrom, Appellees 
were required to demonstrate, without inference, that the y would 
have faced substantial difficulties in obtaining competent counsel 
in the relevant market without the risk -enhancement multiplier.  
See Little v. Bath & Kitchen Boutique, LLC, 435 So. 3d 1142, 1150 (Fla. 3d DCA 2026) (citing Foot & Ankle , 412 So. 3d at 829).   
 
Appellees did not testify at the attorney’s fees hearing; and 
their expert witness, who admitted under oath that he did not 
handle first- party property insurance cases such as the instant 
claim nor did he speak with Appellees, testified that he made no 
inquiry as to whether any other attorneys would have accepted

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 this type of case without the possibility of a contingency fee 
multiplier.  See Impex Caribe Corp. v. Carl Levin, P.A., 338 So. 3d 
13, 15 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022) (recognizing that the party seeking 
application of the multiplier “must establish ‘that a party would 
have difficulty securing counsel without the opportunity for a 
multiplier’” (quoting Citizens Prop. Ins. v. Laguerre, 259 So. 3d 
169, 177 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018)) );  see also Bankers Life & Cas. v . 
Borew, 430 So. 3d 124, 128 (Fla. 4 th DCA 2026) (“So, to award the 
multiplier, the record evidence must show that without risk -
enhancement[,] plaintiff would have faced substantial difficulties 
in finding counsel in the . . . relevant market.” (alteration in original) (citation omitted)).   
 
Instructive on this issue is this court’s decision in PHH 
Mortgage Corp. v. Schreiber, 397 So. 3d 1159 (Fla. 5th DCA 2024) , 
where the a ppellant challenged an attorney’s fees award with a 
contingency fee multiplier in a foreclosure case.  Id. at 1159 .  The 
appellees’ expert there testified that for “almost all [foreclosure] 
clients, because they couldn’t pay their mortgage, they can’t pay 
their attorney or . . . they pay very little as compared to the amount 
of work involved.”  Id. at 1160  (alteration in original).  The expert 
further opined that, because of  the client’s inability to pay, most 
foreclosures involved some type of contingency fee.  Id.  
 Concluding that this testimony said nothing about whether a 
foreclosure client could have obtained competent counsel without 
a multiplier, we reversed and remanded for entry of an amended judgment without the contingency multiplier.  Id.  
 Appellees’ expert’s testimony here was similarly lacking as to 
whether Appellees could have obtained competent counsel in the 
relevant market  absent the possibility of a multiplier.   We 
therefore hold, without further elaboration, that Appellees failed 
to meet their evidentiary burden under the first Q uanstro m factor 
to support the imposition of the contingency risk multiplier.  
 
III 
 
 We further find that Appellees did not present competent 
substantial evidence of the second Quanstrom factor that counsel 
was unable to mitigate the risk of nonpayment in any way.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 “Generally, the controlling consideration in determining whether 
an attorney can mitigate the risk of nonpayment . . . is whether the plaintiffs can afford a retainer or hourly fees.”  Certain 
Underwriters at Lloyd’s London v. Candelaria, 339 So. 3d 463, 470 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022) (quoting Wesson v. Fla. Peninsula Ins., 296 So. 3d 572, 573 (Fla. 1st DCA 2020)).  Simply stated, there was no 
specific, non-inferential evidence before the trial court that 
Appellees could not have afforded or lacked the financial means to 
either pay a retainer fee or counsel’s hourly rate.  
  
Accordingly, we conclude that the trial court erred in applying 
the 2.0 contingency risk multiplier to the lodestar attorney’s fees 
amount.  We therefore reverse that portion of the final judgment 
and remand  with directions to  the trial court to enter an amended 
final judgment that awards to Appellees the $125,080.00  lodestar 
attorney’s fees figure previously determined, with no multiplier.
2 
  
REVERSED and  REMANDED  with directions.   
 
EDWARDS and  BOATWRIGHT , JJ.,  concur.  
 
 
2 On a final note, effective March 24, 2023, the Florida 
Legislature amended section 57.104, Florida Statutes, to provide 
that “[i]n any action in which attorney fees are determined or 
awarded by the court, there is a strong presumption that a lodestar fee is sufficient and reasonable,” and that “[t]his presumption may 
be overcome only in a rare and exceptional circumstance with 
evidence that competent counsel could not otherwise be retained.”  
§ 57.104(2), Fla. Stat.  Security First’s second argument for 
reversal here briefly argu ed that this statute  should be applied 
retroactively a nd that this was not the rare and exceptional case 
to overcome the strong presumption that the lodestar fee awarded 
was sufficient and reasonable.  
While the record in this appeal supports Security First’s 
argument that this case was not  rare and exceptional, b ased upon 
our disposition of Security First’s first issue on appeal, we find it 
unnecessary to address the retroactive applicability of section 
57.104(2).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 _____________________________  
 
Not final until disposition of any timely and 
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 9.331.  
_____________________________

items.summary:
Holding: The evidence did not support either a relevant-market need for a contingency multiplier or inability to mitigate nonpayment risk. The court eliminated a 2.0 multiplier while preserving the unchallenged lodestar. The claim predates repeal of section 627.428; the court expressly declined to decide retroactivity of section 57.104(2).
Disposition: Reversed multiplier award and remanded for an amended fee judgment of $125,080 without a multiplier.
Author: Judge Lambert. Edwards and Boatwright concur.

citations.quote:
DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA  
SECOND DISTRICT  
 
 
LaVONNE WASHINGTON and MICHAEL WASHINGTON , 
 
Appellants,  
 
v. 
 
GINA JUSTICE and VICTOR CRIST, solely in his official capacity as 
CLERK OF CIRCUIT COURT & COMPTROLLER, HILLSBOROUGH 
COUNTY , 
 
Appellees.  
 
No. 2D2025 -2678  
 
October 7, 2026  
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for Hillsborough County; Kemba Damali 
Johnson Lewis, Judge . 
 
LaVonne Washington  and Michae l Washington, pro se . 
 
James Uthmeier, Attorney General, Tallahassee, and Juliana Tirado, 
Assistant Attorney General , Tampa, for Appellee Gina Justice . 
 
Kristen M. Fiore of Akerman LLP, Tallahassee; and Jason L. Margolin, 
and Keenan Ryan Molaskey of Akerman LLP, Tampa, for Appellee  Victor 
Crist.  
 
 
PER CURIAM . 
 
LaVonne and Michael Washington  filed a notice of  appeal seeking 
review of a final order dismissing their complaint entered in lower 
tribunal case 24 -CA-010301 , resulting in this proceeding.  The

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 Washingtons submitted an initial brief citing eleven cases that this court 
could not locate.  We issued an order that directed them to either provide 
copies of the eleven cases or show cause why sanctions should not be 
imposed for submitting a brief that r elied on fictitious case law.  
Considering  the Washingtons ' numerous meritless filings in this case 
and two others related to lower tribunal case 24 -CA-010301, our order 
specifically named dismissal and an order barring further pro se filing s 
as possible sanctions.  
The Washingtons did not provide copies of the eleven cases named 
in our order to show cause .  Rather, they describe the citations as 
scrivener's errors "resulting from intense logistical pressure."  They claim 
they were "forced to manually consolidate overlapping fully briefed legal 
arguments across three distinct appellate tracks . . . without professional 
legal verification softwar e."  The Washingtons claim the fake case 
citations were the result of the volume and page numbers being 
"mangled" during drafting.   The Washingtons also insist that their brief 
was filed prior to the promulgation of Florida Rule of General Practice 
and Judicial Administration 2.515(d)(2)(D), see In re Amends . to Fla . R. of 
Gen. Prac. & Jud . Admin . 2.515 , 435 So. 3d 5 (Fla. 2026), and that this 
court cannot apply that rule retroactively to sanction them.  
The Washingtons'  response fails to adequately explain the inclusion 
of the fabricated case citations.  Their response neither confesses nor 
denies that the fictitious case citations were the result of using 
generative artificial intelligence.  See generally  Russell v. Mells , 426 So. 
3d 913, 918 n.3 (Fla. 2d DCA 2025) (explaining generative artificial 
intelligence models and hallucinations).  It is likely that the inclusion of 
the fake case citations is the result of generative artificial intelligence. 
See id. at 919 -20 ("None of us can recall an instance when an attorney

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 
 accidentally  submitted a completely fabricated case as a legal authority 
to a court of law —not until the recent advent of generative artificial 
intelligence.").  Regardless , it is not the source of the fictitious cases that 
concern s us, but the Washingtons' reliance on them in their brief.  
Several courts, including this one, have held that the submission of 
fictitious cases is sanctionable.  See, e.g., Clerk of Ct . & Comptroller for 
13th Jud . Cir., Hillsborough Cnty. v. Rangel , 427 So. 3d 1069, 1071 (Fla. 
2d DCA 2025); Gouveia v. Meridian Fin. Invs.,  LLC, 432 So. 3d 49, 51 
(Fla. 4th DCA 2026); Hessert v. Hessert , 431 So. 3d 610, 614 (Fla. 6th 
DCA 2026); Takefman v. Pickleball Club, LLC , 418 So. 3d 826, 827 (Fla. 
3d DCA 2025); Gutierrez v. Gutierrez , 399 So. 3d 1185, 1188 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2024).  Such submissions are  sanctionable because they abuse the 
adversary system, waste the time of the court, and could harm the 
reputation of judges and parties whose names are falsely invoked in 
connection with the hallucinated citations.  Goya v. Hayashida , 418 So. 
3d 652, 655 -56 (Fla. 4th DCA 2025).  The Washingtons' response fails to 
justify or excuse their submission of fake case citations.  
And this court need not retroactively apply rule 2.515(d)(2)(D) to 
impose sanctions.  To specifically address the issue of fictitious case 
citations generated by generative artificial intelligence tools, the supreme 
court amended rule 2.515(d)(2) to provide that the signer of a filing 
certifies the legal authorities identified in the filing "exist and are 
accurately cited."   In re Amend s. to Fla. Rule of Gen. Prac . & Jud . Admin. 
2.515 , 435 So. 3d at 6.  Prior to the amendment, courts applied the 
earlier version of rule 2.515(d)(2) and held that pro se parties and 
attorneys  represent ed the accuracy of a filing by signing it.  See Hessert , 
431 So. 3d at 613 ("Florida's appellate courts, like other courts, require 
pro se litigants and attorneys to sign their filings and thereby represent

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 
 the accuracy thereof."); see also  Davidson v. Chang -Warner , 51 Fla. L. 
Weekly D1311 , D1311 (Fla. 6th DCA June 26, 2026) (" [T]he explicit 
requirements and sanctions authority of the amendments to rule 
2.515(d)(2) merely clarify what already fell within the scope of the pre -
existing requirements of rule 2.515(d)(2) .").  Because a citation to a 
nonexistent case is not accurate, signing a filing that contains fictitious 
citations breaches that representation.  Under rule 9.410(a), this court 
has the authority to sanction such a breach  without reliance on the 
amended version of the rule .  See Davidson , 51 Fla. L. Weekly at D1311.  
("[R]ule 2.515(d)(2) as amended now explicitly authorizes what Florida 
Rule of Appellate Procedure 9.410(a) already allowed —namely, for 
appellate courts to sanction pro se litigants and attorneys for failing to 
follow the requirements of rule 2.515(d)(2)." ). 
In deciding whether sanctions are warranted, w e also consider the 
Washingtons ' history of filing across this case and the other two 
proceedings identified in our order to show cause, 2D2025 -1883 and 
2D2025 -2170.   Appeal 2D2025 -1883 was dismissed as from a nonfinal, 
nonappealable order.  In case 2D2025 -2170, we denied the Washingtons ' 
meritless petition for writ of quo warranto and all writs.  Across all three 
cases, the Washingtons  raised meritless challenges to this court's fee 
orders  and filed meritless motions for rehearing.  "[A]ny  citizen . . . 
abuses the right to pro se access [to the courts] by filing repetitious and 
frivolous pleadings, thereby diminishing the ability of the courts to 
devote their finite resources to the consideration of legitimate claims."   
State v. Spencer , 751 So. 2d 47, 48 (Fla. 1999).   
Based on  the Washingtons' reliance on fictious cases, unavailing 
response to this court's order , and pattern of frivol ous filings , we dismiss 
this appeal.  See Fla. R. App. P. 9.410(a) .  Further, we direct the clerk of

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 
 this court to place in an inactive file any original proceedings or notices 
of appeal filed by LaVonne or Michael Washington related to Hillsborough 
County Circuit Court case 24 -CA-010301 unless the filing is signed by a 
member in good standing of The Florida Bar  or related to a proceeding 
pending at the time this opinion issues.1   
Affirmed.  
 
NORTHCUTT, KELLY, and MORRIS , JJ., Concur.  
 
 
Opinion subject to revision prior to official publication.  
 
1 We note that the Washingtons have other proceedings  pending in 
this court unrelated to the lower tribunal case at issue in this appeal.  
We caution that further frivolous filings or the submission of fictitious 
case citations in those cases may result in additional sanctions.

items.summary:
Holding: Fabricated citations, an inadequate response to a show-cause order, and a pattern of frivolous filings supported sanctions under rule 9.410(a), without retroactive application of the amended rule 2.515. The court did not establish whether generative AI actually produced the citations.
Disposition: The reasoning dismisses the appeal and imposes a qualified filing restriction for the specified underlying case, but the closing disposition says Affirmed; this inconsistency remains unresolved.
Author: Per curiam. Northcutt, Kelly and Morris concur.
Official opinion retrieved October 12, 2026; issuance date stated in document and index. Any printed rehearing or revision qualification is preserved; subsequent docket finality and treatment not independently verified.
Recorded discrepancy: Page 4 says the court dismisses the appeal; page 5 concludes Affirmed. Both official statements are preserved without deciding which controls.

FIRST DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
No. 1D2025- 2879  
_____________________________  
 
CHAUDRA BLACKMON 
PATTERSON , 
 
Appellant,  
 
v. 
 
RUSSELL VAN DIEPEN , 
 
Appellee.  
_____________________________  
 
 On appeal from the County Court for Escambia County.  
Barry E. Dickson, Jr., Judge.  
 
 
October 7, 2026  
 
P
ER CURIAM . 
 
Appellee Russell Van Diepen and his  wife co-own a single-
family residence which they lease d to Appellant Chaudra 
Blackmon-Patterson (“Tenant”). After Van Diepen  filed this 
residential eviction action, Tenant failed to timely deposit the 
required past-due rent into the court registry. As a result, the trial 
court entered a final judgment for possession and awarded Van 
Diepen a $7,800 judgment for damages. For the following reasons, 
we affirm the judgment for possession but reverse and remand the 
judgment for damages. 
 
We affirm the default judgment for possession because  
Tenant’s nonpayment of the accrued rent into the court registry

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 entitled Van Diepen to “an immediate default judgment for 
removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without 
further notice or hearing thereon.” § 83.60(2), Fla. Stat. (2025) . 
Tenant asserts on appeal that the trial court erred by not 
dismissing the action due to the nonparty status of Van Diepen’s 
wife, whom Tenant claims was an indispensable party. But, at 
least with respect to the judgment for possession, the trial court 
properly  denied  Tenant’s motion to dismiss based on the defense 
of Van Diepen’s alleged failure to join an indispensable party. 
Tenant’s failure to pay the rent into the court registry waived any such defense to the claim for possession . See § 83.60(2), Fla. Stat. 
(nonpayment of the accrued rent “constitutes an absolute waiver 
of the tenant’s defenses other than payment”); see also  Fla. R. Civ. 
P. 1.140(b) ( identifying “failure to join indispensable parties” as a 
“defense” ).  
 As to the judgment for damages, however, we reverse and 
remand for further proceedings. The trial court ruled that Tenant 
“failed to deposit rent monies into the court registry . . . to qualify 
for a trial in this case.” But the registry deposit provisions in 
section 83.60(2) only apply to “an action by the landlord for 
possession of a dwelling unit,”  not to an action for damages.  
§ 83.60(2), Fla. Stat. In First Hanover v. Vazquez, the Third 
District concluded that a default judgment and writ of possession  
issued under section 83.60(2)  would not apply to a separate cause 
of action for damages. 848 So. 2d 1188, 1191 (Fla. 3d DCA 2003) ; 
see also  Zambrano v. Quintana, 435 So. 3d 687, 688 –89 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2026)  (same).  Other districts have decided similarly. See  
Famsun Invest, LLC v. Therault, 95 So. 3d 961, 963 –64 (Fla. 4th 
DCA 2012) (“A default under [the registry deposit statute] determines only the possessory interest and does not resolve a 
dispute for damages .”); Premici v. United Growth Props., L.P., 648 
So. 2d 1241, 1243 –44 (Fla. 5th DCA 1995) (holding that a registry-
based  default only “results in a default for possession ,” so the lower 
court “should have tried” the disputed damages claim  before 
entering a final judgment).
* We agree with the reasoning of our 
 
* Although these cases applied the statutory provisions 
governing nonresidential tenancies, not residential tenancies, both statutes similarly provide that a failure to pay the outstanding 
rent into the court registry entitles the landlord to an immediate

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 sister districts and conclude that Tenant’s failure to deposit the 
accrued rent into the court registry did not entitle Van Diepen to 
judgment on his damages claim. The damages claim must be 
separately adjudicated by  the trial court. In doing  so, the trial 
court may consider any defenses properly raised by Tenant, about which we express no opinion.  
 
A
FFIRMED in part;  REVERSED  in part and  REMANDED . 
 
ROBERTS , WINOKUR , and  TREADWELL , JJ.,  concur.  
 
_____________________________  
 Not final until disposition of any timely and authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 9.331.  
_____________________________  
  
Daniel Clibbon and Patrick W. Jennings of Legal Services of North Florida, Tallahassee, for Appellant.  
 No appearance  for Appellee.  
 
default for “possession.” §§ 83.232(5), 83.60(2), Fla. Stat.; see also  
Zambrano, 435 So. 3d at  688 (noting the similarity between the 
nonresidential statute, section 83.232(5), and the residential 
statute, section 83.60(2)). We therefore find such cases to be 
persuasive in the residential context.

items.summary:
Holding: Failure to deposit residential rent into the registry waived the asserted indispensable-party defense to possession, but did not authorize a damages judgment. Damages require separate adjudication, including properly raised defenses; the court did not decide their merits.
Disposition: Possession judgment affirmed; $7,800 damages judgment reversed and remanded.
Author: Per curiam. Roberts, Winokur and Treadwell concur.

FIRST DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
No. 1D2026- 0971  
_____________________________  
 
AMANDA CLARK , 
 
Appellant,  
 
v. 
 
AMAZON .COM SERVICES , LLC;  
ZURICH AMERICAN INSURANCE 
COMPANY ; and S EDGWICK CMS, 
 
Appellee s. 
_____________________________  
 
 On appeal from the Office of the Judges of Compensation Claims.  
Brian J. Anthony, Judge.  
 Date of Accident: April 18, 2022 . 
  
October 7, 2026  
 
O
N MOTION FOR REVIEW OF INSOLVENCY DETERMINATION  
 P
ER CURIAM .  
 
During the pendency of this workers’ compensation appeal, 
the Judge of Compensation Claims (JCC) denied Claimant’s 
petition for relief from the cost of the record on appeal , and 
Claimant sought review. We reverse.  
 The JCC’s thoughtful nine-page order explains that, although 
Claimant’s financial affidavit discloses her husband’s $1700 -a

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 month contribution to household expenses, her admission on cross-
examination that he earns $3200 per month reveals that she did 
not “satisfy all the requirements” of statute or comply with the 
applicable appellate rule. Section 440.25(5)(b), Florida Statutes, 
notes that “[f]ailure to state in the affidavit all assets and income, including marital assets and income, shall be grounds for denying 
the petition with prejudice. ” And Florida Rule of Appellate 
Procedure 9.180(g)(3)(D) uses equally forceful language: “ With the 
verified petition to be relieved of costs, the appellant must file a 
sworn financial affidavit listing income and assets, including 
marital income and assets, and expenses and liabilities.”  
 
But Claimant argues that “marital assets and income” are not 
solicited by the affidavit form suggested by the Office of the Judges 
of Compensation Claims (OJCC). This form, titled “Financial 
Affidavit in Support of Verified Petition for Relief from Paying 
Costs” (item 12 at https://www.jcc.state.fl.us/JCC/forms/, visited 
September 10, 2026) , instead states, “If anyone contributes to your 
income or helps pay your expenses, complete the following ,” then 
designates only three fields:  “Name of Contributor; Relationship to 
Claimant/Appellant; Total Monthly Amount of Contribution.” The 
appendix in the appellate docket confirms that Claimant 
“completed every field on the official form exactly as written.”  In 
other words, the form provided by OJCC does not include all the 
necessary information required by the statute.  Claimant suggests 
that correctly completing the provided form should not be used as 
a basis for denial.   
 
The JCC acknowledged that he “must look at the totality of 
circumstances” in determining insolvency, yet he concluded that 
he is “constrained” by statute. The totality of circumstances in this 
case, however, includes not just the affidavit but also the  
discrepancy between statute and the OJCC’s form—not to mention 
Claimant’s sworn testimony of her spouse’s income (which might  
cure its absence on the affidavit), her testimony that his income  
was wholly inaccessible to her, and the JCC’s own finding that the 
workers’ compensation benefits at issue would accrue solely to 
Claimant and not her spouse. The true remedy here is to fix the 
form. In the meantime, we reverse the order and remand for the 
JCC to re consider the totality of the circumstances.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 REVERSED  and REMANDED . 
 
LEWIS , M.K.  THOMAS , and LONG, JJ., concur.  
 
_____________________________  
 
Not final until disposition of any timely and 
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 
9.331.  
_____________________________  
 
 
Amanda Clark, pro se, Appellant.  
 
No appearance for Appellees.

items.summary:
Holding: On review of a workers’ compensation appellate-cost insolvency determination, the court required reconsideration of the total circumstances, including a mismatch it identified between the official financial-affidavit form and statutory marital-income requirements, the claimant’s testimony and inaccessibility of spousal income. It did not grant insolvency relief outright or announce a general exemption from full disclosure. The underlying form was described in this opinion, not independently verified in this review.
Disposition: Insolvency order reversed and remanded for reconsideration.
Author: Per curiam. Lewis, M.K. Thomas and Long concur.
