citations.quote:
Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 7, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D25 -1280  
Lower Tribunal No. 23-17090 -CA-01 
________________  
 
 
Meb Loan Trust VI , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Albert Isaacs, et al. , 
Appellee s. 
 
 
 
 An Appeal from a non -final order from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Reemberto Diaz , Judge.  
 
 McCalla Raymer Leibert Pierce, LL C, and Robinson Keith Ustler  
(Orlando) , for appellant.  
 
 Markowitz, Ringel, Trusty & Hartog, P.A., and Adrian Carlington 
Delancy , for appellee  Albert Isaacs . 
 
  
Before  SCALES , C.J., and FERNANDEZ , and REBULL,  JJ.  
 
 REBULL, J.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 In a mortgage foreclosure action must  an incapacitated  ward be 
personally named as a defendant where a probate court has already  
appointed a guardian to act on behalf of the ward’s real property?  Or must 
the guardian be substituted as a named defendant in place of the 
incapacitated ward? 
I. 
MEB Loan Trust VI appeals an order dismissing defendant Albert 
Isaacs from its foreclosure suit, contending the trial court erroneously 
dismissed Isaacs under Florida Rule of Civil Procedure  1.260(a) and (b). We 
review the dismissal de novo. Grove Isle Ass ’n, Inc. v. Grove Isle Assoc., 
LLLP , 137 So. 3d 1081 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014) ; see also  Hamza v. McLemore , 
421 So. 3d 742, 743 (Fla. 5th DCA 2025) ( “We review de novo the trial court’s 
dismissal under Rule 1.260. ”).   
 MEB filed t his foreclosure action in May 2023 against Albert Isaacs, 
among other defendants. Isaacs was a co-owner of the property,  and he 
executed the mortgage MEB  is seeking to enforce . When MEB filed this 
action , it knew that the probate court had already adjudicated Isaacs totally 
incapacitated and appointed Adrian Delancy as Guardian for the property of 
Isaacs as his  Ward.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3  The probate court ’s Letters of Plenary Guardianship of the Property 
declare that Delancy had “full power ” to, among other things, “take 
possession of and to hold for the benefit of the Ward, all property and income 
of the Ward. ” The Letters empowered Delancy to administer and take 
possession of Isaacs ’ property, but they did not divest Isaacs  of title or 
ownership. In a later order, the probate court authorized Delancy “to file 
pleadings in the foreclosure action . . . to protect the Ward ’s interest in real 
properties and business. ”  
Delancy filed an answer and affirmative defenses to the foreclosure 
complaint “in his official capacity of Guardian of the Property of Albert 
Isaacs.” Delancy later moved to dismiss Isaacs  as a party defendant  and 
argued  that MEB’s failure to substitute Delancy as party defendant was 
required by Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.260(a)(1) , and that any 
judgment against Isaacs would be void. MEB responded  that Isaacs, as a 
record title  property owner, was an indispensable party who could not be 
substituted.  
The trial court initially denied the motion to dismiss , but when Delancy 
moved for reconsideration of the order, asserting that dismissal was

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 mandatory under Rule 1.260 , the court granted the motion for 
reconsideration and dismissed Isaacs from the case. This appeal followed.1  
II. 
A. 
The legal issue raised in this appeal is whether, under Florida Rule of 
Civil Procedure 1.260 , the trial court was required to dismiss MEB ’s 
foreclosure complaint because it failed to file a motion substituting Delancy 
for Isaacs within ninety  days after Delancy filed a statement that Isaacs was 
incapacitated.  The simple answer is no, and  we conclude  the trial court erred 
in dismissing Isaacs as a party.  
As happened here,  an incapacitated  person’s right to defend a lawsuit 
can be delegated by court order to a guardian . See § 744.3215(3)(b), Fla. 
Stat. (2025) . When that happens, the ward or incapacitated person remains 
an indispensable  defendant in a n action to foreclose their ownership interest , 
 
1 During the pendency of this appeal, Delancy filed a suggestion of death, 
indicating Isaacs died on June 1, 2026. We express no opinion on the 
application of Rule 1.260 below, following the death of Isaacs and the filing 
of any suggestion of death in the trial court. We merely take this opportunity 
to note: “The courts of this state have a long -standing tradition in favor of the 
disposition of an action on its merits. Further, this court has recognized that 
rule 1.260 has been liberally interpreted to permit substitution beyond the 
ninety -day time period.  Moreover, we have explained that all doubt should 
be resolved in favor of allowing trial upon the merits. ” Sammons v. Adam 
Greenfield, D.O. , 270 So. 3d 534, 535 (Fla. 2d DCA 2019)  (citation modified).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 but they are not  “substituted ” as a party by the guardian. Rather, the guardian 
“may . . . defend on behalf of  the . . . incompetent person. ”2 See Fla. R. Civ. 
P. 1.210(b)  (emphasis added).  As a record title holder, the ward  must remain  
as a named defendant .3 The guardianship did not have the legal effect of 
divesting him of his ownership interest in the property ; it merely empowered 
the guardian to act on his behalf and for his benefit as it relates to the 
property he owned.  
Community Federal Sav ings & Loan Ass ociation  of Palm Beaches v. 
Wright , 452 So. 2d 638 (Fla. 4th DCA 1984) , illustrates this proposition.  
There,  a lender  filed a foreclosure action against  the guardian of the minor 
title holder. The complaint named as the sole defendant “Karen L. Wright as 
guardian of the person and property of Robert W. Olsker, Jr. ” When the 
guardian failed to file responsive papers , a default final judgment was 
entered,  and the property was sold at a foreclosure sale.  
 
2 The Florida Rules of Civil Procedure use the terms “[i]ncompetency ” and 
“incompetent ” person. The Florida Guardianship Law, Chapter 744, Florida 
Statutes, uses the terms “Incapacitated Person ” and “incapacity. ” We use 
the term “incapacitated person ” as that is also the terminology  used by the 
probate court in its orders adjudicating Isaacs and appointing Delancy.  For 
purposes of this opinion, we treat the phrase “incompetent person ” as 
synonymous with “incapacitated person. ”  
3 A precise and complete naming of a ward as a party defendant  would  be: 
“Albert Isaacs, by Adrian Delancy, as guardian. ” Or “Albert Isaacs, a ward, 
by Adrian Delancy, as guardian of the property. ”

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 When the minor was evicted, he (through a guardian ad litem) moved 
to set aside the default judgment and foreclosure sale. The trial court granted 
the motion and set aside the judgment and the sale. On appeal the Fourth 
DCA affirmed and  held in pertinent part  that the minor4 was an indispensable 
party as he was the holder of fee simple title to the property . Because the 
minor was not named  a party to the foreclosure suit, the judgment of 
foreclosure was void. Id. at 641. The same can be said for a minor and an 
incapacitated person, as Isaacs was in this case. 39 C.J.S. Guardian and 
Ward §1 (2026) ( “A guardian is a person who legally has the care of the 
person or property, or both, of another person, who is incompetent to act for 
themself. ”). As the court did in Wright , we reiterate that an incapacitated  title 
holder to property, such as Isaacs, is an indispensable party in a suit to 
foreclose on that property. See Meh Byron 4 LLC v. Federal Nat. Mortg . 
Ass’n, 187 So. 3d 335, 335 (Fla. 3d DCA 2016) (“One who holds legal title 
to mortgaged property is an indispensable party defendant in a suit to 
foreclose a mortgage  . . . .” (quoting Davanzo v. Resolute Ins. Co. , 346 So. 
2d 1227, 1228 (Fla. 3d DCA 1977) ). 
 
4 The court cited to 39 C.J.S. Guardian and Ward §179, at 359 -60 for the 
proposition that “A ward is a necessary party to a suit affecting his title to real 
property and cannot be bound by such an action brought against the 
guardian alone. ” Community Federal Sav. & Loan Ass ’n of Palm Beaches v. 
Wright , 452 So. 2d 638 , 641  (Fla. 4th DCA 1984) .

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 B. 
Having  answered the question posed at the outset that an 
incapacitated ward who holds title to realty must be named as a party 
defendant in a foreclosure suit, we further hold that Rule 1.260 did not require 
dismissal in this case. Indeed, that rule did not apply here at all. The Rule 
provides  in pertinent part:  
(a)  Death.  
 
If a party dies and the claim is not thereby extinguished, the court 
may order substitution of the proper parties.  
 
(b) Incompetency.  If a party becomes incompetent, the court, 
upon motion filed and served as provided in subdivision (a) of 
this rule, may allow the action to be continued by or against that 
person’s representative.  
 
The Rule plainly covers a situation where an existing party to a civil 
action dies or becomes  “incompetent. ” When that happens,  the Rule 
contemplates that the court in that action, upon proper filing and service of a 
motion, may order substitution (in the case of death) or continuation of the 
action against an “incompetent ” person’s representative.  
Here, all parties agree that MEB knew Isaacs had a guardian before it 
filed the foreclosure action , because MEB tried to effect service of initial 
process on Isaacs at the Guardian ’s place of business. Indeed, service of

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8 process on the Guardian was legally correct under section 48.042 of the 
Florida Statutes:  
48.042  Service on incompetent. — 
 
(1) Process against an incompetent shall be served:  
 
(a) By serving two copies of the process to the person who has 
care or custody of the incompetent or, when there is a legal 
guardian appointed for the incompetent, by serving the guardian 
as provided in s. 48.031.  
 
In the end, the only issue that existed with MEB ’s complaint was – at 
worst – a misnomer. MEB, knowing he was incapacitated and had a 
guardian, sued “Albert Isaacs ” without qualification or any indication of his 
incapacity. As we have noted, the better practice would have been for MEB 
to note his incapacity and guardianship by, for example, naming him as: 
“Albert Isaacs, a ward, by Adrian Delancy, as guardian of the property. ” But 
even with this misnomer, the rules of civil procedure provide a remedy:  
RULE 1.120. PLEADING SPECIAL MATTERS  
 
(a) Capacity. It is not necessary to aver the capacity of a  party to 
sue or be sued, the authority of a party to sue or be sued in  a 
representative capacity, or the legal existence of an organized  
association of persons that is made a party, except to the extent  
required to show the jurisdiction of the court. The initial pleading  
served on behalf of a minor party shall specifically aver the age 
of the minor party. When a party desires to raise an issue as to . 
. . the capacity of any party to sue or be sued  . . . that party shall 
do so by specific negative averment which shall include such 
supporting particulars as are peculiarly within the pleader ’s 
knowledge.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 9
citations.quote:
9  
In other words, Delancy  could have raised by specific negative averment that 
Albert Isaacs was incapacitated and was his ward, and that he was acting 
as his guardian  in the action. Lastly, the other remedy for misnomer of a party 
is – of course – amendment by interlineation.  “The long -standing general rule 
in Florida with respect to amendments changing the description of a 
defendant is that amendment by interlineation is proper and will relate back 
to the original filing of the complaint if the mis -description [of the defendant ] 
is interpreted merely as a misnomer or defect in the characterization of the 
party....” See Barone v. Scandinavian World Cruises (Bahamas), Ltd ., 531 
So. 2d 1036, 1039 –40 (Fla. 3d DCA 1988)  (citation modified ). 
III. 
 For these reasons, it was error for the trial court to dismiss Isaacs as a 
party defendant on the ground that MEB failed to comply with Rule 1.260 by 
failing to substitute the Guardian in his place.    
 Reversed and remanded .

items.summary:
Holding: A ward who held title remained an indispensable foreclosure defendant notwithstanding a previously appointed property guardian. Rule 1.260 did not require substitution for incapacity existing before suit; the guardian defends for the ward under rule 1.210(b). Omitting the guardianship designation was at worst a curable misnomer. The court expressly left later death-substitution issues undecided.
Disposition: Dismissal of Isaacs reversed and remanded.
Author: Judge Rebull. Panel: Chief Judge Scales, Fernandez and Rebull.

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
O
pinion filed  October 7, 2026.  
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing. 
_
_______________ 
N
o. 3D25 -2523  
Lower Tribunal No. 22-17871 -CA-01 
________________ 
865 East 49th Street Associates LLC , 
Appellant,  
v
s. 
Valdo Auto Sales Corp. , et al. , 
Appellee s. 
A
n Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, Valerie R. 
Manno Schurr , Circuit Court Judge.  
P
eter C. Bianchi, Jr., for appellant.  
N
o appearance , for appellee s. 
B
efore  FERNANDEZ , GORDO and REBULL,  JJ. 
GORDO, J.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 865 East appeals summary judgment  order s determining liability and 
granting damages in its favor against Valdo Auto Sales Corp.  We have 
jurisdiction.   See Fla. R. App. P. 9.030(b)(1)(A).  865 East argues the trial 
court erred in granting summary judgment and awarding it zero damages as 
to its fraud and unjust enrichment claims.1  We find that contention fails here 
based on the record before us.   
We review de novo an order granting summary judgment.   Arbor Grove 
Dev., LLC v. ECS1,  Inc., 425 So.  3d 699, 700  n.4 (Fla. 3d DCA 2025) .  The 
“legal operation and effect of a judgment” are reviewed de novo.   
Boynton v. Canal Authority , 311 So.  2d 412, 415 (Fla. 1st DCA 1975) 
(footnote omitted ).  “[T]he lack of a transcript is usually fatal to an appellant.”   
Florida Wellness  & Rehab. Ctr.,  Inc. v. Mark J. Feldman,  P.A., 262 So.  3d 
234, 238 n.4 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018).   But an order on appeal remains 
reviewable and reversible where “error appears on the face of the order.”   Id.   
At issue is the trial court’s award of zero damages despite its 
determination of liability on 865 East’s fraud and unjust enrichment claims.  
Although the existence and amount of damages  ordinarily present questions 
of fact, those questions may be resolved on summary judgment where no 
 
1 The court found liability on 865 East’s claims —including its fraud and unjust 
enrichment claims —but only awarded $76,199.37 as past due rent  for 
breach of the commercial lease.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 genuine dispute of material fact exists.   See R. Plants,  Inc. v. Dome 
Enterprises,  Inc., 221 So.  3d 752, 754 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017)  (“[A]ny claim for 
damages, liquidated or unliquidated, or for attorneys fees and costs can be 
decided by summary judgment  . . . . Without a genuine issue of material fact 
on the amount of damages caused by the breach, summary judgment was 
appropriate. ” (citation omitted)); Avant Design Grp.,  Inc. v. Aquastar 
Holdings  LLC, 351 So. 3d 62, 70 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022) (“The general rule is 
that the extent of damages determined by a trial court is a question of fact 
which will be affirmed on appeal if supported by competent, substantial 
evidence .” (internal quotation marks omitted) (quotation omitted)).    
Critically, 865 East  was required to establish damages  separate and 
distinct from the $76,199.37 rent judgment  entered against Valdo—rather 
than a prohibited double recovery on the “same element of damages.”   
Montage Grp.,  Ltd. v. Athle -Tech Comput. Sys.,  Inc., 889  So. 2d 180, 199 
(Fla. 2d DCA 2004) ( finding f raud or unjust -enrichment damages are 
duplicative of a contract award where the plaintiff offers no evidence that they 
are separate and distinct from the damages suffered on the contract).    
Whether the evidence  created a genuine issue of fact as to separate 
damages  necessarily depends on the record  before the trial court .  The trial 
court resolved liability, damages and rehearing only after holding full in court

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 hearings on each —yet 865 East supplied no transcript of any hearing .  The 
gap is compounded by the nature of the liability order.   The operative 
judgment is titled “Agreed Summary Final Judgment as to Liability.”  Nothing 
in the record reveals the scope of what the parties agreed to —including 
whether 865 East, in agreeing to that judgment, preserved or instead waived 
any position on the existence, compensability or amount of damages.  That 
agreement was reached at a hearing 865 East did not transcribe, and it 
furnished no approved statement of the evidence from which the terms of the agreement, or any waiver, might be reconstructed.  Accordingly, this 
Court cannot assume the “agreed” judgment resolved anything more than 
the liability it recites, or that 865 East preserved a claim to damages the order 
does not mention.    
We agree with the trial court that 865 East failed to raise  a genuine 
issue of material fact  as to a compensable non duplicative amount of 
damages on its fraud and unjust enrichment claims  based on the record 
before us.   That failure of proof is fatal because 865 East is not entitled to a 
non-zero award as a matter of law.   A plaintiff who establishes liability can 
still recover nothing.   For fraud, a liability judgment does not  necessarily  
establish compensable damages  and the plaintiff must separately meet the 
actual and distinct damages element to recover.   See  Nat’l Equip.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 Rental,  Ltd. v. Little Italy Rest. & Delicatessen,  Inc., 362 So.  2d 338 , 339  
(Fla. 4th DCA 1978) ( reversing a damages award because “ the judgment 
debtors produced no facts or evidence to show that they had sustained any 
damages in type or amount  . . . [and reiteratin g that a]ctual damages and the 
measure thereof are essential as a matter of law in establishing a claim of 
fraud ”); Steinbauer Associates,  Inc. v. Smith , 599 So.  2d 746, 748 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 1992) ( recognizing that a “zero [damages ] verdict will be upheld” in a 
fraud action notwithstanding a finding of liability where the evidence supports 
a finding that the plaintiff sustained no damages);  Morgan 
Stanley  & Co. Inc. v. Coleman (Parent) Holdings  Inc., 955 So.  2d 1124 (Fla. 
4th DCA 2007)  (internal quotation marks omitted)  (citation omitte d) (affirming 
the jury’s finding of fraud liability but reversing the damages award w here the 
plaintiff failed to prove damages under the proper measure , stating 
“[d]amage is of the very essence of an action for fraud or deceit  [and w]ithout 
proof of actual damage the fraud is not actionable ”).   
Unjust enrichment is no different.   Without competent, quantified 
evidence of the value of the benefit conferred, the plaintiff cannot establish compensable damages.   See Alvarez  v. All Star Boxing,  Inc. (“Alvarez I”) , 
258 So.  3d 508, 512 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018) ( holding that “[b]ecause unjust 
enrichment damages are economic damages, the amount of damages must

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 be measurable and quantifiable” such that they are not “founded on jury 
speculation or guesswork” but “must rest on some reasonable factual 
basis”); Alvarez  v. All Star Boxing,  Inc. (“Alvarez  II”), 409 So.  3d 192, 196 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2025) (“Where there is no evidence to justify any amount on a claim for economic damages [under unjust enrichment], defendant is entitled 
to judgment on the claim.”  (citation omitted )); Am. Safety Ins. 
Serv.,  Inc. v. Griggs , 959  So. 2d 322, 332 (Fla. 5th DCA 2007) (finding the 
plaintiff “only presented evidence of the money they hoped to receive” and 
“presented no evidence of the value of the benefit conferred ”).   
Affirmed.

items.summary:
Holding: A liability determination did not guarantee additional fraud or unjust-enrichment damages beyond the rent award. The appellant failed on this record to establish distinct, quantified, nonduplicative damages, and supplied neither hearing transcripts nor an approved substitute explaining the agreed liability judgment.
Disposition: Summary judgments affirmed, including zero additional fraud and unjust-enrichment damages beyond the $76,199.37 rent award.
Author: Judge Gordo. Panel: Fernandez, Gordo and Rebull.

citations.quote:
Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 7, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D25 -2538  
Lower Tribunal No. 25-SC-575-K 
________________  
 
 
John Gregorian , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
New Century Alhambra Automobiles , Inc., 
Appellee.  
 
 
 
 An Appeal from the County Court for M onroe  County, Albert L. Kelley , 
Judge.  
 
 Zermay Law, P.A., and Zachary Z. Zermay , and Matthew Larosiere,  for 
appellant.  
 
 Selz & Muvdi Selz, P.A., and Steven M. Selz (Jupiter) , for appellee.  
 
 
Before  FERNANDEZ, MILLER, and LOBREE, JJ.  
 
 MILLER, J . 
ON APPELLANT’S MOTION FOR REHEARING

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2  
Upon consideration of Appellant ’s motion for rehearing , we grant 
rehearing, withdraw  our decision dated July 29, 2026 , and issue the  following 
opinion in its place.  
Appellant , John Gregorian, challenges  a final order dismissing his 
statement of claim against appellee, New Century Alhambra Automobiles, 
Inc., for lack of personal jurisdiction.   On appeal, Gregorian contends that 
the trial court reversibly erred in failing to first consider his outstanding 
jurisdictional discovery before dismissing his claim.  Consistent with  the 
holding in  Gleneagle Ship Mgmt. Co. v. Leondakos , 602 So. 2d 1282, 1284 
(Fla. 1992), we reverse and remand  for further proceedings.  
I 
Gregorian filed suit alleging that New Century surreptitiously 
embedded trackers known as “spy pixels” into marketing emails and then 
shared consumer information with third parties, in violation of section 934.27, 
Florida Statutes ( 2025).  The amount in controversy placed the dispute within 
the Florida Small Claims Rules.   See Fla. Sm. Cl. R. 7.010(b).  The unverified 
statement of claim alleged personal jurisdiction based on tortious acts 
committed in the State of Florida, along with substantial and not isolated 
activity  within the state , including selling goods and services, direct

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 advertising, and maintaining a dedicated  Florida  website .  See § 
48.193(1)(a)2., Fla. Stat. (2025) (providing  acts subjecting a person “to the 
jurisdiction of the courts of this state ”).  New Century filed a motion to dismiss 
for lack of personal jurisdiction, supported  by the affidavit of its corporate 
representative, Daniel Linn.  Linn attested that New Century had no physical 
presence in the state and lacked  continuous  and systematic general 
business contacts with Florida.   
A few  weeks later, Gregorian propounded jurisdictional discovery.  
New Century answered the request for admissions but objected to the 
remaining discovery.   Gregorian moved to compel and filed the affidavit of 
his attorney,  detailing  outstanding discovery  and unsuccessful attempts to 
coordinate depositions with opposing counsel . 
The trial court convened a hearing on the competing motions .  The 
court granted the motion to dismiss and denied the motion to compel 
discovery as moot.  The court reasoned that  under Venetian Salami Co. v. 
Parthenais , 554 So. 2d 499 (Fla.1989),  Gregorian’s failure to traverse Linn’s  
jurisdictional  affidavit was dispositiv e and therefore discovery was 
unwarranted .  This appeal ensued.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 II 
A 
Gregorian contends the trial court applied the incorrect legal 
framework .  He asserts that the trial court  put the proverbial “cart before the 
horse” by finding that his failure to contravene Linn’s affidavit was fatal  to his 
motion to compel  without first affording him limited jurisdictional discovery.  
In the bedrock  case of  Gleneagle Ship Mgmt. Co. v. Leondakos , 602 
So. 2d 1282  (Fla. 1992), the Florida Supreme Court  exercised jurisdiction to 
resolve a conflict as to “whether discovery is appropriate on jurisdictional 
issues while the jurisdictional question is still pending before the trial court.”  
Id. at 1282.  Noting that “[f]ederal courts permit discovery for the purpose of 
determining issues such a s whether jurisdiction exists,” the Gleneagle  court 
reasoned that “limited discovery in such instances will provide the trial court 
with additional information on which to base its decision regarding  
jurisdiction.”  Id. at 128 4 (citing Oppenheimer Fund, Inc. v. Sanders , 437 U.S. 
340, 351 n.13 (1978 )).  The court therefore adopted the federal courts’ policy.  
Id. 
In so doing, the court explained  that allowing jurisdictional discovery 
does not conflict with the procedures set forth in  Venetian Salami .  Under 
Venetian  Salami , “a defendant wishing to contest the allegations of the

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 complaint concerning jurisdiction or to raise a contention of minimum 
contacts must file affidavits in support of his position .”  554 So. 2d at 502.  
The burden then shifts to  the plaintiff “to prove by affidavit the basis upon 
which jurisdiction may be obtained. ”  Id.  If the affidavits are capable of 
harmonization , “the court will be in a position to make a decision based upon 
facts which are essentially undisputed .”  Id. at 502 –03.  But if not, an 
evidentiary hearing is required.  Id. 
The court  further recognized  “that averments  made in good faith may 
not always rise to assertions which could be made under oath.”  Gleneagle , 
602 So. 2d  at 1284.  Consistent with this observation , “a plaintiff should be 
able to conduct limited discovery  on the jurisdictional question in order to 
gather facts and file an opposing affidavit. ”  Id.  Once discovery on the 
jurisdictional issue is conducted , “the procedure outlined in  Venetian  
Salami  should be followed by the trial court .”  Id. 
Gleneagle  does  not, however,  create a bright -line rule .  See Posner v. 
Essex Ins. Co. , 178 F.3d 1209, 1214 n.7 (11th Cir. 1999) ( Gleneagle  
recognize s a “qualified right to conduct jurisdictional discovery” ).  Instead,  
the trial court retains the discretion to control  the availability and scope of  
discovery.  J urisdictional  discovery “is appropriate where  the existing record 
is ‘inadequate’ to support personal jurisdiction and ‘a party demonstrates that

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 it can supplement its jurisdictional allegations through discovery. ’”  Trintec 
Indus., Inc. v Pedre Promotional Prod., Inc. , 395 F.3d 1275, 1283 (Fed.  Cir. 
2005) (quoting GTE New Media Svcs ., Inc. v. BellSouth Corp. , 199 F.3d 
1343, 1351 –52 (D.C.  Cir. 2000) ).  But as the gatekeeper, the trial court is 
charged with guarding against “ broad, onerous or expansive ” discovery and 
that which  is designed to “ address the merits of the case.”  Gleneagle , 602 
So. 2d at 1284.    
In this vein, courts have  distinguished between timely discovery 
requests and the failure to seek disclosures  until the so -called “eleventh 
hour.”  See Estes v. Rodin , 259 So. 3d 183 , 198  (Fla. 3d DCA 2018) ; Bosdorf 
v. Beach , 79 F. Supp. 2d 1337, 1342 n.9 (S.D. Fla. 1999)  (“[P]recedent  from 
the Eleventh Circuit and Florida courts support a qualified right to conduct 
jurisdictional discovery ” where “ plaintiffs actually served interrogatories or 
production requests before the motion to dismiss was ruled on.” (citing Eaton 
v. Dorchester Dev., Inc. , 692 F.2d 727, 729 –31 (11th Cir.  1982) and 
Gleneagle , 602 So. 2d at 1284 )); Bosdorf , 79 F. Supp. 2d at 1342  (“Plaintiffs ’ 
failure to obtain jurisdictional discovery in the state case resulted more from 
Plaintiffs own inaction than it d id the trial court ’s denial of their ‘right’ to seek 
discovery.  Plaintiffs did not serve or propound any discovery requests ,” and 
therefore “[t] he state court  . . . did not so much deny discovery as it dismissed

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 the case before discovery was taken.”) .  Courts similarly take a dim view of 
vague allusions to the necessity of acquiring jurisdictional facts.   See Posner , 
178 F.3d at 1214 n.7 (distinguishing Gleneagle  and denying request for 
jurisdictional discovery where “no discovery efforts were made in the eight 
months between the time Plaintiffs filed the complaint and the time it was 
dismissed” and the “only allusion to jurisdictional discovery was on the first 
page of their memorandum in opposition to the motion to dismiss filed seven 
and one -half months after the complaint and more than five months after the 
filing of the motion to dismiss”).   And absent a “colorable basis” that 
jurisdiction exists, a denial of discovery may be proper.  Lang v. Morris , 823 
F. Supp. 2d 966, 979 (N.D. Cal. 2011)  (citation omitted) . 
B 
Against these principles, we examine the case at hand .  As the trial 
court astutely observed, small claims cases in Florida are to be resolved 
expeditiously and efficiently.  But where both parties are represented by 
counsel, discovery, including jurisdictional discovery, is governed by t he 
Florida Rules of Civil Procedure.  See Fla. Sm. Cl . R. 7.020 (b) (“Any party 
represented by an attorney is subject to discovery pursuant to  Florida Rules 
of Civil Procedure 1.280 -1.380  directed at said party, without order of 
court.”) .

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8 Though unverified, the statement of claim contai ned a colorable basis  
for jurisdiction.  Under Gleneagle  and its progeny, th e fact that  Gregorian 
failed to file a contravening affidavit did not  bar him from seeking information 
to corroborate his own jurisdictional allegations and testing the accuracy of 
Linn’s affidavit .   
Given that there was no evidence Gregorian engaged in dilatory 
tactics, we conclude that the trial court should have first considered the 
merits of the motion to compel.  We therefore reverse and remand for 
renewed  consideration .  See Volkswagen Aktiengesellschaft v. Jones , 227 
So. 3d 150, 152 (Fla. 2d DCA 2017)  (reversing an order denying a motion to 
dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction and remanding “for the trial court to 
consider in the first instance [plaintiff’s] motion to compel to the extent that 
the motion sought discovery relevant to personal juris diction”) .    
Reversed and remande d.

items.summary:
Holding: On rehearing, the court expressly withdrew its July 29 opinion. With a colorable jurisdictional basis and timely discovery efforts, failure to counter the defendant’s affidavit did not justify dismissing the claim before considering the pending motion to compel jurisdictional discovery. The right is qualified: trial courts retain control of scope and may reject dilatory, speculative or merits-directed discovery. Both small-claims parties here had counsel. The withdrawn July text has not been reconstructed from this replacement.
Disposition: Rehearing granted; July 29, 2026 opinion withdrawn and replaced; dismissal reversed and remanded for renewed consideration.
Author: Judge Miller. Panel: Fernandez, Miller and Lobree.
Official opinion retrieved October 12, 2026; issuance date stated in document and index. Any printed rehearing or revision qualification is preserved; subsequent docket finality and treatment not independently verified.

citations.quote:
Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  October 7, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D25 -1480  
Lower Tribunal No. 25-4087 -CA-01 
________________  
 
 
Juan Gonzalez , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Resolvion, LLC , 
Appellee.  
 
 An Appeal from a non -final order from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Daryl E. Trawick , Judge.  
 
 Law Office of Gustavo Martinez, and Gustavo Martinez , for appellant.  
 
 Winget, Spadafora & Schwartzberg, LLP, and Zachary S. Knoblock, 
for appellee.  
 
 
Before LOGUE, LINDSEY, and GOODEN, JJ.  
 
 LOGUE, J.  
 The plaintiff below, Juan Gonzalez, appeals from the trial court’s 
nonfinal order granting defendant  Resolvion, LLC’s  Motion to Stay the Case

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 and Compel Arbitration  pursuant to a n arbitration provision in the lease 
agreement  between Gonzalez and American Honda Finance Corporation  to 
which Resolvion was not a signatory . The facts at this preliminary point in 
the litigation indicate Resolvion repossessed Gonzalez’s 2018 Honda Civic 
under the mistaken impression that Gonzalez had failed to make payments 
to Honda under the lease agreement . In fact, Gonzalez had purchased the 
vehicle pursuant to the lease agreement  and financed the purchase through 
another finance company . As such, Honda had no lien or claim on the 
vehicle. In the underlying action, Honda was not made a party  to the litigation  
and Gonzalez’s cause s of action  against Resolvion did not cite to or rely 
upon the lease agreement. Under these circumstances, the trial court erred 
in finding that Gonzalez was equitably estopped from refusing to arbitrate his 
claims against Resolvion .   
BACKGROUND  
 Gonzalez filed a complaint against Resolvion . The complaint alleged  
that on February 1, 2022, Resolvion wrongfully seized and removed  his 
vehicle  from the front of his residence without his consent . On the day the 
vehicle was taken, Gonzalez  was the title holder and registered owner of his 
vehicle  and there was no lienholder or claimant who had a lawful right to 
repossess, use, or take his vehicle.  Further, the complaint alleged Resolvion

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 
 was not acting on behalf of anyone who had a lien, security interest, or lawful 
right to repossess the vehicle.  Gonzalez repeatedly requested Resolvion  
return the vehicle, but Resolvion refused. The complaint asserted claims for 
civil theft, conversion, trespass to chattel, negligence, gross negligence, and  
unlawful removal of a vehicle  under section 715.07, Florida Statutes (2021) .  
 In response, Resolvion filed a motion to stay the case and compel 
arbitration, relying on an arbitration provision in the 36-month lease 
agreement  for the vehicle  between Gonzalez and  Honda  executed on 
September 25, 2018.  The lease agreement contain ed the following 
arbitration provision:  
By agreeing to arbitrate, the right to go to court is waived and 
instead claims, disputes, or controversies are submitted to 
binding arbitration. . . .  
 
By signing the Arbitration Consent, YOU  elect to have disputes 
resolved by arbitration. YOU, HONDA[1] or any involved third 
party may pursue a Claim. “Claim” means any dispute between 
YOU, HONDA , or any involved third party relating to your 
account, this Lease, or our relationship, including any 
application; the Vehicle , its performance and any 
representations; omissions or warranties. “Claim” does not 
 
1 The arbitration provision defines “Honda” as follows : “HONDA  means the 
Lessor, Dealer, Honda Leas e Trust, American Honda Finance Corporation 
(AHFC), American Honda Motor Co., Inc., Honda Finance Exchange, Inc., 
Acura Financial Services (AFS), Honda Financial Services (HFS), HVT, Inc., 
their parents, subsidiaries, predecessors, successors, assignees, and  
officers, employees, representatives, and agents. YOU  means Lessee and 
Co-Lessee.”

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 
 include personal injury or wrongful death claims. YOU  or HONDA  
may seek remedies in small claims court or provisional judicial 
remedies without arbitrating.  
 
 . . . . 
 
This provision survives termination of this Lease or relationship, 
bankruptcy, assignment, or transfer.  . . . 
 
The lease agreement also allowed Honda to repossess the vehicle if 
Gonzalez defaulted . 
In support of its motion to compel arbitration, Resolvion filed the sworn 
affidavit of its Vice President, Wendy Radmall.  In her affidavit, Radmall  
averred  that Resolvion had an agreement with Honda  to provide automobile 
recovery and repossession services.  In late 2021 or early 2022, Honda 
contacted Resolvion to repossess Gonzalez’s  vehicle because he had 
violated the lease agreement.  Resolvion then engaged a non -party tow truck 
company to reposse ss the vehicle. At all relevant times, Resolvion was 
acting with the sole purpose of assisting Honda in enforcing its rights under 
the lease agreement.   
In its motion,  Resolvion acknowledged that the general rule is that a  
non-signatory  to a contract containing  an arbitration agreement cannot 
compel a signatory to submit to arbitration . Reso lvion, however,  asserted 
that Florida and federal courts  have applied the principles of equitable

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 
 estoppel to allow  a non -signatory , such as Resolvion,  to compel arbitration 
against a signatory to the contract, such as Gonzalez .  
In this regard, Resolvion claimed  that, while the complaint was “crafted 
in a way to avoid implicating the arbitration provision, [Gonzalez ’s] reference 
to the vehicle, his alleged possessory interest right to [the vehicle] , and the 
repossession of the vehicle pursuant to Honda’s instructions nevertheless 
invokes the lease agreement that he signed with Honda.” In addition, 
Resolvion argued , the arbitration provision provide d that Gonzalez agreed to 
arbitrate all claims or disputes with Honda and its affiliates, assignees, and 
agents, and Resolvion was acti ng as Honda’s  agent.  
 Gonzalez countered by filing his own affidavit. In it, he averred  that he 
satisfied all financial obligations to Honda under the lease agreement ; the 
lease agreement en ded when he purchased the vehicle on January 14, 
2022 ; and t he causes of action he asserted against Resolvion are based on 
incidents that occurred following the lease period and are completely 
unrelated to the lease agreement.  Moreover, when he purchased the vehicle, 
he financed a portion of the purchase price with Capital One Auto Finance, 
not Honda , and o n January 15, 2022, Capital One placed a lien on the 
vehicle , and Honda removed any lien it had on the vehicle.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 
 Further, in late January 2022, Gonzalez check ed Florida’s Department 
of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles ’ website, which confirmed that Honda 
no longer had a lien on the vehicle ; Capital One was the sole lienholder ; and 
he was the sole registered owner of the vehicle with the title being issued on 
January 15, 2022. Nonetheless, on February 1, 2022, Resolvion entered his 
private property and stole his vehicle.  In addition, Gonzalez averred that 
once  the vehicle was stolen, he communicated with several Honda entities, 
including Honda and the dealership. The Honda entities admitted that 
Gonzalez was the sole lawful owner of the vehicle ; he did not owe anything 
to Honda and/or its affiliated corporate entities ; no Honda entity had a lien 
on the vehicle ; Resolvion was not enforcing any of Honda’s  rights under the 
lease agreement ; the lease was over because Gonzalez had purchased the 
vehicle ; and Resolvion did not have the authority to repossess the vehicle on 
its behalf.  
Gonzalez also asserted that he presented this evidence to Resolvion,  
but Resolvion  refused to return the vehicle for weeks.  Gonzalez further 
argued that, a ssuming Resolvion , which  was not a party to the lease 
agreement , does have standing to enforce the arbitration provision, the 
communications between  Gonzalez , Honda , and the dealership “prove that 
Resolvion’s tortious conduct [fell] well outside the scope of the arbitration

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 
 provision.” Gonzalez also  asserted that Resolvion’s characterization of what 
occurred as a “repossession” was misleading.  
The trial court conducted a hearing on Resolvion’s motion to stay and  
compel arbitration . Following arguments of  the parties’ counsel s, the trial 
court granted Resolvion’s motion  to stay and compel arbitration.  In doing so, 
the trial court determined that the first circumstance in which  a non -signatory 
can use equitable estoppel to enforce an arbitration provision —when the 
signatory’s claims allege substantially interdependent and concerted 
misconduct by another signatory and the non -signatory —was not applicable. 
The trial court, however, determined the second  circumstance —when the 
claims relate directly to the contract and the signatory relies  on the contract 
to assert its claims against the non -signatory —was applicable.  In ruling that 
the second circumstance was applicable, the trial court stated:  
The plaintiff asserts that this dispute  is based in tort and is 
not based upon the lease,  which had expired, and that the lien 
was no longer in  effect, and as a result, this action is not 
dependent  upon the lease. The defendant, on the other hand,  
makes the argument that this dispute is dependent upon  the 
lease. It would not have arisen, but for the  existence of the lease 
in the first place.  
               
 The Court here agrees with the defense.  While the plaintiff 
may assert that this case is not  dependent upon the lease and 
that it expired, this  dispute is premised -- this dispute would not 
have reached this stage but for the existence of the lease  in the 
first place. The Court looks at the provisions  of the lease, and the

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8 
 provision that the Court is  relying upon has been referred to by 
both sides.  
 
Where it says “By signing the  arbitration agreement, you 
elect to have disputes  resolved by arbitration. You, Honda, or 
any involved  third party may pursue a claim. Claim means any  
dispute between you, Honda, or any involved third  party relating 
to your account, ” the Court finds that  language to be convincing.  
                
In addition, the agreement states “This provision survives 
termination of this lease, ” et cetera. Given the explicit terms of 
the lease and the  Court ’s findings regarding the fact that this 
case is  in fact premised upon the lease, despite the fact that  the 
plaintiff has brought tort actions, the Court is  going to grant the 
motion to stay the case and send  this case to arbitration.  
 
The trial court  entered an order granting Resolvion’s motion to stay and 
compel arbitration “for the reasons stated in the record. ” Gonzalez timely 
appealed . 
ANALYSIS  
Florida courts consider three elements  when ruling on a motion to 
compel arbitration  of a given dispute : “(1) whether a valid written agreement 
to arbitrate exists; (2) whether an arbitrable issue exists; and (3) whether the 
right to arbitration was waived.” Seifert v. U.S. Home Corp. , 750 So. 2d 633, 
636 (Fla. 1999) .  
In Florida, the general rule is that  “a non -signatory to a contract  
containing an arbitration  agreement  cannot compel a signatory to submit to 
arbitration.”  Rolls -Royce PLC v. Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd. , 960 So. 2d

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 9
citations.quote:
9 
 768, 770 (Fla. 3d DCA 2007) ; see also  Fla. Roads Trucking , LLC v. Zion  
Jacksonville, LLC , 384 So. 3d  817, 819 (Fla. 5th DCA 2024)  (“The normal 
rule, of course, is that ‘a party cannot compel arbitration under an arbitration 
agreement to which it was not a party.’” (quoting Beck Auto Sales, Inc. v. 
Asbury Jax Ford, LLC , 249 So. 3d 765, 767 (Fla. 1st DCA 2018) )). Florida  
courts,  however, “have recognized that principles of equitable estoppel 
sometimes allow a non -signatory to compel arbitration against someone who 
had signed an arbitration agreement.” Beck Auto Sales , 249 So. 3d at 767 . 
“The doctrine of equitable estoppel ‘precludes a party from asserting 
rights he otherwise would have had against another when his own conduct 
renders assertion of those rights contrary to equity. ’” Marcus v. Fl a. Bagels, 
LLC, 112 So. 3d 631, 634 (Fla. 4th DCA 2013)  (quoting R.J. Griffin & Co. v. 
Beach Club II Homeowners Ass’n , 384 F.3d 157, 160 (4th Cir. 2004) ). In the 
context of arbitration, a non -signatory may use equitable estoppel to compel 
arbitration where  “a signatory plaintiff should not be allowed to sue to 
essentially enforce its rights under a contract and, at the same time, evade 
an arbitration agreement in the contract, simply by naming as defendants 
parties who were not signatories to the contract. ” Allscripts Healthcare Sols., 
Inc. v. Pain Clinic of N w. Fla., Inc. , 158 So. 3d 644, 646 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014) .

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 10
citations.quote:
10 
 Thus, the non-signatory can compel arbitration and the signatory will 
be equitabl y estopped from refusing to arbitrate (1) when the signatory’s 
claims allege “substantially interdependent and concerted misconduct by 
another signatory and the non -signatory,” Fla. Roads Trucking , 384 So. 3d 
at 819 (cleaned up); or (2) “when the claims relate directly to the contract 
and the signatory is relying on the contract to assert its claims against the 
non-signatory.” Id. Significantly, this equitable  estoppel analysis focuses on 
the legal claims and defenses of the signatory who is being estopped, not on 
the legal claims and defenses of the non-signatory trying to enforce the 
estoppel. If either of these circumstances exist, the court must then 
determine whether the dispute that the non -signatory to the contract seeks 
to have arbitrated is included in the arbitration clause.  
Here, t he trial court relied on the second circumstance to grant the 
motion to compel arbitration, namely “when the claims relate directly to the 
contract and the signatory is relying on the contract to assert its claims 
against the non -signatory.”  Id.2 It reasoned that Gonzalez obtained 
ownership of the vehicle from Honda and therefore  the lease was sufficiently 
 
2 The trial court found the first circumstance did not apply. Resolvion d id not 
appeal this determination.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 11
citations.quote:
11 
 implicated in Gonzalez’s claim s for Gonzalez to be equitably estopped from 
refusing to arbitrate his claim s against Resolvion.  
The circumstance whereby a party obtain ed ownership of property in 
litigation through a contract with an arbitration clause without more , however,  
“does not constitute the actual dependence on the underlying contract that 
equitable estoppel requires. Instead, reliance on the contract in this context 
requires that a party must actually depend on the underlying contract to 
assert its claims. ” Allscripts , 158 So. 3d at 647  (internal citations and 
quotation marks omitted ). For this reason , “the claim . . . must, at a minimum, 
raise some issue the resolution of which requires reference to or construction 
of some portion of the contract  itself.”  Id. (quoting Rolls -Royce , 960 So. 2d 
at 771). For example, “[i]f the contract places the parties in a unique 
relationship that creates new duties not otherwise imposed by law, then a 
dispute regarding a breach of a contractually -imposed duty is one that arises 
from the contract. ” Seifert , 750 So. 2d at 6 39 (quoting Dusold v. Porta -John 
Corp. , 807 P.2d 526 , 531  (Ariz. Ct. App. 1990)) .  
In Allscripts , for example, Allscripts , the defendant, marketed its 
healthcare software to plaintiffs —doctors  who purchased software from 
subsidiaries of Allscripts. The contracts between the Allscript s subsidiaries 
and the doctors contained an arbitration provision.  Allscripts , 158 So. 3d at

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 12
citations.quote:
12 
 645. Allscripts was not a signatory to the agreements . Id. After the software 
failed to support the doctors’ compliance with federal regulations,  Allscripts 
directly contacted the doctors to offer them a replacement upgrade that 
cause d the doctors to incur  substantial  costs . Id. at 646 . The doctors sued 
Allscripts  claiming the upgrade was defective. Allscripts moved to compel 
arbitration based on the doctors ’ agreements  with the subsidiaries under  
which the doctors had originally obtained ownership of the software . Id.  
The Court explained , “[a] plaintiff’s dependence on the contract in this 
sense means more than that plaintiff would not own the product except for 
the contract : ‘A simple but -for relationship does not constitute the actual 
dependence on the underlying contract that equitable estoppel requires .’” Id. 
at 647  (quoting Bailey v. ERG Enter s., L.P., 705 F.3d 1311, 1321 –22 (11 th 
Cir. 2013)) . Accordingly, the Court held that Allscripts could not compel 
arbitration through the provisions in the master agreements , noting that  while 
the “lawsuit would not exist but for the fact that the [d]octors purchased the 
software licenses [,] . . . the allegations in the Complaint reach beyond the 
master agreements to encompass actions that Allscripts took outside the 
scope of the agreements [.]” Allscripts , 158 So. 3d at 647 . 
Gonzalez’s claims  are filed against only Resolvion, not Honda. Honda 
is not a party. Gonzalez asserts claims of civil theft, conversion, trespass to

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 13
citations.quote:
13 
 chattel, negligence, gross negligence, and  unlawful removal of a vehicle  
under  section 715.07 , Florida Statutes  (2021) . These claims arise from 
general duties “ otherwise imposed by law .” They do not depend on the lease 
agreement. Accordingly , because Gonzalez’s claims against Resolvion are 
not based on the provisions of the lease , Resolvion cannot avail itself of 
equitable estoppel to compel arbitration  under the lease  agreement  it never 
signed . Seifert , 750 So. 2d at 640 ; Allscripts , 158 So. 3d at 647 . 
Reversed and remanded.

items.summary:
Holding: A nonsignatory repossession company could not compel arbitration by equitable estoppel merely because an expired vehicle lease was a but-for link to ownership. The pleaded tort and statutory claims depended on duties imposed by law, not enforcement or construction of the lease. The ruling addresses the equitable-estoppel basis decided below; it does not establish a universal rule against nonsignatory arbitration.
Disposition: Order staying the case and compelling arbitration reversed and remanded.
Author: Judge Logue. Panel: Logue, Lindsey and Gooden.

citations.quote:
Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  October 7, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________ 
 
No. 3D26 -1268  
Lower Tribunal No.   26-4885- CA -01 
________________ 
 
  
Gratigny Park Condominium No. 1, Inc.,  
Petitioner,  
 
vs. 
 
Reinier Vargas Perez and Alina Garcia Gonzalez, 
Respondent s. 
 
 
  A Writ of  Certiorari to the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, William 
Thomas , Judge.  
  Vernis & Bowling of Miami, P.A ., and Evelynn Greenstone Kammet, 
and Waynice  Amoii Green- Musgrove, for petitioner . 
  Gomez Law, and Eduardo Gomez , for respondents.  
 Before  FERNANDEZ, MILLER and GOODEN , JJ.  
 
 GOODEN, J .

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 Petitioner Gratigny Park Condominium No. 1, Inc.  seeks  a writ of 
certiorari to quash the trial court’s order denying its motion to dismiss  for 
failure to comply with presuit requirements of section 617.07401, Florida 
Statutes , which governs derivative suits .1  Because we find the subject 
lawsuit is subject to the presuit requirements  and the Respondents did not 
comply with those requirements , we grant the petition and quash the order.   
Respondents Reinier Vargas Perez and Alina Garcia Gonzalez own a 
unit within a 79- unit condominium.   Gratigny Park , a non- profit corporation,  
functions as the homeowner’s association that manages and maintains the 
condominium.  All unit owners are members of the association.   
Without complying with section 617.07401, Florida Statutes, Perez and 
Gonzalez  sued Gratigny  and Sun City Condo Solutions, Inc. for injunctive 
and declaratory relief.2  The complaint alleges breach of fiduciary duty, 
corporate mismanagement, and improper corporate expenditures in violation 
of the declaration of condominium, its bylaws, and articles of incorporation.  
 
1 Section  617.07401, Florida Statutes, has since been  repealed.  See Ch. 
2026 -168, § 168, Laws of Fla. (eff. July 1, 2026).  In the same bill, the 
Legislature enacted section 617.0742, Florida Statutes.  Id. § 35.  This 
section specifies certain requirements for a complaint brought in the right of 
a corporation.  
   
2 The claims against Sun City were dismissed below.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 
 Among other things, the complaint alleges that association funds were paid 
to both the maintenance provider, Sun City, and the association’s president 
for the same services.    The wherefore clause provided:  
WHEREFORE, Plaintiffs REINI ER VARGAS PEREZ and ALlNA 
GARCIA GONZALEZ request that t his Court enter an Injunction 
to compel Defendant Association to: (a) immediately cease 
making, any and all payments to the Association President for 
“Janitorial Services ” or any other services for which he should 
not have been compensated; (b) terminate the Property 
Management Services  Agreement with Sun City Condo 
Solutions, Inc. due to the Manager ’s violation of the licensing  
requirements of § 718.111(3)(g) and the Agreement itself; (c) 
establish and maintain the online portal required by § 718.111(12)(g) for unit owner access to official records; (d) 
comply with its governing documents in all respects; and (e) 
award reasonabl e attorney ’s fees and costs pursuant to  Fla. Stat. 
§§ 718.303, 57.105(7), Section 12.2 of the Declaration and applicable Florida law and for any other relief this Court deems just and proper.  
 
Asserting the claims were derivative in nature, Gratigny Park moved to 
dismiss for want of compliance with section 617.07401, Florida Statutes.  But 
Perez and Gonzalez maintained that their claims were not derivative and 
section 718.303(1), Florida Statutes, provides unit owners a direct right of 
action.   
After  a hearing, the trial court denied Gratigny Park’s motion.  It ruled  
that section 718.303(1), Florida Statutes, authorizes a unit owner to bring an 
action  against the association for violating Chapter 718 , the declaration, and 
the association rules.  It explained: “ This statute creates a direct right of

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 
 action for individual unit owners and does not condition that right upon 
compliance with the derivative pre -suit demand requirements of Section 
617.07401. ”  Gratigny moved for reconsideration , which  was denied .  This 
petition timely followed.   
To obtain a writ of certiorari, a party must demonstrate a departure 
from the essential requirements of the law that results in material injury that cannot be corrected on plenary appeal.  Reeves v. Fleetwood Homes of Fla ., 
Inc., 889 So. 2d 812, 822 (Fla. 2004) .  Failure to enforce statutory presuit 
mandates satisfies the irreparable  harm requirement for certiorari review.   
See, e.g. , Moss & Assocs. , LLC v. Peterson , 406 So. 3d 344, 348 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2025) ; Citizens Prop. Ins. Corp. v. Walden , 395 So. 3d 216, 21 7–18 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2024) ; Dial 4 Care, Inc. v. Brinson , 319 So. 3d 111, 115 (Fla. 
3d DCA 2021) .  Such failure deprives a party of its statutory right to presuit 
notice, demand , and investigation —a right that cannot be meaningfully 
enforced or restored on plenary appeal.   
To determine whether a departure of the essential requirements of law 
occurred, we turn to  the statutory framework.   First, we will start with general 
business organization laws .  Pertinent here, Chapter 617 addresses 
nonprofits corporations.  See § 617.01011, Fla. (2025).  A condominium

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 
 association  organized under Chapter 617 has certain powers, including the 
power to “[s]ue and be sued.”  § 617.0302(2 ), Fla. Stat. (2025).   
Section  617.07401, Florida Statutes, places restrictions o n its 
members’ ability to bring derivative suits.  It provides:  
(1) A person may not commence a proceeding in the right of a 
domestic or foreign corporation unless the person was a 
member of the corporation when the transaction complained 
of occurred or unless the person became a member through 
transfer by operation of  law from one who was a member at 
that time.  
 
(2) A complaint in a proceeding brought in the right of a domestic 
or foreign corporation must be verified and allege with 
particularity the demand made to obtain action by the board of directors and that the demand was refused or ignored by the board of d irectors for at least 90 days after the date of the 
first demand unless, before the expiration of the 90 days, the 
person was notified in writing that the corporation rejected the 
demand, or unless irreparable injury to the corporation would 
result by wait ing for the expiration of the 90 -day period.  If the 
corporation commences an investigation of the charges made 
in the demand or complaint, the court may stay any proceeding until the investigation is completed.  
 
§ 617.07401 , Fla. Stat. (2025).   
Next, we turn to the specific laws governing condominiums —Chapter 
718.  This Chapter requires condominiums to be operated by an association.  
§ 718.111 (1)(a) , Fla. Stat.  (2025).  Unit owners are members of that 
association and the officers and board of directors have a fiduciary duty to 
those members.  Id.  But “[a]  unit owner does not have any authority to act

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 
 for the association by reason of being a unit owner. ”  Id. at (1)(c).   Like it 
does under Chapter 617, an association has the power to “sue, and be sued.”  
Id. at (3).   
Section 718.303, Florida Statutes, states:  
(1) Each unit owner, tenant and other invitee, and association is 
governed by, and must comply with  the provisions of , this 
chapter, the declaration, the documents creating the 
association, and the association bylaws which are expressly incorporated into any lease of a unit.  Actions at law or in 
equity, or both, for failure to comply with these provisions may be brought by the association or by a unit owner against:  
 
(a) The association.  
 
(b) A unit owner.  
 
(c) Directors designated by the developer, for actions taken by them before control of the association is assumed by unit owners other than the developer.  
 
(d) Any director who willfully and knowingly fails to comply 
with these provisions . 
 
(e) Any tenant leasing a unit, and any other invitee occupying a unit.  
 § 718.303 (1), Fla. Stat. (2025).   
The Legislature has provided guidance as to how to interpret Chapters 
617 and 718.  See  § 617.1703, Fla. Stat.  (2025).  Chapter 617 applies to 
corporations that operate under Chapter 718 —but  only to the extent that it 
does not conflict with, or yield to a specific provision in, the applicable

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 
 community -association statute.   Id.  Simply stated , if there is any conflict 
between the two chapters, Chapter 718 controls.  
Yet there is no conflict here.  These two statutes can be read in 
harmony  without rendering either one superfluous or contradictor y.  See 
generally  Antonin Scalia & Bryan Garner, Reading Law: The Interpretation 
of Legal Texts  180 (2012) (“The provisions of a text should be interpreted in 
a way that renders them compatible, not contradictory.”) ; Forsythe v. 
Longboat Key Beach Erosion Control Dist. , 604 So. 2d 452, 455 (Fla. 1992)  
(“Where possible, courts must give full effect to all statutory provisions and 
construe related statutory provisions in harmony with one another. ”). 
Section 718.303(1) , Florida Statutes,  provides a cause of action for 
certain condominium -related violations , while section  617.07401 , Florida 
Statutes,  governs the procedures for bringing derivative actions.  A claim 
under section 718.303(1) , Florida Statutes,  may or may not be derivative 
depending on the nature of the right asserted and the injury alleged.  Thus, 
section 718.303(1) , Florida Statutes,  establishes the substantive cause of 
action, while section 617.07401 , Florida Statutes,  supplies  the procedural 
prerequisites for pursuing that claim  derivatively.    
Although section 718.303(1) , Florida Statutes,  authorizes a unit owner 
to sue a condominium association, it does not follow that every action

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8 
 brought under that provision is direct in nature or exempt from the procedural 
requirements governing derivative proceedings.   Our sister courts have 
reached similar conclusion s.  See Iezzi Fam.  Ltd. P ’ship v. Edgewater Beach 
Owners Ass’n, Inc. , 254 So. 3d 584 , 585  (Fla. 1st DCA 2018) ; Mineo v. Do , 
435 So. 3d 1058, 1060 (Fla. 4th DCA 2026) .   
So the remaining question is whether this lawsuit is derivative.   We 
answer in the affirmative.  See  Dinuro Invs., LLC v. Camacho, 141 So.  3d 
731, 738–41 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014) (holding that Florida requires a direct harm and special injury to a corporation member, or a special duty owed, for a 
member to maintain an individual action compared to a derivative one); 
Braun v. Buyers Choice Mortg. Corp. ex rel. McAloon , 851 So.  2d 199, 203 
(Fla. 4th DCA 2003) (holding that the claims were derivative because the 
body of the complaint  alleged injuries that equally affected other corporation 
shareholders).   The allegations of the complaint and the wherefore clause 
demonstrate this is an action in which a unit owner seeks to enforce a right 
existing in the corporation.  The injury sustained by the unit owner is the very 
same injury sustained by other unit owners.  Leppert v. Lakebreeze 
Homeowners Ass ’n, Inc. , 500 So.  2d 250, 252 (Fla. 1st DCA 1986) .   
Labeling it a direct action does not change this analysis.  “[P] laintiffs 
may not decide that they are not subject to statutory requirements merely by

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 9
citations.quote:
9 
 labeling their allegations in an effort to avoid them. ”  Iezzi Fam . Ltd. P ’ship, 
254 So. 3d at  586.  It is the substance of the complaint that controls.  And 
the substance here shows this is derivative.   
Because the complaint alleges derivative claims, Perez and Gonzalez  
were required to comply with the presuit requirements of section 617.07401 , 
Florida Statutes .  The trial court departed from the essential requirements of 
the law.  Therefore, we grant the petition and quash the order.   
Petition granted; order quashed.

items.summary:
Holding: The complaint sought to enforce association rights for injuries shared by unit owners and was derivative in substance. Section 718.303 did not exempt it from the presuit requirements of section 617.07401 applied in the case. The opinion expressly notes that chapter 2026-168 repealed that provision effective July 1 and enacted section 617.0742; do not treat its quotation of the 2025 statute as the current complaint requirements.
Disposition: Certiorari petition granted; order denying dismissal quashed.
Author: Judge Gooden. Panel: Fernandez, Miller and Gooden.
Official opinion retrieved October 12, 2026; issuance date stated in document and index. Any printed rehearing or revision qualification is preserved; subsequent docket finality and treatment not independently verified.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 1
citations.quote:
DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA  
FOURTH DISTRICT  
 
KID INTERNATIONAL, LLC, a Florida limited liability company, 
LICHI, LLC, a Florida limited liability company, and 
YARON KATZ, an individual, 
Appellants, 
 
v. 
 
CITY NATIONAL BANK OF FLORIDA, and 2655 SW 25, LLC,  
a Florida limited liability company, 
Appellees. 
 
No. 4D2025-2599 
 
[October 7, 2026] 
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit, 
Broward County; Jeffrey R. Levenson, Judge; L.T. Case No. 
062024CA012184AXXXCE. 
 
Winsor Daniel Jr., of The Daniel Firm, Weston, for appellants. 
 
Christopher B. Spuches of Lynx Law PLLC, Coral Gables, for appellees. 
 S
HAW, J. 
 
The plaintiffs appeal from the final summary judgment entered for the 
defendants.  This case boils down to one issue: whether the circuit court 
correctly determined that the plaintiffs’ claims were barred by the statute 
of limitations.  The record and applicable case law establish the circuit 
court was correct.  Accordingly, we affirm without further discussion. 
 
We now address the defendants’ motion for sanctions against the 
plaintiffs and their counsel.  Therein, the defendants state that the 
plaintiffs repeatedly cited to fabricated case law, both in the lower tribunal 
and in their initial b rief, misrepresented the holdings of actual cases, and 
included fictional quotations from actual cases.  The defendants note that 
this conduct compelled them to waste valuable time and money searching 
for cases that did not exist or reviewing cases which had no bearing on the 
issues on appeal.  As a result, the defendants request that we grant their 
sanctions motion and award their reasonable attorney’s fees and costs.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 Our opinion will focus on the plaintiffs’ initial brief filed here, not the 
plaintiffs’ conduct in the circuit court.1 
 
Our independent review confirms that the plaintiffs’ initial brief 
contained the following errors: (i) relying heavily on a federal case involving 
the same defendant bank, City Nat ional Bank of Florida  v. Louisiana  Apple, 
LLC, No. 24-CV-23285, 2024 WL 4212910 (S.D. Fla. Sept. 17, 2024), to 
falsely assert (including with fictional quotations) that the defendant bank made various admissions impacting this case;
2 (ii) citing a hallucinated 
case, Ogilvie v. Sebring Airport Authority , 841 So. 2d 529 (Fla. 2d DCA 
2003), seven times and including a fictional quotation from this non-
existent case; (iii) citing Mansolillo v. Parties by Lynn, Inc., 173 So. 3d 112 
(Fla. 4th DCA 2015), for a legal proposition and including a quotation from 
that case, even though that case has a different citation, came from a 
different court, was entered in a different year, did not stand for the proposition cited, and did not include the quotation; (iv) attributing a quote 
to Seaboard Air Line Railroad  Co. v. Holt , 92 So. 2d 169, 170–71 (Fla. 
1956), which does not appear in the opinion; and (v) relying heavily on  
Silvestrone v. Edell, 721 So. 2d 1173 (Fla. 1998), for several propositions 
which are not accurately excerpted from the opinion.  
Because of these fabricated references to non-existent cases and 
inaccurately cited legal authorities, we issued an order to the plaintiffs to 
show cause why we should not strike the initial brief or impose other 
sanctions.  See Order to Show Cause, Kid Int’l , LLC  v. City Nat’l Bank of 
Fla., No. 4D2025-2599 (Fla. 4th DCA Aug. 7, 2024) (unreported) (citing 
Fla. R. App. P. 9.410(a) and In re Amends. to Fla. R. Gen. Prac. & Jud. 
Admin. 2.515, 435 So. 3d 5, 6 (Fla. 2026) (amending rule 2.515(d)(2) to 
provide that a court may impose sanctions after providing the signer with “notice and an opportunity to be heard[,] ” and to specify that “sanctions 
may include . . . striking of the document . . . or other sanctions”)). 
 
The plaintiffs filed a timely response.  Therein, the plaintiffs’ counsel 
 
1 In the circuit court, t he plaintiffs (proceeding pro se) commenced this action 
with a complaint that contained extensive citation errors , presumably from the 
use of artificial intelligence when drafting the complaint.  The pro se complaint 
cited thirty -two cases total —fifteen were non- existent cases, two were accurately 
cited but misstated the holding, fourteen were inaccurately cited and contained 
misstated holdings, and only one of which was accurately cited with the correct holding.  The defendants moved to dismiss the complaint, and the plaintiffs 
subsequently filed an amended complaint (through an attorney) which did not 
contain those hallucinated  or inaccurately  cited legal authorities . 
2 The plaintiffs go so far as to argue that th e federal  case “is devastating to [the 
defendant bank’s] position .”

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 
 acknowledged the seriousness of the issues which we had  identified and 
admitted that the initial brief “contained legal authorities, citations, 
quotations, and/or characterizations that were not adequately verified 
before filing.”  He continued, “[c]ertain authorities did not exist as cited, 
while other citations or propositions attributed to authorities were 
inaccurate.”  Ultimately, he fully accepted responsibility for these issues.   
 
The plaintiffs’ counsel also explained how the errors occurred.  He 
stated that, in an effort to manage his work efficiently and control litigation 
expense, he accepted his client’s offer to assist by providing research materials and authorities for his consideration (unaware at the time of the 
citation issues in the plaintiffs’ initial complaint).  Additionally, counsel’s  
law firm incorporated generative artificial-intelligence (“AI”) technology as 
one component of the legal research and drafting process.  Ultimately, 
counsel concluded that the initial brief’s errors occurred because his 
“verification process failed to identify before filing that certain authorities did not exist, were inaccurately cited, or did not support the propositions 
attributed[.]”   
 
Counsel stated that after we brought the citation issues to his attention, 
he attempted to correct the problem.  He sought permission to replace the 
initial brief with an amended brief (though, alas, as counsel admitted, the amended brief did not resolve all the citation issues).  He also represented 
that he has changed his legal research and drafting procedures to ensure 
that legal authorities relied upon in court filings are independently located 
and checked against authoritative legal sources before filing. 
 Based on counsel’s response to the order to show cause, we  decided to 
proceed with the initial brief as filed, while disregarding the hallucinated 
citations and quotations, as well as the misrepresented holdings.  See 
Friend v. Serpa , 425 So. 3d 51, 51 (Fla. 4th DCA 2025) (“Such phantom 
authority cannot assist any litigant and must be expressly disregarded by 
this court.”).  As stated above, we affirm without discussing the merits. 
 But there is still the matter of the defendants’ motion for sanctions.   
Recent cases have established that a party’s submission of hallucinated 
and inaccurately cited case law is sanctionable.  See Francois v. Vive Fin., 
LLC, 433 So. 3d 795, 795 (Fla. 4th DCA 2026) (“The submission of 
fictitious or fabricated case law—whether the product of carelessness, misunderstanding, or reliance on generative artificial-intelligence tools—
is sanctionable.”) (collecting cases); Eclectic Synergy, LLC v. Seredin, 435 
So. 3d 1074, 1077–79 (Fla. 4th DCA 2026) (sanctioning attorney, who had 
filed a petition that misstated the law and cited to non-existent caselaw, 
with referral to The Florida Bar); Clerk of Ct. & Comptroller for 13th Jud.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 
 Cir., Hillsborough Cnty. v. Rangel, 427 So. 3d 1069, 1071 (Fla. 2d DCA 
2025) (deeming sanctions against attorney were proper where the answer 
brief contained one hallucinated case citation, fourteen fabricated 
quotations from real cases, and misstated court holdings in nine cited 
cases).  While these cases involved an appellate court’s own authority to 
sanction a party under Florida Rule of Appellate Procedure 9.410(a), we conclude that their reasoning should be extended to cases such as this 
one, where a party moves for attorney’s fees as a sanction pursuant to 
Florida Rule of Appellate Procedure 9.410(b) (2026). 
 
As noted by Judge Matthewman in the United States District Court for 
the Southern District of Florida, “counsel who decide to enter a case to 
litigate must ensure that they carefully evaluate, elucidate, and advocate—not hallucinate.”  Versant Funding LLC v. Teras Breakbulk Ocean 
Navigation Enters., LLC, No. 17-CV-81140, 2025 WL 1440351, at *7 (S.D. Fla. May 20, 2025).  In Versant Funding LLC, the trial court awarded the  
plaintiff all reasonable attorney’s fees and costs incurred by its counsel for 
the time spent researching and replying to a response that contained one hallucinated citation.  Id.  Here, as admitted by the plaintiffs in their 
response to the order to show cause, the  initial brief—which was drafted 
with the assistance of AI and input from the plaintiffs—contained 
hallucinated cases, fabricated quotations from real cases, and cases that 
did not stand for the proposition cited.    
Given the foregoing, we grant the defendants’ motion for sanctions and 
award defendants their reasonable attorney’s fees incurred in litigating 
this appeal.  On remand, the circuit court shall set the amount of the 
reasonable attorney’s fees to be awarded for this appellate case.  If a 
motion for rehearing is filed in this court, then services rendered in 
connection with the filing of the motion, including, but not limited to, 
preparation of a responsive pleading, shall be considered in computing the 
amount of the fees.   The plaintiffs and their counsel shall be jointly and 
severally liable for the payment of this award.    
Affirmed; motion for sanctions granted; remanded with directions.  
 G
ERBER , C.J.,  and L OTT, J., concur. 
 
*            *            * 
 
Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

items.summary:
Holding: The court affirmed limitations-based summary judgment without merits discussion and granted the appellees’ rule 9.410(b) sanctions motion for fabricated cases, quotations and mischaracterized holdings in the initial brief. Plaintiffs and counsel were made jointly and severally liable for reasonable appellate attorney fees, with amount determined on remand and rehearing services included if applicable.
Disposition: Affirmed; sanctions granted; remanded to set reasonable appellate attorney fees.
Author: Judge Shaw. Chief Judge Gerber and Lott concur.
Official opinion retrieved October 12, 2026; issuance date stated in document and index. Any printed rehearing or revision qualification is preserved; subsequent docket finality and treatment not independently verified.
Recorded discrepancy: Page 2 cites a show-cause order dated August 7, 2024 in this 2025-numbered appeal while describing that order as citing a 2026 rule amendment. The chronology is preserved as printed; the actual show-cause docket date was not independently verified.
