citations.quote:
DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA  
FOURTH DISTRICT  
 
GUY BENNETT RUBIN and STEPHANIE RUBIN, 
Appellants, 
 
v. 
 
SAILFISH POINT PROPERTY OWNERS and COUNTRY CLUB 
ASSOCIATION, INC., GLORIA DITTUS, CKENA5 HOLDINGS, LLC, 
CHARLES LAROCCO, and KATHLEEN LAROCCO, 
Appellees. 
 
No. 4D2024-2398 
 
_____________________________ 
 
GUY BENNETT RUBIN and STEPHANIE RUBIN, 
Appellants, 
 
v. 
 
SAILFISH POINT PROPERTY OWNERS and COUNTRY CLUB 
ASSOCIATION, INC., GLORIA DITTUS, CKENA5 HOLDINGS, LLC, 
CHARLES LAROCCO, and KATHLEEN LAROCCO, 
Appellees. 
 
No. 4D2025-1575 
 
[October 7, 2026] 
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit, 
Martin County; Nancy F. Alley, Judge; L.T. Case No. 
432021CA000548CAAXMX.   
 
Guy Bennett Rubin of Rubin & Rubin, Stuart, for appellants. 
 
Tim B. Wright, Paul J. Parton, and Jesus M. Hernandez of Wright, 
Ponsoldt & Lozeau Trial Attorneys, L.L.P., Stuart, for appellees CKENA5 
Holdings, LLC, Charles LaRocco, and Kathleen LaRocco. 
 
Gary A. Woodfield and Alejandra S. Alv arez of Nason Yeager Gerson 
Harris & Fumero, P.A., Palm Beach Gardens, for appellee Gloria Dittus.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 Michael Kissner of Block & Scarpa, P.A., Vero Beach, for appellee 
Joseph Vessely. 
 
MAY, J. 
 
 A dispute over a purchase agreement for a residence in a private 
residential community and the assignment of that agreement wound up in 
litigation.  The buyer1 appeals a final judgment in favor of the assignee of 
the purchase agreement.  The buyer argues the trial court erred in (1) 
entering a judgment for the assignee without considering whether 
rescission was warranted due to impossibility of performance; (2) failing to 
address the buyer’s theories of mutual mistake and lack of consideration; 
(3) awarding attorney’s fees to the assignee; and (4) failing to award costs 
against a back-up buyer.  We find no merit to the issues raised in the 
appeal of the underlying judgment and affirm.   
 
 In a consolidated appeal, the purchaser appeals an attorneys’ fees 
judgment in favor of the assignee.  He argues the trial court erred in awarding attorney’s fees because the assignment agreement contained no attorney’s fees provision.  We agree and reverse. 
 
• The Facts 
 
 The sellers contracted to sell the property to the buyer.  Under the 
community’s declarations and covenants, the sale could not close without 
an approval certificate issued by Sailfish Point Property Owners’ and 
Country Club Association, Inc. (“association”). 
 
 When the purchase agreement was entered into, the buyer was leasing 
a residence in the community and had been approved by the association.  
Nevertheless, the association required the buyer to submit a second 
membership application before closing.   The sellers also signed a backup 
contract with another buyer, which would become effective only if the 
buyer’s contract did not close.  
 
1 The appellants are a husband and wife who sought to purchase real property.  
They were both plaintiffs in the lawsuit, but only the husband signed the 
purchase agreement and the subsequent assignment.  For ease of reference, the buyers will be referred to as “buyer” throughout the opinion.   
 
 The assignees are a husband and wife, but the assignment was made to a 
limited liability company they owned.  For ease of reference, the opinion will refer 
to them as assignees.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 
  As luck would have it, the association denied the buyer’s membership 
application and the appeal of that denial.  The association, however, 
conditionally approved the backup buyer’s membership application, 
contingent upon closing under the backup contract. 
 
 Trying to preserve the original purchase agreement, the buyer proposed 
assigning the rights under the purchase agreement to another community 
resident through CKENA5 Holdings, LLC, an entity owned by those 
residents.  Those residents were already approved association members.  
Before executing the assignment, the buyer and assignee consulted the 
closing agent, who advised that the purchase agreement remained valid 
and assignable.  The assignees also contacted the association, which 
confirmed they could proceed with the assignment. 
 
The buyer assigned the rights and obligations under the purchase 
agreement to the assignees.  Under the assignment, the assignees agreed to pay the buyer $37,181.25.  Less than one day later, the association 
informed the assignees and the closing agent that it would not permit the 
transaction to close because it considered the purchase agreement to have automatically terminated upon the association’s denial of the buyer’s 
membership application, leaving no agreement to assign.  Because the 
association refused to issue the approval necessary for closing, the sale did not occur. 
 
o The Litigation  
  
 The buyers filed an  action for declaratory and injunctive relief, tortious 
interference with a business relationship, and negligent misrepresentation 
against the association, and filed a notice of lis pendens against the 
property.  The buyer also sought to rescind the assignment based on lack of consideration, impossibility of performance, frustration of purpose, and 
mutual mistake.  These claims made up the operative Third Amended 
Complaint.   
  
 The assignees counterclaimed for declaratory relief, seeking a 
declaration that the assignment remained valid and enforceable and that they were entitled to purchase the property under the assigned agreement.  
The backup buyer sought a declaration that the buyer’s agreement had 
terminated and that the backup contract had become effective.   The trial court entered a partial final judgment on the declaratory 
judgment claim, finding that the purchase agreement had never been terminated; the assignment was valid and could not be rescinded; the

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 
 assignees could proceed to close; and the backup contract never became 
effective. 
  
 In disposing of the buyer’s rescission claim, the trial court found the 
assignment was supported by sufficient consideration, as payment was 
not due until closing.  Further, the buyer failed to establish a mutual 
mistake, because any mistake concerning the association’s approval 
related to a future event rather than an existing fact. 
 
 A jury returned a verdict for the buyer against the association in the 
amount of $1,430,000. 
 
 The buyers filed an amended motion to tax costs against all defendants, 
including the backup buyer, pursuant to sections 57.041 and 86.081, 
Florida Statutes (2021).  The buyer argued he prevailed on the competing 
declaratory judgment claims because the trial court found the purchase 
agreement never terminated, the assignment remained valid and 
enforceable, the assignees were entitled to close, and the backup buyer’s 
contract never became effective.  Accordingly, the buyer asserted he was entitled to recover taxable costs. 
 
 The backup buyer, not surprisingly, opposed the motion, arguing that 
any taxable costs should be assessed against the association because the 
litigation principally arose from the association’s denial of the buyer’s 
membership application.  The backup buyer merely held a contingent 
contract and was not alleged to have committed any wrongdoing.  
Specifically, the backup buyer maintained that the requested mediation fees, court reporter fees, deposition transcripts, subpoenas, and trial 
transcripts would have been incurred regardless of her participation in the 
litigation.   
 The trial court denied the buyer’s amended motion to tax costs against 
the backup buyers. 
 
 The buyers now appeal the trial court’s partial final judgment, the order 
denying rehearing, and the order denying costs against the backup buyer. 
 
• Analysis 
 
First, the buyer argues the trial court erred in entering judgment for 
the assignees on the buyer’s rescission claim because it failed to consider his theories of impossibility and frustration of purpose.  The assignees respond that neither of the buyer’s theories warranted rescission.  We 
agree with the assignees.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 
 “We have de novo review of a trial court’s ruling on a motion for directed 
verdict.”  Feldman v. Citizens Property  Ins. Corp., 373 So. 3d 636, 639 (Fla. 
4th DCA 2023) (citing Young v. Becker & Poliakoff, P.A., 88 So. 3d 1002, 
1011 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012)). 
Written findings are required only when mandated by statute, rule, or 
governing law.  See Gidden v. State, 613 So. 2d 457, 458 (Fla. 1993); Julia 
v. Ramos-Baez , 395 So. 3d 1121, 1124 n.4 (Fla. 6th DCA 2024) 
Here, the buyer knew the trial court would decide his rescission claim 
at the close of the case and had an opportunity to oppose the assignee’s 
motion.  After hearing arguments, the trial court ruled from the bench and 
disposed of the rescission claim.  The trial court later entered a written 
order concluding that the assignment was valid, had never been rescinded, and was not subject to rescission. 
Although the written order expressly addressed only consideration and 
mutual mistake, the trial court was not required to separately address each theory supporting rescission in writing.  See Julia , 395 So. 3d at 1124 
n.4.  We therefore affirm this issue. 
We similarly affirm the trial court’s rejection of the buyer’s mutual 
mistake and consideration arguments without further discussion. 
In his third issue, the buyer argues the trial court erred in awarding 
attorneys’ fees to the assignees.  The buyer argues that, although 
attorney’s fee entitlement is generally not ripe for appellate review until the 
amount of fees is determined, we should review the issue because the 
entitlement determination was included in the partial final judgment.  
Addressing entitlement now, he argues, would conserve judicial resources by avoiding unnecessary fee proceedings and a second appeal.  The 
assignees respond that the issue is not ripe for appellate review because 
the partial final judgment merely reserved jurisdiction over those issues. 
An attorney’s fee determination is generally not ripe for appellate review 
until the trial court has determined both entitlement to attorney’s fees and the amount of the award.  See Dania Beach Boat Club Condo. Ass’n v. 
Forcier, 290 So. 3d 99, 102 (Fla. 4th DCA 2020). 
Here, the buyer’s challenge to attorney’s fees is not properly before us 
on this appeal.  The partial final judgment contained no determination on entitlement to attorney’s fees nor the amount of the fee award.  Rather, the 
trial court merely retained jurisdiction to consider future motions for 
attorney’s fees and costs.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 
 We agree with the assignees on this issue and affirm.2   
And last, the buyer argues the trial court abused its discretion by 
denying his request for taxable costs against the backup buyer because 
the buyer prevailed against the backup buyer on her declaratory judgment 
claim.  The buyer argues that, as the prevailing party, he was entitled to 
recover taxable costs as a matter of law, pursuant to section 57.041, 
Florida Statutes (2021). 
The backup buyer responds that section 86.081, rather than section 
57.041, governs costs in declaratory judgment actions and vests the trial 
court with discretion to award costs as are equitable.  The backup buyer 
argues the trial court properly exercised that discretion because: (1) the 
underlying dispute primarily concerned the association’s conduct in preventing the buyer’s purchase of the property, (2) the backup buyer played only a limited role as the holder of a backup purchase contract, (3) 
the buyer failed to apportion the costs attributable to the backup buyer, 
and (4) the association has already satisfied the final judgment, including 
the buyer’s taxable costs. 
We agree with the backup buyer. 
“A trial court’s award of costs is generally reviewed for an abuse of 
discretion, but the standard of review is de novo to the extent the issue 
involves statutory construction or the legal determination of whether costs 
may be awarded.”  Fla. Dep’t of Health v. Woliner, 397 So. 3d 121, 123 (Fla. 
1st DCA 2024) (citing Cornfeld v. Plaza of the Americas Club, Inc., 306 So. 
3d 1136, 1139 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020)). 
Section 57.041 generally requires an award of taxable costs to the party 
recovering judgment.  See § 57.041(1), Fla. Stat. (2021).  However, section 
57.041 applies only where a more specific statutory costs provision does not govern.  Woliner, 397 So. 3d at 123–24.   
In declaratory judgment actions, section 86.081 controls and provides 
that “[t]he court may award costs as are equitable.”  § 86.081, Fla. Stat. 
(2021).  Accordingly, the assessment of costs in a declaratory judgment 
action is committed to the sound discretion of the trial court.  First 
 
2 The attorney’s fees award is the subject of the second consolidated appeal.  We 
address the merits below.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 
 Protective Ins. Co. v. Featherston, 978 So. 2d 881, 884–85 (Fla. 2d DCA 
2008). 
Here, although the buyer relies on section 57.041 to argue that he was 
entitled to taxable costs as the prevailing party, that statute does not govern his claims against the backup buyer.  The buyer’s claims against 
the backup buyer sought declaratory relief concerning the parties’ 
competing contractual rights.  Accordingly, section 86.081 governed, 
meaning the trial court had discretion in assessing taxable costs.  See 
Featherston, 978 So. 2d at 884–85.  The trial court acted within its 
discretion in declining to tax costs against the backup buyer.  We affirm 
this issue as well.  
Attorney’s Fees Appeal – Case No. 2025-1575 
 
 Following the trial, the assignees moved for attorneys’ fees and costs 
against the buyer, pursuant to Paragraph 17 of the purchase agreement 
and section 57.041, Florida Statutes (2021).  The assignees argued they 
were entitled to reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs because:  
(1) they were the prevailing parties on the rescission claim;   (2) the assignment expressly incorporated the terms of the 
 purchase agreement; and 
 
(3) the buyer remained liable because the agreement provided 
that buyers/assignors would not be released from liability 
upon assignment. 
  
 The buyer responded that the only contractual basis for fees was 
Paragraph 17 of the purchase agreement.  The assignment  did not include 
an attorney’s fee provision.  The buyer argued that Paragraph 17 did not 
authorize fees for litigation between the buyer and the assignee.   
 
 The buyer alternatively argued that he ceased to be the “buyer” once he 
assigned the purchase agreement, and the buyer’s wife was never a party to either the purchase agreement or the assignment contract.  The buyer 
further argued the assignees were not pr evailing parties because the buyer 
prevailed on his principal claim against the association. 
  
 At the hearing on the motion, the assignees argued that the rescission 
claim could not be separated from enforcement of the purchase agreement 
because the purchase agreement’s validity necessarily had to be litigated in defending against rescission of the assignment.  The trial court rejected

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8 
 the assignees’ request for fees on all claims and ruled that any fees would 
be assessed against only the buyer husband and only for the rescission 
claim.  The trial court subsequently entered a written order and reserved jurisdiction to determine the fee and cost amounts. 
 
 Subsequently, the trial court concluded that all the claims were 
inextricably intertwined because they incorporated the same factual 
allegations, the issues were interrelated, and enforcement of the 
assignment and defense of the rescission claim were “part and parcel” of 
one another.  The trial court found the buyer failed to show that the claims 
were separable, but the assignees proved that allocating attorney time 
among the various claims was not feasible.  The trial court determined that 
its prior order limiting fee entitlement to the rescission claim was “in error” 
and “superseded by this holding,” concluding the assignees were entitled 
to recover “all the fees incurred.”  
 
 The trial court then awarded the assignees $248,767.50 in attorney’s 
fees, $8,852.55 in taxable costs and expert witness fees, and $11,951.83 in prejudgment interest, for a total judgment of $269,571.88.  
 The buyer moved for rehearing, which the trial court denied. 
 
 The buyer now appeals the multiple orders and final judgment 
awarding attorneys’ fees to the assignees and the order denying rehearing. 
 
• Analysis  
 The buyer argues the trial court erred in awarding attorneys’ fees to the 
assignees because the assignment did not contain an attorneys’ fees provision.  Instead, the trial court improperly relied on Paragraph 17 of the 
purchase agreement, which authorized attorneys’ fees in disputes between 
the buyer and the sellers.  Although the assignees succeeded to the buyer’s rights under that purchase agreement, they did not assume the sellers’  
rights.  Thus, the fee provision does not apply to a dispute between the 
buyer and the assignees, who both occupy the “buyer” position under the 
purchase agreement.  
 
 The assignees respond that the trial court properly awarded them 
attorneys’ fees because the purchase agreement expressly provided that 
an assignment does not release the buyer from the purchase agreement 
absent a written release or novation. 
  We have de novo review of entitlement to attorney’s fees based on 
contract interpretation.  Michelis v. Nugent , 412 So. 3d 786, 790 (Fla. 4th

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 9
citations.quote:
9 
 DCA 2025) (quoting Waverly at Las Olas Condo. Ass’n, Inc. v. Waverly Las 
Olas, LLC, 88 So. 3d 386, 389 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012)). 
 
 Attorneys’ fees are not recoverable unless provided by statute or 
contract.  State Farm Fire & Cas. Co. v. Palma , 629 So. 2d 830, 832 (Fla. 
1993).  “The right to attorney’s fees under any contractual provision is 
limited by the terms of such provision.  Attorney’s fees are not necessarily 
recoverable as to any and all litigation relating to a contract that provides 
for attorney’s fees.”  Bay Lincoln-Mercury-Dodge, Inc. v. Transouth Mortg. 
Corp. of Fla., 531 So. 2d 1027, 1028 (Fla. 1st DCA 1988) (quoting Bowman 
v. Kingsland Dev., Inc., 432 So. 2d 660, 664 (Fla. 5th DCA 1983)). 
  
 An assignee “stands in the shoes” of the assignor and is subject to all 
rights and defenses that could have been asserted against the assignor.  
Lauren Kyle Holdings, Inc. v. Heath-Peterson Constr. Corp., 864 So. 2d 55, 58 (Fla. 5th DCA 2003) (citing Dove v. McCormick, 698 So. 2d 585 (Fla. 5th 
DCA 1997); State Farm Fire and Cas. Co. v. Ray, 556 So. 2d 811 (Fla. 5th 
DCA 1990)).  Accordingly, an assignee may enforce a contract’s prevailing-
party attorney’s fee provision where the contract provides for it.  See First 
Fin. Nw., Inc. v. Laver, 410 So. 3d 1, 4 (Fla. 4th DCA 2025).  
 Here, the only basis for attorneys’ fees was under Paragraph 17 of the 
purchase agreement.  That provision provided: 
 
17. ATTORNEY’S FEES; COSTS: The parties will split equally 
any mediation fee incurred in any mediation permitted by this 
Contract, and each party will pay their own costs, expenses and fees, including attorney’s fees, incurred in conducting the 
mediation. In any litigation permitted by this Contract, the 
prevailing party shall be entitled to recover from the non-prevailing party costs and fees, including reasonable 
attorney’s fees, incurred in conducting the litigation. This Paragraph 17 shall survive Closing or termination of this 
Contract. 
 
The assignment contained no attorney’s fee provision. 
 
 Here, the trial court awarded fees against the buyer/assignor in favor 
of the assignees.  While the assignment placed the assignees in the buyer’s shoes with respect to the sellers, it did not place the assignees in the sellers’ shoes such that they could recover attorney’s fees against the 
buyer.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 10
citations.quote:
10 
  Accordingly, there is no contractual basis for the assignees’ entitlement 
to attorney’s fees.  Neither Paragraph 17 of the purchase agreement, nor 
any provision of the assignment, entitles the assignees to recover fees.  The 
trial court erred in its fee entitlement determination.  We therefore reverse 
the attorney’s fees award. 
 
Affirmed on all issues in case number 2024-2398.  Reversed on the 
attorney’s fees award in case number 2025-1575. 
 
GROSS and C IKLIN, JJ., concur. 
 
*            *            * 
 
Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

items.summary:
Holding: An assignment placing assignees in the buyer’s position did not give them the seller’s contractual right to recover fees against the assignor, and the assignment itself had no fee provision. The court separately upheld rejection of rescission and discretionary denial of costs against the backup buyer under the declaratory-judgment costs statute, section 86.081.
Disposition: All issues affirmed in 2024-2398; attorney-fee award reversed in 2025-1575.
Author: Judge May. Gross and Ciklin concur.

1 
 DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA  
FOURTH DISTRICT  
 
FEDERAL INSURANCE COMPANY, HAROLD 
PEERENBOOM, and WILLIAM MARVIN DOUBERLEY,  
Appellants, 
 
v. 
 
ISAAC (“IKE”) PERLMUTTER and LAURA PERLMUTTER, 
Appellees. 
 
Nos. 4D2022-1558, 4D2022-1560 and 4D2022-1562 
 
[October 7, 2026] 
 
Consolidated appeals of nonfinal orders from the Circuit Court for the 
Fifteenth Judicial Circuit, Palm Beach County; G. Joseph Curley, Judge; L.T. 
Case No. 502013CA015257XXXXMB. 
 
Joseph H. Lang, Jr., and Jeffrey A. Cohen of Carlton Fields, P.A., Tampa, and 
Kristen D. Perkins of Kennedys CMK LLP, Fort Lauderdale, for appellant Federal 
Insurance Company. 
 Ethan A. Arthur of Wicker Smith O’Hara McCoy & Ford, P.A., Tampa, and 
Jordan S. Cohen and Victoria N. Sosa of Wicker Smith O’Hara McCoy & Ford, P.A., Fort Lauderdale, for appellant Harold Peerenboom. 
 
Travis J. Foels, Steven J. Rothman, and Danielle L. Jakeman of Jones Foster 
P.A., West Palm Beach, for appellant William Marvin Douberley. 
 Jesse Panuccio, David Costello, and Dante Ficarelli of Boies Schiller Flexner 
LLP, Fort Lauderdale, and Joshua E. Dubin of Joshua E. Dubin, P.A., Miami, for appellees. 
 
ON REMAND FROM THE FLORIDA SUPREME COURT 
 
C
ONNER , J. 
 In this consolidated appeal, Federal Insurance Company (“Federal”), Harold 
Peerenboom (“Peerenboom”), and William Douberley (“Douberley”) (collectively, 
“the appellants”) separately appeal trial court orders granting Isaac and Laura 
Perlmutter’s (“the Perlmutters”) motions to amend their counterclaims to seek punitive damages from the appellants.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 
 We initially reversed the trial court’s orders.  Fed. Ins. Co. v. Perlmutter, 376 
So. 3d 24 (Fla. 4th DCA 2023) (“Perlmutter I”).  However, the Florida Supreme 
Court quashed Perlmutter I and remanded the case for our re-examination  
consistent with the Court’s opinion.  Perlmutter v. Fed. Ins. Co., 434 So. 3d 681 
(Fla. 2026) (“Perlmutter II”). 
 
Upon completing our re-examination, we affirm without discussion the trial 
court’s order permitting amendment of the Perlmutters’ counterclaims to assert punitive damages against Peerenboom.  However, as explained below, we reverse 
the orders permitting amendment of counterclaims against Douberley and 
Federal. 
 In short, the Perlmutters’ proposed second amended counterclaim (“proposed 
counterclaim”) lacks sufficient allegations and evidentiary support of Douberley’s 
intentional misconduct to support punitive damages.  Regarding Federal, the “vicarious liability” theory fails because of our reversal as to Douberley, and 
independently because the proffered evidence was insufficient to show that a 
managing agent knew of and “condoned, ratified, or participated” in an 
employee’s intentional misconduct, as required by the governing statute. 
 For our reconsideration, we have relied on the background facts and 
procedural history as discussed in Perlmutter I, 376 So. 3d at 28-30, and 
Perlmutter II, 434 So. 3d at 686-87.
1 
 
Standard of Review  
Appellate courts review de novo an order granting leave to amend to assert 
punitive damages.  See Estancia US Ltd. P’ship v. Aji -Dawkins , No. 6D2025-0673, 
2026 WL 2363549, at *3 (Fla. 6th DCA Aug. 14, 2026) (decided after Perlmutter 
II); Liston v. Salvi , 436 So. 3d 499, 501 (Fla. 4th DCA 2026) .  In conducting de 
novo review, we evaluate the sufficiency of the claimant’s proposed pleading and 
evidentiary proffer, just as the trial court must do.  McLane Foodservice Inc. v. 
 
1 After remand, we ordered supplemental briefing on the S upreme Court’s clarified 
standards for ruling on a motion to amend to assert punitive damages.  In supplemental 
briefing, both sides have raised issues that were not raised in the initial briefing.  We 
read the remand instructions as directing us to reexamine the trial court’s decision 
using the S upreme Court’s clarified guidance as to the arguments raised in the initial 
appeal.  Accordingly, we decline to consider new arguments first raised in supplemental briefing.  Additionally, the Perlmutters’ supplemental briefing asserts facts about the 
trial court proceedings after the notice of appeal was filed in this case.  We cannot  
consider facts occurring after the notice of appeal was filed.  See Lauderdale Marine Ctr., 
Ltd. v. MYD Marine Distribs, Inc. , 31 So. 3d 256, 257 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010) (“This court 
may review only proceedings occurring prior to the date of appellant's notice of appeal. ”) 
(citing Fla. R. App. P. 9.110(h )).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 
 Wool, 400 So. 3d 757, 761 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024) (citations omitted).  And, like the 
trial court, we view the evidentiary proffer in the light most favorable to the 
claimant but may not accept conclusory labels and characterizations as 
substitutes for competent substantial evidence.  Id. 
 
Foundational Statutes and Caselaw 
 
Section 768.72, Florida Statutes (2013), the general statutory authority for 
the imposition of punitive damages, provides: 
 
(1) In any civil action, no claim for punitive damages shall be 
permitted unless there is a reasonable showing by evidence in the 
record or proffered by the claimant which would provide a 
reasonable basis for recovery of such damages.  The claimant may 
move to amend her or his complaint to assert a claim for punitive 
damages as allowed by the rules of civil procedure.  The rules of civil procedure shall be liberally construed so as to allow the claimant 
discovery of evidence which appears reasonably calculated to lead 
to admissible evidence on the issue of punitive damages. . . .  
(2) A defendant may be held liable for punitive damages only if the 
trier of fact, based on clear and convincing evidence, finds that the defendant was personally guilty of intentional misconduct or gross 
negligence.  As used in this section, the term:  
(a) “Intentional misconduct” means that the defendant had actual 
knowledge of the wrongfulness of the conduct and the high 
probability that injury or damage to the claimant would result and, 
despite that knowledge, intentionally pursued that course of 
conduct, resulting in injury or damage. 
 (b) “Gross negligence” means that the defendant’s conduct was so 
reckless or wanting in care that it constituted a conscious disregard 
or indifference to the life, safety, or rights of persons exposed to such 
conduct. 
 
(3) In the case of an employer, principal, corporation, or other legal 
entity, punitive damages may be imposed for the conduct of an 
employee or agent only if the conduct of the employee or agent meets 
the criteria specified in subsection (2) and: 
 
(a) The employer, principal, corporation, or other legal entity 
actively and knowingly participated in such conduct;

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 
 (b) The officers, directors, or managers of the employer, principal, 
corporation, or other legal entity knowingly condoned, ratified, or 
consented to such conduct; or 
 
(c) The employer, principal, corporation, or other legal entity 
engaged in conduct that constituted gross negligence and that 
contributed to the loss, damages, or injury suffered by the claimant.  
 (4) The provisions of this section shall be applied to all causes of 
action arising after the effective date of this act. 
 
§ 768.72, Fla. Stat. (2013) (emphasis added).  The underlined phrases form the 
bases for our reversal. 
 Perlmutter II recognized the well-settled principle that the statute “creates a 
substantive legal right not to be subjected to a punitive damages claim and ensuing financial worth discovery until the trial court makes a determination 
that there is a reasonable evidentiary basis for recovery of punitive damages.”  
434 So. 3d at 685 (citations omitted). 
 The Supreme Court’s objective in Perlmutter II was to clarify the showing a 
movant must make to amend a pleading to seek punitive damages.  Id. at 684.  
In doing so, Perlmutter II considered the interplay among subsections (1), (2), and 
(3) of section 768.72.
2  Id. at 688-90.  
 
The Supreme Court identified four clarifications as to the movant’s showing 
which are the most pertinent for our remand review. 
 First, in a proceeding under section 768.72(1), the trial court should consider 
only the evidence identified or proffered by the claimant, not any evidentiary 
counter-submission from the opponent.  Id. at 688. 
 
Second, the test for evidentiary sufficiency under section 768.72(1) is 
“whether a reasonable person could conclude, based on the claimant's evidence, that the defendant committed ‘intentional misconduct’ or ‘gross negligence,’ as 
defined in section 768.72(2).”  Id. 
 Third (relevant to Federal), “[i]f the claimant seeks to plead punitive damages 
against an employer under a theory of vicarious liability, the evidentiary sufficiency test must also ask whether a reasonable person could conclude that 
the claimant’s evidence satisfies the substantive legal criteria set out in section 
768.72(3).”  Id. 
 
2 Here, t he interplay between subsections (1) and (2) applies to Douberley.  The interplay 
between all three subsections applies to Federal.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 
  
Fourth, and particularly pertinent to this case, “‘[b]ecause punitive damages 
never stand alone,’ the trial court must ‘review the request for punitive damages 
in the context of the underlying claims.’”  Id. at 688 (alteration in original) 
(quoting LoanFlight Lending, LLC v. Wood, 388 So. 3d 1027, 1031 (Fla. 3d DCA 
2024)); see also Estancia, 2026 WL 2363549, at *3 (applying Perlmutter II and 
LoanFlight). 
 
In Perlmutter II, the Supreme Court clarified that “in reviewing the sufficiency 
of the evidence under section 768.72(1) at the pleading stage, the trial court 
should not apply the clear and convincing evidence standard of proof.”  
Perlmutter II, 434 So. 3d at 688-89.  The Supreme Court further explained that 
the trial court does not act as a factfinder at this stage and must not weigh the 
claimant’s evidence.  Id. at 689.  Rather, the trial court must consider the record 
and proffered evidence in the light most favorable to the plaintiff.  Id. (citation 
omitted).  The Supreme Court emphasized that the allegations contained in the 
claimant’s proposed amended complaint are not evidence.  Id.  Thus, the purpose 
of the proceeding under section 768.72(1) at the pleading sta ge “is to determine 
whether the claimant can show reasonable evidentiary support for those 
allegations.”  Id. 
 Consequently, we turn to the proposed counterclaim.  
The Proposed Counterclaim 
Perlmutter II did not specifically address the sufficiency of the proposed 
counterclaim but instead remanded the case for us to re-examine the proposed 
counterclaim under the clarified standards at the pleading stage.  Id. at 691. 
 
Section 768.72(1) states in part: “The claimant may move to amend her or his 
complaint to assert a claim for punitive damages as allowed by the rules of civil procedure.”  § 768.72(1), Fla. Stat. (2013).  Pursuant to Florida Rule of Civil 
Procedure 1.190(a), “[i]f a party files a motion to amend a pleading, the party 
shall attach the proposed amended pleading to the motion.” 
 
Applying the plain language of section 768.72(1) and rule 1.190(a), we again 
adopt our statement in Perlmutter I that “[g]iven the nature of the applicable 
statute and rule, the court must consider both the pleading component and the 
evidentiary component of each motion to amend to assert punitive damage 
claims.”  376 So. 3d at 32 (first quoting Varnedore v. Copeland, 210 So. 3d 741, 744 (Fla. 5th DCA 2017); and then citing Henn v. Sandler, 589 So. 2d 1334, 
1335-36 (Fla. 4th DCA 1991)).  We also reiterate Perlmutter II’s reminder that 
punitive damages “never stand alone,” and “the trial court must ‘review the request for punitive damages in the context of the underlying claims.’”  434 So. 
3d at 688 (citation modified) (citations omitted).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 
 Caselaw has further explained that in ruling on a motion to amend, the trial 
court “must first analyze whether the proposed amended complaint seeking 
punitive damages contains sufficient allegations to support such a claim.”  Keen 
v. Jennings, 327 So. 3d 435, 438 (Fla. 5th DCA 2021) (citing Varnedore, 210 So. 
3d at 745).  We also agree with the Fifth District’s comments in Varnedore that: 
 
In order to perform its function as a gatekeeper, the trial court must 
understand the specific claim proposed by the plaintiff that may 
justify an award of punitive damages.  “Litigants in civil 
controversies must state their legal positions within a particular 
document, a pleading, so that the parties and the court are 
absolutely clear what the issues to be adjudicated are.”  Bank of Am. 
Nat’l Ass’n v. Asbury , 165 So. 3d 808, 809 (Fla 2d DCA 2015).  Thus, 
when entertaining a motion to amend in order to add a claim for 
punitive damages, the trial court must first consider whether the proposed amended complaint actually sets forth a claim that the 
defendants’ conduct was [intentional misconduct], as defined by 
statute.  Absent sufficient allegations, there would be neither a 
reason nor a framework for analyzing the proffered evidentiary basis 
for a punitive damages claim. 
 
210 So. 3d at 745 (emphasis added). 
 Importantly, “[i]f the evidentiary showing does not match the amended 
complaint’s allegations, the trial court should not permit the punitive damages claim.”  Perlmutter I, 376 So. 3d at 32  (citing Desanto v. Grahn, 362 So. 3d 247, 
248-50 (Fla. 4th DCA 2023) (reversing order granting leave to amend because the allegations of the motion to amend did not match any record evidence); and HRB Tax Grp., Inc. v. Fla. Investigation Bureau, Inc., 360 So. 3d 1159 (Fla. 4th 
DCA 2023) (reversing order permitting amendment because the trial court 
improperly considered allegations and evidence not relevant to the claim for 
which punitive damages were sought))). 
 
Intentional Misconduct Alleged 
 
The Perlmutters’ proposed counterclaim asserts intentional misconduct, 
rather than gross negligence, as grounds for punitive damages.  The Perlmutters’ 
motion to amend the counterclaim uses the phrase “gross negligence” four times 
but only to point out that section 768.72(2) allows punitive damages for 
intentional misconduct and gross negligence as defined within the statute.  The 
motion does not assert a theory of gross negligence as grounds for punitive 
damages and, in the evidentiary proffer attached to that motion, the phrase 
“gross negligence” appears once—in an attachment containing a copy of section 
768.72.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 
 Because the proposed counterclaim’s allegations control the first component 
of our analysis, we reject the Perlmutters’ arguments on appeal that we should 
affirm the orders allowing the punitive damages amendment against Douberley 
and Federal based on a gross negligence showing. 
 Thus, our re-examination considers whether the trial court properly allowed 
amendment of the counterclaim to assert punitive damages based on intentional 
misconduct.  In Perlmutter I, we described the caselaw characterizations of 
intentional misconduct as follows: 
 
As the Supreme Court in Cooper Industries [v. Leatherman Tool 
Group, Inc.] observed, “[I]n deciding whether [the punitive damages] 
line has been crossed, we have focused on the same general criteria: 
the degree of the defendant’s reprehensibility or culpability.”  532 
U.S. [424,] 435, 121 S. Ct. 1678 [(2001)] (emphasis added).  “[L]ong-established precedent dictates that actions which deserve 
punitive sanctions involve outrageous conduct, malicious motive, 
or wrongful intention.”  William Dorsky Assocs., Inc. v. Highlands 
Cnty. Title & Guar. Land Co., 528 So. 2d 411, 412 (Fla. 2d DCA 
1988).  “[P]unitive damages are reserved for truly ‘culpable 
conduct,’” where the conduct is “so outrageous in character, and 
so extreme in degree ... [that] the facts [of the case] to an average 
member of the community would arouse his resentment against the 
actor, and lead him to exclaim, ‘Outrageous!’” [Cleveland Clinic Fla. 
Health Sys. Nonprofit Corp. v.] Oriolo, 357 So. 3d [703,] 706 [(Fla. 4th 
DCA 2023)]; see also W.R. Grace & Co.— Conn v. Waters, 638 So. 2d 
502, 503 (Fla. 1994) (“Punitive damages are appropriate when a 
defendant engages in conduct which is fraudulent, malicious, 
deliberately violent or oppressive, or committed with such gross negligence as to indicate a wanton disregard for the rights of 
others.”); Lee Cnty. Bank v. Winson, 444 So. 2d 459, 463 (Fla. 2d 
DCA 1983) (“Punitive damages may be properly awarded only where a tort involves malice, moral turpitude, or wanton and outrageous 
disregard of a plaintiff’s rights.” (citing Winn & Lovett Grocery Co. 
v. Archer, 126 Fla. 308, 171 So. 214 (1936))). 
 376 So. 3d at 36 (Emphasis added). 
 
Because section 768.72(2)(a) defines “intentional misconduct” to mean that 
“the defendant had actual knowledge of the wrongfulness of the conduct and the 
high probability that injury or damage to the claimant would result and, despite 
that knowledge, intentionally pursued that course of conduct, resulting in injury 
or damage,” we reaffirm our statement in Perlmutter I that intentional 
misconduct justifying punitive damages requires “specific intent, not general

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8 
 intent, to knowingly engage in wrongful conduct.”  376 So. 3d at 35 (emphasis 
in original). 
 
The Perlmutters’ proposed counterclaim repeats and succinctly states the 
overarching theme for punitive damages in two paragraphs: 
 
39. Peerenboom thus enlisted Chubb[3] (including its employee 
Douberley) . . . to form a conspiracy to collect, test, and disclose the Perlmutters’ genetic information without the Perlmutters’ knowledge or consent, and manipulate the results of such genetic testing to 
falsely implicate the Perlmutters in allegedly illegal activity (the 
“DNA theft scheme”), for purposes of intimidation and retaliation. 
 . . .  
162. As part of the wrongful acts described above, each of the 
Conspirators[
4] and other, unnamed co-conspirators, knowingly, 
falsely, and intentionally agreed to participate in an overarching 
conspiracy to harm the Perlmutters, and each carried out one or 
more overt acts, as described herein. 
 
(Emphasis added). 
 As stated, we affirm without comment the trial court’s ruling as to 
Peerenboom.  Thus, we turn our analysis to Douberley and Federal and address  
the pleading and evidentiary proffer as to them. 
 
Douberley 
 
Pleading Component—Douberley 
 
The proposed counterclaim asserts punitive damages claims against 
Douberley for Count I (Conversion), Count II (Abuse of Process), and Count VII (Civil Conspiracy). 
 
 
3 Chubb Insurance Company of Canada is a separate corporate division of Federal.  
Federal was not initially a party to the suit below.  Chubb handled the insurance claim 
against Peerenboom as an adjuster  in the Kay- Dee litigation .  Douberley, an employee 
of Federal, handled the legal defense in the same suit .  Tracy Murphy, the Chubb claims 
adjuster handling the insurance claim against Peerenboom, is not mentioned in the 
proposed counterclaim.  
4 The amended counterclaim repeatedly refer s to “the Conspirators,” who were 
specifically identified in the counterclaim as Peerenboom, Douberl ey, Federal, and 
Speckin Forensics.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 9
citations.quote:
9 
 The Perlmutters’ overarching theme for punitive damages alleges a conspiracy 
by Peerenboom, Douberley, Federal, and Speckin Forensics to surreptitiously 
collect, test, and manipulate DNA test results to intentionally and falsely 
implicate the Perlmutters in illegal hate mail activity (the “DNA theft scheme”), 
for purposes of intimidation, retaliation, and hurting Isaac Perlmutter’s financial 
connections with Disney. 
 
The principal problem with the proposed counterclaim is its reliance on the 
repeated use of “Conspirators” to refer collectively to all the counterclaim 
defendants, lumping them together and failing to differentiate which defendants 
engaged in the alleged wrongful conduct.5  More specifically, the proposed 
counterclaim fails to allege with sufficient specificity which acts Douberley 
committed individually or in concert with another counterclaim defendant that 
constituted intentional misconduct with the specific intent to harm either of the 
Perlmutters.  Additionally, the proposed counterclaim does not clearly allege that 
Douberley intended to fabricate false evidence to defame the Perlmutters or to 
harm Isaac Perlmutter’s business relationship with Disney.  Finally, the 
proposed counterclaim does not contain any allegations that Douberley acted for 
personal profit or with malicious motive. 
 
Stated another way, the proposed counterclaim fails to allege intentional 
misconduct that is “so outrageous in character, and so extreme in 
degree . . . [that] the facts [of the case] to an average member of the community 
would arouse his resentment against the actor, and lead him to exclaim, 
‘Outrageous!’” or that demonstrates “malicious motive, or wrongful intention.”  
Perlmutter I, 376 So. 3d at 36 (alterations in original) (citations omitted). 
 
For these reasons, we conclude the proposed counterclaim fails to support 
punitive damages against Douberley.  Thus, the trial court erred in granting the 
motion to amend as to Douberley.  See Keen, 327 So. 3d at 438-39 (trial court 
“must first analyze whether the proposed amended complaint seeking punitive 
damages contains sufficient allegations to support such a claim.” (citing 
Varnedore, 210 So. 3d at 745)). 
 
Even so, we analyze the evidentiary proffer component as an alternative basis 
for reversing as to Douberley.  See Varnedore, 210 So. 3d at 745 (“Absent 
sufficient allegations, there would be neither a reason nor a framework for 
analyzing the proffered evidentiary basis for a punitive damages claim.”). 
 
5 For example, m ultiple paragraphs of the proposed counterclaim alleg e acts by 
“Peerenboom  and his agents,” making it unclear whether the other counterclaim 
defendants (“the Conspirators”) were involved, or other people and entities Peerenboom 
hired to investigate the hate mail against him but not identified in the counterclaim as 
“the Conspira tors.”

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 10
citations.quote:
10 
 Evidentiary Proffer Component—Douberley 
 
Douberley correctly argues that if the evidentiary proffer does not support 
punitive damages liability under either the conversion or abuse of process counts  
against him, the evidentiary proffer also fails for the civil conspiracy count 
against him.  Soffer v. R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., 187 So. 3d 1219, 1221 (Fla. 
2016) (“[A] demand for punitive damages [for conspiracy] is ‘not a separate and 
distinct cause of action; rather it is auxiliary to, and dependent upon, the 
existence of an underlying claim.’” (quoting Liggett Grp., Inc. v. Engle, 853 So. 2d 
434, 456 (Fla. 3d DCA 2003), quashed in part by, 945 So. 2d 1246, 1254 (Fla. 
2016))). 
 Conversion  
On the conversion count, Douberley focuses on the physical aspects of Laura 
Perlmutter’s DNA sample to argue that one cannot be guilty of conversion if the 
property (DNA sample) was not directly taken from Laura’s body and instead was 
collected from a bottle.  However, Douberley does not effectively address the 
Perlmutters’ contention that Douberley assisted in converting (stealing) 
information to which Laura Perlmutter had privacy and property rights. 
 
Nonetheless, we agree with Douberley that the evidentiary proffer did not 
show he had “actual knowledge” that he was violating section 760.40, Florida 
Statutes (2013), or DNA information rights.  Again, the “actual knowledge” 
requirement means that specific intent is required rather than general intent.  Stated another way, “should have known” does not qualify in the context of 
intentional misconduct under section 768.72(2)(a).  See Selz v. McKagen, 386 So. 
3d 933, 937 (Fla. 4th DCA 2024) (“Punitive damages liability based on a ‘should have known’ standard does not meet the specific intent requirement for 
intentional misconduct as defined in section 768.72(2).”). 
 We also find merit in Douberley’s argument that “[t]his is the first case known 
to the litigants -- or cited to the trial court in over 9 years of litigation -- that has 
permitted a party to seek monetary damages for the alleged conversion of contact DNA taken from abandoned objects touched by claimants.”  If an evidentiary 
proffer does not show that the defendant intentionally violated a law which he 
knew about, the defendant’s actions cannot qualify as intentional misconduct 
deserving punishment, i.e., outrageous, malicious, or fraudulent conduct. 
 
Thus, we agree with Douberley that the Perlmutters’ evidentiary proffer on 
their conversion (theft) count was insufficient to support punitive damages 
against him.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 11
citations.quote:
11 
 Abuse of Process 
 
We also agree with several arguments which Douberley has raised regarding 
the abuse of process count.  “Where the process was used to accomplish the result for which it was intended, ‘regardless of an incidental or concurrent motive 
of spite or ulterior purpose,’ there is no abuse of process.”  S&I Invest. v. Payless 
Flea Mkt., Inc., 36 So. 3d 909, 917 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010) (quoting Scozari v. Barone, 
546 So. 2d 750, 751 (Fla. 3d DCA 1989))  (emphasis in original).  The fact that 
collecting DNA may have been an “incidental or concurrent motive” or “ulterior 
purpose” for taking the Perlmutters’ depositions does not change the fact that 
the process was properly used for the intended purpose for which it was 
created—to subpoena witnesses to offer relevant testimony.  Id. 
 
The Perlmutters’ evidentiary proffers failed to show Douberley lacked a valid 
reason to depose them in the Kay-Dee litigation.  Their depositions yielded 
information useful to Peerenboom’s defense.  Thus, the Perlmutters’ conclusory 
claim that Douberley lacked a legitimate basis to subpoena them for a deposition in that case is unsupported.  See McLane Foodservice Inc., 400 So. 3d at 761 
(recognizing conclusory labels and characterizations are not substitutes for 
competent evidentiary support). 
 
We also agree with Douberley that “[i]t is also inconceivable that taking 
depositions authorized by a court order could be considered punitive conduct.”  
Thus, we agree with Douberley that the Perlmutters’ abuse of process count was 
insufficient to support punitive damages against him. 
 
Conspiracy 
 
Because the evidentiary proffer does not support punitive damages against 
Douberley under the conversion and abuse of process counts (Counts I and II), the evidentiary proffer for punitive damages under the conspiracy count (Count 
VII) also fails.  Soffer, 187 So. 3d at 1221. 
 
Conclusion as to Douberley 
 Having concluded the amended pleading and evidentiary proffer are 
insufficient to support punitive damages against Douberley, we reverse the order 
allowing the counterclaim to be amended to assert punitive damages against 
him. 
 
Federal 
 
Pleading Component—Federal

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 12
citations.quote:
12 
 We begin with our conclusion that Federal waived any challenge to pleading 
deficiencies in the Perlmutters’ proposed counterclaim.  Federal’s answer brief’s 
summary of argument states that the Perlmutters were required to “first allege 
and proffer sufficient evidence” to be entitled to punitive damages.  However, nowhere in that brief does Federal make any argument, beyond conclusory 
statements, that the amended counterclaim insufficiently pled grounds for punitive damages.
6  Thus, Federal waived any challenge to the pleading 
component for punitive damages.  See Desilvio v. Desilvio, 433 So. 3d 847, 847 (Fla. 4th DCA 2026) (“Claims for which an appellant has not presented any 
argument, or for which he provides only conclusory argument, are insufficiently 
presented for review and are waived.” (quoting Hammond v. State, 34 So. 3d 58, 59 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010))). 
 Evidentiary Proffer Component—Federal 
 Given the Perlmutters’ acknowledgments in their answer briefs that they 
assert vicarious, rather than direct, liability against Federal, we review the claim 
accordingly.
7  Section 768.72(3) governs an employer’s vicarious liability for 
punitive damages caused by an employee’s wrongful conduct.8 
 
The primary disagreement on appeal between Federal and the Perlmutters is 
whether an employer’s vicarious liability under section 768.72(3) for an 
employee’s intentional misconduct, as defined by section 768.72(2)(a), requires 
 
6 Again, we will not consider arguments raised in supplemental briefing that were not 
made in the initial briefing.  
7 The Perlmutters’ initial answer brief unequivocally states: “In this case, the Perlmutters 
seek damages against Federal based on vicarious liability under section 768.72.”  They 
further state: “Which is to say, under a vicarious theory of liability, Federal is liable for  
the actions of its employees (Douberley, Murphy) if any of the three conditions in section 768.72(3) are met.”  Thereafter, Federal  states: “The point is that under a vicarious 
theory of liability, Federal is liable for the actions of its employees —Douberley and 
Murphy —if it was made aware of the misconduct and did nothing to prevent or 
subsequently remedy the misconduct.  That is what happened here.” 
 
Likewise, the Perlmutters’ supplemental answer brief states: “Because Douberley’s 
conduct meets section 768.72(2), his employer —Federal —is liable for punitive damages 
if a Federal ‘manager[ ]’ ‘knowingly condoned, ratified, or consented to [Douberley’s] 
conduct.’”  
 
8 The Perlmutters ’ supplemental briefing  appear s to seek affirmance of Federal’s 
vicarious liability under section 768.72(3) based on gross  negligence.  Having 
determined the proposed counterclaim asserts an overall theory of intentional 
misconduct, rather than gross negligence, we decline to consider new arguments first 
raised in supplemental briefing.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 13
citations.quote:
13 
 a “managing agent” to know of the employee’s misconduct and knowingly  
participate in, condone, ratify, or consent to that misconduct. 
 
Caselaw defines a “managing agent” as “more than just a manager or a mid-
level employee,” such as a job foreman, bank vice president, or hotel manager.  
Fla. Power & Light Co. v. Dominguez, 295 So. 3d 1202, 1205 (Fla. 2d DCA 2019) (citations omitted).  Rather, a managing agent would be someone like a corporate 
president or primary corporate owner, who holds a “position with the corporation 
which might result in his acts being deemed the acts of the corporation.”  Id.  
(citation omitted). 
 
Federal argues that by enacting the definition of “intentional misconduct” in 
section 768.72(2)(a) in 1999, the legislature rejected the previous common law standard for imposing employer vicarious liability for punitive damages and 
imposed a heightened standard.  Although section 768.72(3) does not use the 
term “managing agent,” Federal argues that the post-1999 caselaw interpreting section 768.72(3) has clearly held that the employer’s vicarious liability is based 
on wrongful conduct as demonstrated by one or more “managing agents.” 
 
The Perlmutters respond that “[t]he plain language of section 768.72(3) 
codifies Florida’s longstanding rule that corporate vicarious liability does not include a ‘requirement that the independent negligent conduct by the 
corporation be attributed to a managing agent.’”  The Perlmutters cite several 
cases in support of their argument.  However, we conclude the cases do not 
support their argument. 
 We agree with Federal’s arguments and cited caselaw that the concept of 
“managing agent” applies to all three subsections of section 768.72(3).  See Napleton’s N. Palm Auto Park, Inc. v. Agosto, 364 So. 3d 1103, 1106-07 (Fla. 4th DCA 2023) (holding that a platform manager, service manager, and assistant 
service manager were not managing agents because a corporation cannot act on 
its own and a plaintiff must identify a managing agent with “ultimate decision-
making authority for the company” (citation omitted)); HCA Health Servs. of 
Fla., Inc. v. Byers-McPheeters, 201 So. 3d 669, 670 (Fla. 4th DCA 2016) (holding 
“[u]nder section 768.72(3), the legislature established a heightened standard for 
imposing punitive damages on an employer rather than adopting the common law rules of agency and vicarious liability” (citation omitted)); Tallahassee Mem’l 
Healthcare, Inc. v. Dukes, 272 So. 3d 824, 826 (Fla. 1st DCA 2019) (quashing an 
order permitting amendment under subsection (3)(b) and explaining: “[w]hat is 
missing from Ms. Dukes’s motion and proffer, however, is an allegation or 
evidence that corporate management knowingly condoned, ratified or consented to the alleged misconduct”); Fetlar, LLC v. Suarez, 230 So. 3d 97, 100 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2017) (no liability under any subsection of 768.72(3) because individual 
construction managers, superintendents, construction workers were not officers 
or managing members of the limited liability companies); Coronado Condo. Ass’n

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 14
citations.quote:
14 
 v. La Corte, 103 So. 3d 239, 241 (Fla. 3d DCA 2012) (no employer vicarious 
liability under section 768.72(3) because the property manager was “not a 
controlling officer, director, or ‘manager’ of the Association as a corporate entity” 
and the alleged actions of the contractor’s employees “do not involve active, 
knowing participation by, or the consent or gross negligence of, the Association 
as an entity” (footnote omitted)). 
 
Having determined the role of managing agents for asserting an employer’s 
vicarious liability for punitive damages, we turn to the Perlmutters’ motion to 
amend to seek punitive damages against Federal. 
 
Because the Perlmutters concede they seek to vicariously impose punitive 
damages against Federal based on Douberley’s and Tracy Murphy’s misconduct, 
our reversal of the order allowing the proposed counterclaim to assert punitive 
damages against Douberley also negates any claim against Federal based on 
Douberley’s alleged misconduct.  Soffer, 187 So. 3d at 1221.  Additionally, we 
determine that the Perlmutter’s proffer does not provide evidence that either 
Douberley or Murphy were managing agents of either Federal or Chubb, a threshold requirement for imposing vicarious punitive damages liability against Federal, as stated above. 
 We also agree with Federal that the Perlmutters’ evidentiary proffer used 
highly selective and parsed snippets from record documents to support their contention that Federal was part of the conspiracy (“the DNA scheme”) to use false DNA evidence to accuse the Perlmutters of being involved in criminal 
activity relating to the hate mail against Peerenboom.  More importantly, those  
snippets do not support that contention. 
 Additionally, the Perlmutters’ evidentiary proffer, like their amended 
counterclaim, repeatedly lumps the actions of Peerenboom as proof of 
Douberley’s, Murphy’s, and Federal’s misconduct.  Because punitive damages 
for intentional misconduct require specific intent and actual knowledge of the 
wrongfulness of the conduct, one defendant’s intentional misconduct cannot 
establish another’s direct liability for punitive damages to another defendant.  Perlmutter I, 376 So. 3d at 35. 
 Likewise, in the context of section 768.72(3), vicarious liability for an 
employee’s intentional misconduct cannot be imposed on the employer absent 
proof that the requirements of at least one of the subsections of section 768.72(3)  
have been met.  See § 768.72(3)(a)-(c), Fla. Stat. (2013).  The Perlmutters’ 
arguments lumping proof of acts of intentional misconduct by Peerenboom as proof of acts of intentional misconduct by either Douberley or Murphy to meet the requirements of section 768.72(3) have no merit.  Moreover, Federal’s 
vicarious liability under section 768.72(3) also requires more than showing intentional misconduct by either Douberley or Murphy.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 15
citations.quote:
15 
 Thus, we conclude the Perlmutters’ evidentiary proffer fails to support 
punitive damages against Federal. 
 
Conclusion As to Federal 
 
Having concluded the evidentiary proffer is insufficient to support punitive 
damages against Federal, we reverse the order allowing the counterclaim to be 
amended to assert punitive damages against Federal. 
 
Additional Ground for Reversal—Douberley and Federal 
 
The Perlmutters’ proposed counterclaim alleges that Douberley and Federal 
carried out a “DNA theft scheme” to intimidate and retaliate against the  
Perlmutters and to harm Isaac Perlmutter’s Disney ties.  However, the 
Perlmutters’ evidentiary proffer did not show that Douberley or Federal actually 
intended to improperly harm the Perlmutters, as opposed to pursuing them for alleged defamation of Peerenboom (and possible postal-law violations).  For that 
additional reason, we conclude that the evidentiary proffer failed to establish 
“outrageous” intentional misconduct sufficient to support punitive damages  
against Douberley and Federal.  Perlmutter I, 376 So. 3d at 36; Oriolo, 357 So. 3d at 706. 
 
Conclusion 
 
Having re-examined the trial court orders granting the Perlmutters’ motions 
to amend their counterclaims to assert punitive damages against all three 
appellants, we affirm the trial court as to Peerenboom without discussion but reverse the orders as to Douberley and Federal for the reasons discussed above.  
 Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. 
 L
EVINE and K LINGENSMITH , JJ., concur. 
 
*            *            * 
 
Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

items.summary:
Holding: On Supreme Court remand, the court applied the reasonable-evidentiary-basis test at the punitive-pleading stage, considering claimant evidence favorably without weighing counterevidence or imposing the clear-and-convincing trial burden. The proposed intentional-misconduct allegations and proffer failed as to Douberley; the vicarious claim against Federal also lacked sufficient support, including the managing-agent requirements the opinion applies under section 768.72(3). The court declined newly raised gross-negligence theories and affirmed permission to plead against Peerenboom without discussion. This ruling concerns permission to amend, not an adjudication awarding punitive damages.
Disposition: Affirmed as to Peerenboom; reversed as to Douberley and Federal; remanded.
Author: Judge Conner. Levine and Klingensmith concur.
Official opinion retrieved October 12, 2026; issuance date stated in document and index. Any printed rehearing or revision qualification is preserved; subsequent docket finality and treatment not independently verified.

Florio asserts the trial court erred in entering a directed 
verdict on the contents claim because he presented sufficient

court erred in granting FIGA’s motion in limine restricting him 
from seeking more than the $500,000 statutory cap  on damages.

A. Directed Verdict  
“A trial court’s order directing a verdict is reviewed de novo.”  
Sells v. CSX Transp., Inc. , 170 So. 3d 27, 32 n.2 (Fla. 1st DCA 2015) 
(citation omitted).  “A trial court’s construction of an insurance 
policy to determine coverage is a matter of law subject to de novo 
review.” Am. Integrity Ins. v. Estrada , 276 So. 3d 905, 911 n.13 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2019) (citation omitted).  
“A motion for a directed verdict shall state the specific 
grounds therefor. ”  Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.480(a).  In pursuing directed 
verdict, “the movant admits the truth of all evidentiary facts, as 
well as every reasonable conclusion or inference favorable to the 
opposing party from those facts.”  Dolgen Corp, LLC v. Doty , 383 
So. 3d  864, 866 (Fla. 5th DCA 2024) (citation modified).  “Directed 
verdict is proper only when the evidence, viewed in the light most 
favorable to the non -moving party, shows that a jury could not 
reasonably differ about the existence of a material fact and the

citations.quote:
7 movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.”  Id. (citation 
modified).  “If there are conflicts in the evidence or if different 
reasonable inferences could be drawn from the evidence, then the 
issue is a factual one that should be submitted to the jury and not 
be decided by the trial court as a matter of  law.” Id. (citation 
omitted ). 
FIGA moved for directed verdict on Coverage C damages 
arguing  that, based on the evidence presented , these damages 
would be “purely speculative.”  FIGA assert ed that Florio could not 
establish these damages because  he had failed to submit a 
complete inventory of the damaged contents of his home.   It was 
“based on the argument for lack of a proper inventory in evidence ” 
that the court granted directed verdict as to the personal property . 
However,  because Florio paid an additional premium to insure 
his personal property for its replacement  value —rather than the 
actual cash value3—he did not need to admit evidence beyond proof 
of ownership of damaged property and the associated replacement

293 So. 3d 19, 20 (Fla. 4th DCA 2020) (“An owner of property may 
testify as to its value.”); Reliance Ins. v. Pro -Tech Conditioning & 
Heating , 866 So. 2d  700, 701 (Fla. 5th DCA 2003) (“Florida and 
other jurisdictions permit an owner to testify as to property 
damages and value.”) .  While the defense later argued that there 
was no evidence or testimony regarding  who created the lists, the 
emails were not authenticated, and Florio’s handwritten 
valuations were not substantiated, these objections were waived 
when it stipulated to its admission  without limitation.  See                 
§ 90.107, Fla. Stat. (“When evidence that is admissible as to one 
party or for one purpose, but inadmissible as to another party or 
for another purpose, is admitted, the court, upon request, shall 
 
3.  Personal property insured for actual cash value accounts

364 So. 3d 1121, 1122 (Fla. 6th DCA 2023).

8 restrict such evidence to its proper scope and so inform the jury at 
the time it is admitted. ” (emphasis added) ); see also Rich v. Rich , 
337 So. 3d 138, 148 (Fla. 2d  DCA 2022) (“This stipulation was 
binding and resulted in the waiver of the Former Wife’s obligation 
to lay a foundation for admission and authentication of these 
records.”); Adamson v. R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. , 325 So. 3d 887, 
900 (Fla. 4th DCA 2021) (“Hearsay received without objection 
becomes part of the evidence in the case and is usable as proof just 
as any other evidence, limited only by its rational, persuasive 
power.”  (citation modified)).  
“Because the trial court appropriately received these records 
into evidence, it could not summarily disregard them without even 
considering their substance.”  Rich , 337 So. 3d at 148; see Dortch 
v. State , 137 So. 3d 1173, 1176 (Fla. 1st DCA 2014) (“A stipulation 
cannot be impeached or swept aside merely by the bald statement 
of a party desiring to renege.” (citation modified)); see also Eagle 
FL VI SPE, LLC v. T & A Fam. P’ship, Ltd. , 177 So. 3d 1277, 1280 
(Fla. 2d  DCA 2015) (“The general rule is that a party will be 
relieved from a stipulation entered into under a mistake as to a 
material fact, if there has been reasonable diligence exercised to 
ascertain such fact.  On the other hand, if a party enters into an 
agreement, not as a result of a mistake of fact, but merely due to a 
lack of full knowledge of the facts, caused by the party’s failure to 
exercise due diligence to ascertain them, there is no proper ground 
for relief.” (citation modified)).  
The stipulated admission of Florio’s  content list in Exhibit 15, 
alongside his testimony  and other evidence,  presented sufficient 
support  for a jury to find  some —though perhaps  not all —of his 
claimed personal property damages.4  See Homeowners Choice 
 
4.  Additionally, the defense admitted a professional inventory 
as Defendant’s Exhibit 8  before  Florio rested.  See Padgett v. State , 
53 So. 2d 106, 109 (Fla. 1951) (“Although the trial court has some 
discretionary powers in admitting such exhibits out of the regular 
order, such discretion should be rarely exercised and then only 
when special circumstances render it desirable, and such  practice 
should not be encouraged.”).  After moving for directed verdict, 
however, FIGA sought to withdraw the inventory:

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 9
citations.quote:
9 Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. v. Clark , 410 So. 3d 99, 112 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2025) (“A disagreement between the parties as to the scope and 
extent of the damage is resolved by a factfinder.”), review denied , 
No. SC2025 -0871, 2025 WL 2925370 (Fla. Oct. 15, 2025).   Thus, 
the trial court erred in entering directed verdict on this claim.   See 
Weston v. Universal Prop. & Cas. Ins. , 425 So. 3d 638, 642 (Fla. 2d 
DCA 2025) (“A motion for directed verdict should be granted only 
where no view of the evidence, or inferences made therefrom, could 
support a verdict for the nonmoving party.” (citation modified)), 
reh’g denied  (Jan. 8, 2026); Gelsomino v. ACE Am. Ins. , 207 So. 3d  
288, 293 (Fla. 4th DCA 2016) (“A directed verdict is improper if 
any evidence will support a verdict for the non -moving party.” 
(citation modified)).  And FIGA has not shown that the error was 
harmless.  See GEICO Gen. Ins. v. Tsao , 397 So. 3d 1186, 1190 (Fla. 
5th DCA 2024) (“The burden to demonstrate that an error was 
harmless lies with the beneficiary of the error, who must show that 
 
[Defense Counsel]:  That’s -- I said to the 
Judge, when we were doing housekeeping, we 
moved it into an exhibit for us as a housekeeping 
issue because I didn’t think we’d be arguing 
directed verdict on it.  
THE COURT:  So we have it but it’s your 
exhibit.  
[Defense Counsel]:  It’s mine.  I entered it as an 
exhibit prior to lunch so we could move things 
along.  
Though not raised by Florio on appeal, once admitted, this 
inventory could  only be withdrawn with written  leave of the court.  
See Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.450(b) ; cf. § 22:9. Taking evidence , Trawick, 
Fla. Prac. & Proc. § 22:9 (2026 ed.) (“The defending party must be 
careful in introducing evidence out of order not to jeopardize a 
motion for directed verdict or dismissal at the close of the plaintiff’s 
or petitioner’s case.”) .  No written leave was sought or obtained  
and yet the inventory was excised from the record.   This inventory 
would have added further support for Florio’s claim.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 10
citations.quote:
10 there is no reasonable possibility that the error contributed to the 
verdict.”).  
B. FIGA’s Statutory  Cap 
The trial court’s order granting a motion in limine is reviewed 
for abuse of discretion except as limited by the rules of evidence.  
Tsao , 397 So. 3d at 1188.  “A trial court abuses its discretion if its 
ruling is based on an erroneous view of the law or on a clearly 
erroneous assessment of the evidence.”  Id. (citation modified).  
Statutory construction is reviewed de novo.  Id. 
 
FIGA is  only obligated to pay up to $500,000 for covered 
homeowners’ insurance claims.  § 631.57(1)(a)2., Fla. Stat.   
However, as conceded by FIGA, this statutory cap on its obligation 
to pay covered claims for insolvent insurers  does not prohibit the 
insured  from presenting evidence as to the full extent of his 
damages.  Cf. Jones v. FIGA , 908 So. 2d 435, 438 (Fla. 2005) (noting 
FIGA’s duty “to defend a claim against an insured party is 
identical  to that of the insolvent insurer” (emphasis added)); id. at 
453 (noting FIGA’s statutory cap “becomes applicable only if 
FIGA’s  obligation would otherwise exceed that amount”).  That the 
cap operates a s a post-verdict ceiling tracks with other areas of 
Florida law.  See, e.g. , State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. v. Hudnall , 416 
So. 3d 370, 371 (Fla. 5th DCA 2025) (“Before litigating a first -party 
bad faith claim in an uninsured motorist case, an insured is 
entitled to a jury determination of liability and the full extent of 
his or her damages, which may be in excess of the policy limits.” 
(citation modified)); S. Broward Topeekeegeeyugnee  Park Dist. v. 
Martin , 564 So. 2d 1265, 1267 (Fla. 4th DCA 1990) (“[T]he mere 
fact the legislative act places a cap upon the amount of damages 
recoverable against the governmental entity does not affect the 
plaintiff’s right to a judgment for his full damages.” (quoting 
Gerard v. Dep ’t of Transp. , 472 So. 2d 1170, 1173 (Fla. 1985))).  
 
Because Florio should have been allowed to present evidence 
of damages exceeding FIGA’s statutory cap, the trial court erred in 
granting the motion in limine.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 11
citations.quote:
11 Conclusion  
 
Because the trial court erred in granting directed verdict  on 
the contents claim and in limiting Florio’s evidence of damages to 
$500,000 , we reverse the directed verdict on the personal property 
claim, vacate the order granting FIGA’s motion in limine, and 
remand for further proceedings.  
  
ORDER VACATED ; REVERSED ; and REMANDED  for further 
proceedings . 
 
BOATWRIGHT and  MACIVER, JJ., concur . 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
_____________________________  
 
Not final until disposition of any timely and 
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 
9.331 . 
_____________________________

items.summary:
Holding: Owner testimony, receipts, photographs and a contents list admitted by stipulation supplied enough evidence of some replacement-cost personal-property damages to defeat directed verdict. Evidentiary objections waived by the stipulation could not justify disregarding the admitted material. FIGA’s statutory payment cap did not limit the evidence of total loss that could be presented. The court separately upheld denial of continuances.
Disposition: Personal-property directed verdict reversed; damages-limiting order vacated; remanded for further proceedings.
Author: Judge Kilbane. Boatwright and MacIver concur.
