citations.quote:
FIRST DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
No. 1D2 025-2106  
_____________________________  
 
FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF 
CHILDREN AND FAMILIES , 
 
Appellant,  
 
v. 
 
JOHN L. GAINEY , as Personal 
Representative of the Estate of 
Nazariah Brown;  WORLD WIDE 
WEBB, LLC;  RAPHEAL WEBB, 
individually;  LATORIA 
SINGLETON , individually;  
GABRIEL WOODS , individually;  
CRANDALL MEDICAL 
CONSULTING , LLC;  and  
BRAANDON DAVIS, individually,  
 
Appellee s. 
_____________________________  
 
 On appeal from the Circuit Court for Alachua County.  
Gloria R. Walker, Judge.  
 
October 7, 2026  
 
B
ILBREY , J.  
 
The Florida Department of Children and Families appeals the 
nonfinal order denying its motion for summary judgment.  The 
Department asserted that it was entitled to judgment as a matter 
of law since sovereign immunity was not waived for the alleg ations

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 of negligence in the third amended complaint.  Because the trial 
court applied the incorrect law to deny summary judgment, the 
order on appeal is reversed with instructions that summary final 
judgment be entered for the Department.1  
“Because of the separation of powers principles that animate 
the doctrine, and because it provides both immunity from suit and 
immunity from liability, the Florida Supreme Court instructs that 
‘entitlement to sovereign immunity should be established as early 
in the litigation as possible.’ ”  Fla. Virtual Sch. v. Calfee, 425 So. 3d 
78, 82 (Fla. 6th DCA 2025) (quoting Fla. Highway Patrol v. 
Jackson, 288 So. 3d 1179, 1185 (Fla. 2020) ).  An order denying a 
motion for summary judgment based on sovereign immunity is 
reviewed de novo.  Id.; see also Nocco v. Wilcox, 414 So. 3d 302, 305 
(Fla. 2d DCA 2025).  “[C]ertain ‘discretionary’ governmental 
functions remain immune from tort liability. . . .  Identifying these 
functions is done primarily by distinguishing, through a case-by -
case analysis, the ‘planning’ and ‘operational’ levels of decision-
making by governmental agencies.”  Dep’t of Health & Rehab. 
Servs. v. B.J.M., 656 So. 2d 906, 911 (Fla. 1995)  (footnotes omitted) 
(quoting Com. Carrier Corp. v. Indian River Cnty., 371 So. 2d 1010,  
1022  (Fla. 1979) ).  
 
Nazariah Brown was a young adult man with complex 
medical needs.  He lived with his mother and other family 
members until August 2022 when the family lost the lease to their 
home.  The Department became involved with Mr. Brown in May 2022 at his mother’s request since he needed services and his 
mother knew their housing situation was precarious.  Over the 
several months between May and August 2022, efforts of the 
mother and the Department to locate suitable housing were 
unsuccessful.  The impending loss of the family’s leased residence  
caused an emergency and, to keep Mr. Brown from becoming 
homeless, Department personnel placed Mr. Brown in the only facility they could find that agreed to accept him.  A few days after 
 
1 The nonfinal order on appeal is reviewable under rule 
9.130(a)(3)(F)(iii), Florida Rules of Civil Procedure, because it 
denies a motion that “asserts entitlement to sovereign immunity.”

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 this placement, the Agency for Persons with Disabilities assumed 
responsibility for Mr. Brown’s services.  
While Mr. Brown remained at the facility under the Agency’s 
placement, the Department received two central abuse hotline 
reports.  See § 415.103, Fla. Stat. (2022)  (establishing central 
abuse hotline for reporting abuse, neglect, or exploitation of a 
vulnerable adult).  The reports were investigated by Department 
personnel in the Department’s Adult Protective Services  (APS) 
office, and both cases were eventually closed as “unsubstantiated.”     
In his four-count third amended complaint, John L. Gainey, 
as personal representative of the estate of Mr. Brown, alleged that 
the Department was liable for monetary damages caused by the 
negligence of its employees who acted within the scope of their 
employment.2  In count I, Gainey alleged three bas es for the 
Department’s negligence .  His first allegation was negligence  by 
failing to train and supervise its APS unit staff, resulting in the 
improper protective supervision of Mr. Brown.  See 
§ 415.1051(4) (a), Fla. Stat. (allowing the Department to provide 
protective services with “consent from the caregiver or guardian”).  His second allegation was that the Department was liable for 
failing to supervise APS staff who negligently placed Mr. Brown in 
 
2 The initial complaint was brought by Gainey as Mr. Brown’s 
guardian.  During the litigation, Mr. Brown died and Gainey was substituted as the personal representative of his estate.  Gainey 
alleged both a survival action to the extent that the negligence did 
not cause Mr. Brown’s death and a wrongful death if it did.  Counts 
II, III, and IV of the third amended complaint were dismissed with 
prejudice after the parties stipulated that the three named 
employees were immune from individual liability per section 
768.28(9), Florida Statutes.   Whether  sovereign immunity applies 
to the allegations in count I against the Department is the only 
issue before us.  Because we only have jurisdiction in this nonfinal 
appeal to address the sovereign immunity issue, we do not consider  
the Department’s argument  before the trial court that the third 
amended complaint improperly combined multiple causes of action 
into one count.   See Smith v. Lee, 51 Fla. L. Weekly D1009, D1010, 
2026 WL 1407947, *2 (Fla. 1st DCA May 20, 2026).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 a facility that did not meet  his complex medical needs.  Gainey’s 
third allegation in count I was negligent investigation and closure  
of reports of injury to Mr. Brown.   
On appeal, Gainey concedes that his negligent training and 
negligent supervision claims against the Department are barred 
by sovereign immunity.  We accept this concession.  See Nocco, 414 
So. 3d at 305 (citations omitted) (holding that sovereign immunity 
bars negligent training claims that are based on what subjects to train and how to train those subjects since those issues entail the  
exercise of discretion); Cook ex rel. Est. of Tessier v. Sheriff of 
Monroe Cnty., 402 F.3d 1092, 1117– 19 (11th Cir. 2005) (holding  
that claims targeting the organizational structure and regulatory 
oversight of a government agency inappropriately require the 
judiciary to review policy decisions constitutionally reserved for 
the political branches).  Thus, Gainey has abandoned the negligent 
training and supervision claims against the Department for 
purposes of further proceedings.   
The remaining allegation against the Department in count I 
of the third amended complaint was a claim of negligence by the 
Department due to APS staff members’ investigation and 
premature closure of the two hotline reports received in September 
2022 and October 2022.   These allegations claimed violation of the 
Department’s statutory and common law duties “to properly 
investigate and to take appropriate action to protect” Mr. Brown.  Specifically, the third amended complaint alleged, “At all times 
material, Defendant DCF also had the common law and statutory 
obligations to respond to and investigate calls of abuse or neglect 
of vulnerable adults, and to make sure that it and its personnel took action to remove vulnerable adults from situations where 
their needs and rights were not being provided for.”  As explained 
below, t hese allegations are also subject to sovereign immunity.    
Following the summary judgment hearing held in July 2025, 
the trial court found “there are too many disputed issues of fact 
involving the issue of negligence” to enter summary judgment.  
The court listed many disputed facts about the Department’s provision of services to Mr. Brown, beginning in May 2022 and 
culminating in his placement on an “emergency” basis i n August  
2022.  The court also listed the disputed issues of fact about the

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 two hotline calls received in September and October 2022, and APS 
staff members’ handling and ultimate closure of the cases.  
The trial court concluded that “based on the record evidence, 
sovereign immunity does not apply.”  In its oral pronouncement of 
its ruling, the court stated that “given how many facts are in 
dispute, it’s unclear . . . whether or not sovereign immunity would 
apply because it’s unclear . . . whether or not, based on the facts as 
alleged, DCF did anything wrong.”  The court made no ruling on 
whether the Department’s actions as alleged in  the third amended 
complaint were planning or operational functions.  Additionally, 
the court made no findings that the Department’s sovereign 
immunity was waived under section 768.28, Florida Statues, by any provision in chapter 415, Florida Statutes, or any other 
legislative enactment.   
The trial court misapplied the law when it denied summary 
judgment by treating sovereign immunity as an issue of fact.  
Sovereign immunity is a threshold legal question for the court, not 
a fact question for the jury.  Fla. Dep’t of Corr. v. Campbell, 417 
So. 3d 479 (Fla. 1st DCA 2025) (reversing denial of motion to 
dismiss complaint; classification and assignment of prisoners 
within prison system are discretionary, planning-level decisions to 
which waiver of sovereign immunity does not apply).  “Sovereign 
immunity is the rule, not the exception, and a waiver of sovereign 
immunity must be unequivocal and will not be found by inference.” Univ. of Fla. Bd. of Trs. v. Browning, 387 So. 3d 371, 376 (Fla. 1st 
DCA 2024).   
Immunity, and the limited waiver of sovereign immunity 
under section 768.28, Florida Statutes, are threshold bars to suit 
to be determined independently from “outstanding disputes about 
the existence of a duty of care.”  Fla. Highway Patrol v. Jackson, 288 So. 3d 1179, 1185 (Fla. 2020 ).  It is the nature of the conduct 
challenged, not proof of the facts alleged, that determines whether 
immunity is waived.  Trianon Park Condo. Ass’n, Inc. v. City of 
Hialeah, 468 So. 2d 912, 918 (Fla. 1985).  
“The immunity of the State of Florida and its agencies from 
liability for claims arising under Florida law or common law is 
absolute absent a clear, specific, and unequivocal waiver 
by legislative enactment.”  Dep’t Highway Safety & Motor Vehicles

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 v. Hightower, 306 So. 3d 1193, 1199 –1200 (Fla. 1st DCA 2020) 
(quoting  State, Dep’t of Elder Affs.  v. Caldwell, 199 So. 3d 1107, 
1109 (Fla. 1st DCA 2016) ).  As we held in Caldwell, sovereign 
immunity is not waived under section 768.28 for “statutory 
claims.”  199 So. 3d at 1110.  To the extent that the claims of negligence against the Department depends on its alleg ations of 
failure to properly handle the hotline calls under chapter 415, 
Florida Statutes, a waiver by section 768.28 cannot be assumed or 
inferred.  See Trianon Park Condo. Ass’n, 468 So. 2d at 919 –920 
(holding that enforcement of laws and conducting investigations of 
alleged violations of the law are discretionary functions).   
As for the common law allegations involving negligent 
investigation by the Department, sovereign immunity also applies  
to those allegations.  “A plaintiff suing a governmental entity in 
tort must, therefore, allege and prove that the governmental entity 
owed a duty of care to the plaintiff individually rather than to the 
public in general.”  Miami-Dade Cnty. v. Fente, 949 So. 2d 1101, 
1103 (Fla. 3d DCA 2007) .  “[I]n the absence of a special relationship 
between the individual and the governmental entity, a common 
law duty is not owed to the victim of a criminal offense, even 
though the offense might have been prevented through reasonable 
law enforcement.”  Sams v. Oelrich, 717 So. 2d 1044, 1047 (Fla. 1st 
DCA 1998).   
 
Furthermore, to the extent that the third amended complaint 
alleged that by selecting the placement for Mr. Brown, the 
Department had a special relationship with him and owed him a 
duty beyond that owed to the general public, such placement 
decisions are also subject to sovereign immunity.  See Campbell, 
417 So. 3d at 483 (holding that the classification and assignment 
of persons in the custody of the State were “discretionary, 
planning-level decisions”).  
 
As the Florida Supreme Court has stated: 
 
HRS [the Department’s predecessor agency] is vested 
with broad discretion in exercising its placement 
authority.  For this reason, we believe the placement 
function constituted a “discretionary planning or

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 judgmental function” entitled to immunity even if 
considered as a category IV function.  
 
We also believe the same immunity accorded to 
placement decisions applies to the discretionary decisions 
made by HRS in allocating services to dependents and 
delinquents under the statutory scheme mandated by the 
legislature.  This scheme provides the same broad 
discretion for allocating services as for placement 
decisions. 
 
B.J.M., 656 So. 2d at  913 (citation omitted).3 
 
Because the trial court applied an incorrect standard to 
conclude that “sovereign immunity does not apply,” the order 
denying the Department’s motion for summary judgment is 
reversed.  Sovereign immunity applies to the claims against the Department and summary final judgment must be entered for the 
Department. 
R
EVERSED  with instructions.     
M.K.  THOMAS and  LONG, JJ.,  concur. 
 
_____________________________ 
 
Not final until disposition of any timely and 
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 
9.331. 
_____________________________ 
 
 
Kathryn L. Ender, Ravika R. Marcadis, and Janice Lopez of 
Dinsmore & Shohl LLP, Miami, for Appellant. 
 
3 A category IV function is a “governmental function or 
activity” involving the provision of “professional, education al, and 
general services for the health and welfare of the citizens.”  B.J.M., 
656 So. 2d at 911 (citing Trianon Park  Condo. Ass’n, 468 So. 2d at 
919–21).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8  
David A. Paul, Christine V. Zharvo, and Debora S. Antisdel of Paul Trial Group, Winter Park; Alexis S. Gay and Valentina V. 
Villalobos of Elite Child Advocacy, PLLC, Tampa; Karen Gievers, 
Tallahassee, for Appellee John L. Gainey.

items.summary:
Holding: Disputes about negligence did not themselves resolve the threshold legal sovereign-immunity issue. The court held the pleaded training, supervision, placement and hotline-investigation claims barred and required judgment for DCF; training and supervision were also conceded on appeal. Review did not extend to the separate pleading-joinder objection.
Disposition: Reversed with instructions to enter summary final judgment for DCF.

on an emergency basis.  In August 2022, the Agency for Persons 
with Disabilities (APD) assumed responsibility for Mr. Brown’s 
services under chapter 393, Florida Statutes (2022) .3     
In his amended complaint, Gainey alleged that Crandall 
Medical “served as an APD-licensed medical consulting group” 
responsible for assessing Mr. Brown’s needs, preparing a waiver 
support coordination plan, and monitoring service providers of Mr. Brown’s services.  See  § 393.0651, Fla. Stat.  And Gainey alleged 
that Davis was the Crandall Medical employee responsible for 
preparing Mr. Brown’s waiver support plan and taking actions necessary to protect Mr. Brown’s safety and well-being.  Crandall 
Medical and Davis  admitted the  allegations.  But according to 
Gainey’s amended complaint, Crandall Medical and Davis failed 
their duties to provide Mr. Brown with a waiver support coordination plan, failed to monitor Mr. Brown’s condition, failed to see that Mr. Brown’s needs were met, and failed to transfer Mr. 
Brown to a facility able to meet his needs.  
Count 10 of the a mended complaint alleged that Davis’s 
performance or non- performance of the Medicare Waiver Services 
for Mr. Brown violated Mr. Brown’s rights under section 393.13, Florida Statutes (“The Bill of Rights of Persons with Developmental Disabilities”) and subjected Davis to liability under 
section 393.13(5), Florida Statutes.  In count 11, Gainey alleged 
that Crandall Medical was vicariously liable, under section 
393.13(5), for the negligence of its employees resulting from the 
violation of Mr. Brown’s rights under section 393.13(3) and (4).  
And in count 12, Gainey alleged that Crandall Medical  was 
negligent in hiring, training, and supervising its employees and 
 
3 APD is an agency “housed within the Department of 
Children and Families for administrative purposes only.”  § 20.197,  
Fla. Stat.   APD is responsible for “providing all services provided 
to persons with developmental disabilities under chapter 393, including the operation of all state institutional programs . . . 
established to provide services to persons with developmental 
disabili ties.”  § 20.197(3), Fla. Stat.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 breached its independent duty to ensure that a proper waiver 
support plan for Mr. Brown was in place.   
Section 768.28(9)(a), Florida Statutes, states: 
An officer, employee, or agent of the state or of any 
of its subdivisions may not be held personally liable in 
tort or named as a party defendant in any action for any 
injury or damage suffered as a result of any act, event, or 
omission of action in the scope of her or his employment 
or function, unless such officer, employee, or agent acted 
in bad faith or with malicious purpose or in a manner 
exhibiting wanton and willful disregard of human rights, 
safety, or property. 
But the amended complaint contained no allegations that Crandall 
Medical or Davis acted in bad faith or with malicious purpose or in 
a manner exhibiting wanton and willful disregard of human rights, 
safety, or property.  
Crandall Medical and Davis pleaded their entitlement to 
sovereign immunity under section 768.28(9)(a) , Florida Statutes, 
as an affirmative defense.  In their joint motion for summary 
judgment, they asserted that they were entitled to judgment as a 
matter of law as agents of the State of Florida, acting in the scope 
of their function as contractors performing essential governmental 
functions under the control or direction of APD.  See §§ 393.0651,  
.066, .0663, Fla. Stat.  As agents of State acting through APD, 
Appellants argued that sovereign immunity under section 
768.28(9)(a)  rendered them immune from suit for their acts or 
omissions in providing support coordination services under Florida 
Medicaid Waiver programs.   
To support their motion, Crandall Medical  and Davis 
submitted the transcripts of the depositions of both Daniel 
Crandall, owner and founder of the company, and Davis.  The 
depositions established that they were assigned by APD to Mr. 
Brown’s case in late October or early November 2022.  Davis 
testified in his deposition that he did not act independently of the 
assignment by APD, and he had no discretion to reject the 
assignment.  And Davis stated that he provided case coordination 
only to people referred by APD, used APD forms and templates,

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 completed APD certification and training, and reported his 
activities through a platform monitored by APD.   
Gainey did not contest these facts about the process for 
assignment of and control over the APD services by Crandall 
Medical and Davis.  Instead, to contest their status as agents of 
APD for purposes of section 768.28(9) (a), Gainey presented the 
Medicaid Waiver Services Agreement signed by Davis and an APD representative in November 2018.  Paragraph II.G. of that 
Agreement provided that  Davis acted “as an independent service 
provider” and “ not as an officer, employee, or agent of APD.”     
After hearing the parties’ arguments, the trial court stated 
that “there are just way too many facts in dispute here to grant” 
the motion.  In its written order, the circuit court found:  
[T]here are too many disputed issues of material facts, 
including, but not limited to, whether the Agency for 
Persons with Disabilities (“APD”) controlled Crandall 
and Davis, whether all services provided by Crandall and 
Davis were approved by APD, whether all statutory 
requirements were fulfilled, whether Crandall and Davis operated independently from APD, and whether, given 
the facts of this case, the exceptions to sovereign immunity apply.  
Considering the record materials submitted by the parties in 
support and in opposition to summary judgment under rule 
1.510(c), ( e)(2), Florida Rules of Civil Procedure, the trial court 
applied an incorrect l egal standard to deny summary judgment.  
Whether the party being contracted with is an agent of the 
state turns on the degree of control retained or exercised by the state agency.  Stoll v. Noel, 694 So. 2d 701, 703 (Fla. 1997).  When 
analyzing the issue of control, the focus should be on “the right to 
control, not the actual control . . . .”  Villazon v. Prudential Health 
Care Plan, Inc., 843 So. 2d 842, 846 (Fla. 2003).   In a summary 
judgment proceeding, “[i]f a party fails to . . . properly address 
another party’s assertion of fact” under rule 1.510(c)(2), “the court 
may . . . consider the fact undisputed for purposes of the motion.”  
Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.510(e).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 “Agency status may be decided as a question of law in those 
cases where the party opposing summary judgment is unable to 
point to any conflicting facts or inferences to be drawn from the 
facts.”  Lovelace v. G4S Secure Sols. (USA), Inc. , 320 So. 3d 178, 
188 (Fla. 4th DCA 2021)  (citations omitted).  Appellants submitted 
their depositions supporting their claim to immunity under section 
768.28(9)(a) as agents of APD and the degree of control APD 
retained over their assignment and provision of services.  Gainey’s 
opposition was based only on the language of the Medicaid Waiver 
Services Agreement, and he did not contest the depositions 
submitted by Appellants asserting the facts demonstrating APD’s 
control.  For purposes of the Appellants’ immunity due to their 
status as agents of APD, the contract provision did not preclude 
Appellants’ status as agents under section 768.28(9).  “An ‘express 
intent regarding agency status is to be considered in deciding the 
issue, but is not dispositive. ’”  Lovelace, 320 So. 3d at 188 ( quoting 
G4S Secure Sols. (USA), Inc. v. Morrow, 210 So. 3d 92, 9 4 (Fla. 2d 
DCA 2016)).  “[A]though ‘express intent regarding agency status is 
to be considered in deciding the issue’ of control, ‘it is not 
dispositive.’”  Morrow , 210 So. 3d at 94.  
Gainey’s reliance on the contractual provision making 
Appellants “independent service providers” did not negate 
Appellants’ deposition evidence of the degree of APD’s control over 
their services.  In discussing independent contractors, the Florida 
Supreme Court in Stoll v. Noel stated that “they are not precluded 
from being agents of the state– thereby entitling them to statutory 
immunity from suit and liability  as provided by section 768.28, 
Florida Statutes.”  694 So. 2d at 703.  The trial court’s finding 
disputed issues of “whether the Agency for Persons with 
Disabilities (“APD”) controlled Crandall Medical  and Davis, 
whether all services provided by Crandall Medical and Davis were 
approved by APD” and “whether Crandall and Davis operated independently from APD, ” was unsupported by any admissible 
evidence  submitted by Gainey.  See Fla. R Civ. P. 1.510(c).  The 
facts of APD’s control established by the depositions submitted by 
Appellants were undisputed for purposes of the motion for 
summary judgment.  Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.510(e)(2).   
Gainey did not dispute that APD is a state agency, that 
Crandall Medical  was a certified service provider for APD with no

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 other business than that assigned and supervised by APD, and 
that Davis was an employee of APD.  Under the law as provided by section 768.28(9)(a) and explained by Lovelace v. G4S Secure 
Sols. (USA), Inc. , 320 So. 3d at  188, Appellants were entitled to 
summary judgment as a matter of law on their sovereign immunity  
defense.   See also Naso v. Hall, 338 So. 3d 283 , 287  (Fla. 4th DCA 
2021) .
4    
The order on appeal is reversed with instructions to enter 
summary judgment for the A ppellants.   
REVERSED with instructions.  
M.K.  THOMAS and  LONG, JJ.,  concur.  
 
_____________________________  
 
Not final until disposition of any timely and 
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 
9.331.  
_____________________________  
 
 
 
4 To the extent that Naso and various other cases would apply 
section 768.28(2) and (5) to allow only limited sovereign immunity 
to a corporation rather than absolute immunity under section 
768.28(9), those cases do not apply to Crandall Medical.  Crandall 
Medical is a Florida limited liability company operating under 
chapter 621, Florida Statutes.  The limited sovereign immunity in 
section 768.28(5) applies to “[t]he state and its agencies and 
subdivisions.”  Section 768.28(2) defines “state agencies or 
subdivisions” to include “corporations primarily acting as 
instrumentalities or agencies of the state, counties, or 
municipalities.”  But an LLC such as Crandall Medical is not a 
corporation under Florida law.  See generally chapter 607, Florida 
Statutes; see also  § 607.01401(5), Fla. Stat. (separating 
corporations from LLC); Olmstead v. F.T.C., 44 So. 3d 76, 78 –80 
(Fla. 2010) (explaining LLCs and distinguishing them from 
corporations).

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8 Rogelio J. Fontela and Jessica E. Keeler of Dennis, Jackson, 
Martin, & Fontela, P.A., Tallahassee, for Appellants.  
 
David A. Paul, Christine V. Zharvo, and Debora S. Antisdel of Paul 
Trial Group, Winter Park; Alexis S. Gay and Valentina V. Villalobos of Elite Child Advocacy, PLLC, Tampa; Karen Gievers, 
Tallahassee, for Appellee John L. Gainey.

items.summary:
Holding: Uncontroverted evidence of the agency’s right of control established state-agent immunity under section 768.28(9)(a) on this summary-judgment record. The contract’s independent-provider label was relevant but not dispositive. The complaint did not allege the statutory bad-faith, malicious-purpose or wanton-and-willful exception. The opinion distinguishes the LLC from a corporation for its statutory-immunity analysis.
Disposition: Reversed with instructions to enter summary judgment for Crandall Medical and Davis.
Author: Judge Bilbrey. M.K. Thomas and Long concur.
Official opinion retrieved October 12, 2026; issuance date stated in document and index. Any printed rehearing or revision qualification is preserved; subsequent docket finality and treatment not independently verified.
Recorded discrepancy: Pages 1 and 3 identify Davis as Crandall Medical’s employee; page 7 says he was an employee of APD. Both statements are retained without resolving the employer discrepancy.

citations.quote:
Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  October 7, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D25 -0817  
Lower Tribunal No. 18-591-CP-02 
________________  
 
 
Pauline Walters, as Personal Representative for the Estate of 
Enid May Townsend , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Agency for Healthcare Administration , 
Appellee.  
 
 An Appeal from  a non -final order from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Bertila Soto , Judge.  
 
 Law Office of Dexter F. George, and Dexter F. George (Plantation) , for 
appellant.  
 
 Alexander R. Boler (Tallahassee) , for appellee.  
 
 
Before  LOGUE, LINDSEY, and GOODEN , JJ.  
 
 LOGUE, J.  
Pauline Walters, as Personal Representative for the Estate of Enid

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 2
citations.quote:
2 May Townsend , appeals a trial court order that held a cooperative unit was 
not real property and therefore was not protected  by the Florida 
Constitution’s homestead provisions from forced sale to satisfy debts to a 
creditor  of the Estate.  We held as much when this case was previously 
before us. Walters v. Agency for Health Care Admin. , 288 So. 3d 1215, 1218 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2019) . Subsequently, however, in 2021, the Florida Legislature 
amended section 719.103(25), Florida Statutes (2021) , to provide that an 
interest in a cooperative unit is an interest in real property. The issue in this 
appeal is whether the 2021 amendment to section 719.103(25) applies 
retroactively to the date of  Enid May Townsend’s (“Decedent”) death. The 
trial court held that the amendment did not apply retroactively. We affirm.  
BACKGROUND  
The Decedent died intestate on August 29, 2017. The Decedent’s sole 
heir was her daughter, Pauline Walter s. On February 8, 2018, Walters filed 
a petition for summary administration of the Decedent’s estate. The estate’s 
only asset was the Decedent’s  interest in a cooperative unit , which Walters 
proposed be distributed to herself as protected homestead property .  
On March 21, 2018, the Agency for Health Care Administration (the 
“Agency”) filed a statement of claim against the  Decedent’s  estate for 
$81,276.76 . This amount represented  the Decedent’s debt that resulted from

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 3
citations.quote:
3 her acceptance of Medicaid benefits from the Agency. See §§ 409.910 1, 
414.28 , Fla. Stat. (20 18). 
The following day, on March 22, 2018, Walters filed a petition to 
determine homestead status of the Cooperative Unit. In the petition, Walters 
described the Cooperative Unit as “Cooperative Stock, 16900 NW 14th 
Avenue, Apt. 203, North Miami Beach, FL 33162 .” Walters argued “[t]he 
Property constituted the homestead of the decedent within the meaning of 
Section 4 of Article X of the Constitution of the State of Florida,” and, 
therefore, title to the Cooperative Unit passed to Walters upon the 
Decedent’s death  and the constitutional exemption from claims of the 
Decedent ’s creditors —in this case, the Agency —also inured to Walters’ 
benefit at that time.    
In response, the Agency filed an objection to the Homestead Status 
Petition and argued the Cooperative Unit was not entitled to the homestead 
exemption because it was “not a fee simple interest in land as required by 
law.”   
On June 21, 2018, following a hearing, the trial court entered the 2018 
Homestead Status Order, stating that “the Petition to Declare Decedent’s 
CO-OP Property Homestead for the purpose of descent and distribution is 
denied,” citing, in part, to In re Estate  of Wartel s, 357 So. 2d 708 (Fla. 1978) .

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 4
citations.quote:
4 Walters then appealed th e order to this Court . We affirmed the order  but 
certified to the  Florida  Supreme Court , as one of great public importance , the 
question of whether Wartels  had continuing effect . We also certified conflict 
with Geraci v. Sunstar EMS , 93 So. 3d 384 (Fla. 2d DCA 2012). See Walters , 
288 So. 3d at 1218.  
The Florida Supreme Court accepted jurisdiction to review this Court’s 
decision. See Walters v. Agency for Health Care Admin. , No. SC20 -12, 2020 
WL 3494393 (Fla.  June 29, 2020). While the Florida Supreme Court’s case 
was pending, section 719.103(25), which defined the term “Unit,” was 
amended , see Ch. 2021 -99, § 15, Laws of Fla. , to provide as follows : 
“Unit” means a part of the cooperative property which is subject 
to exclusive use and possession. A unit may be improvements, 
land, or land and improvements together, as specified in the 
cooperative documents. An interest in a unit is an interest in real 
property . 
 
§ 719.103 (25), Fla. Stat . (2021) (emphasis added). The only change 
between the 2017 version of the statute, which was in effect at the time of 
the Decedent’s death, and the amended 2021 version was the addition of 
the last sentence: “A n interest in a unit is an interest in real property. ” § 
719.103 (25), Fla. Stat . (2021). The Chapter Law enacting the amendment 
was signed into law on June 16, 2021, and t he Legislature made the 
amendment effective July 1, 2021. Ch. 2021 -99, § 27, Laws of Fla.

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 5
citations.quote:
5 Following this amendment, on June 23, 2021, the Florida Supreme 
Court discharged its jurisdiction and declined review. See Walters v. Agency 
for Health Care Admin. , No. SC20 -12, 2021 WL 2562698 (Fla. June 23, 
2021) . Thereafter, on June 30, 2021, this Court issued its mandate, which 
stated that “ such further proceedings be had in said cause as may be in 
accordance with the opinion of this Court .”  
Walters then filed an amended petition to determine homestead status 
of real property and again argued the  constitutional homestead exemption 
applied to the Cooperative Unit  under the 2021 Amendment . The trial court 
ruled against Walters:   
The Court finds that the change in law regarding cooperative 
[units]  at section 719.103(25), Florida Statutes (2021), is not 
remedial in nature, and is to be applied only prospectively. The 
Order Denying Petition for Homestead (DIN 21, filed June 21, 
2018) will be upheld.  
 
Walters timely  appeal ed.  
ANALYSIS  
Courts must proceed cautiously when considering whether a statute 
impacting substantive rights applies retroactively.  See, e.g. , Menendez v. 
Progressive Exp ress Ins. Co. , 35 So. 3d 873, 875 (Fla. 2010). “The general 
rule is that in the absence of clear legislative intent to the contrary, a law 
affecting substantive rights, liabilities and duties is presumed to apply

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 6
citations.quote:
6 prospectively.” Metro. Dade Cnty. v. Chase Fed. Hous. Corp. , 737 So. 2d 
494, 499 (Fla. 1999). But “the presumption against retroactivity is only a 
default rule of statutory construction.” Id. at 500. The presumption can be 
“rebutted by clear evidence of legislative intent.” Id. 
The homestead provisions of the Constitution at issue protect 
homestead property from forced sale and bar the owners of homesteaded 
property from devising the property away from their spouse or minor children. 
See Art. X, § 4 (a)(1), Fla. Const.  (“There shall be exempt from forced sale 
under process of any court, and no judgment, decree or execution shall be 
a lien thereon  . . . the following property owned by a natural person:  . . . a 
homestead , if located outside a municipality, to the extent of one hundred 
sixty acres of contiguous land and improvements thereon . . . ; or if located 
within a municipality, to the extent of one -half acre of contiguous land, upon 
which the exemption shall be limited to the residence of the owner or the 
owner ’s family [.]”); Art. X, § 4 (c), Fla. Const.  (“The homestead shall not be 
subject to devise if the owner is survived by spouse or minor child  . . . .”); Art. 
X, § 4 (b), Fla. Const.  (“These exemptions shall inure to the surviving spouse 
or heirs of the owner. ”). 
Thus, the 2021 amendment, to the extent it transforms cooperative 
units  into real property  protected as homestead, impacts the substantive

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 7
citations.quote:
7 rights of diverse parties. The amendment expands the rights of owners and 
heirs of such property to be free from forced sale while commensurately 
diminishing the rights of their creditors to be paid. As importantly, it expands 
the rights of spouses and min or children to inherit while commensurately 
diminishing the rights of the owners to freely devise. These impacts on 
substantive rights trigger “the presumption against retroactivity.” Metro. Dade 
Cnty. , 737 So. 2d at 500.   
In the face of this presumption, we find little evidence of the 
Legislature’s intent that the 2021 amendment  should  apply retroactively. The 
Chapter Law enacting the amendment was signed into law on June 16, 2021, 
and the Legislature provided a future effective date: “This act shall take effect 
July 1, 2021.” Ch. 2021 -99, § 27, Laws of Fla.  At no point , either in the text 
of the 2021 amendment or in the Chapter Law enacting the amendment, 
does the Legislature state the amendment will take effect retroactively.  
We acknowledge that the “presumption in favor of prospective 
application generally does not apply to ‘remedial’ legislation;  rather, 
whenever possible, such legislation should be applied to pending cases in 
order to fully effectuate the legislation ’s intended purpose.”  Smiley v. State , 
966 So. 2d 330, 334 (Fla. 2007)  (quoting Arrow Air, Inc. v. Walsh , 645 So. 
2d 422, 424 (Fla. 1994)) . But, such statutes are recognized as remedial

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 8
citations.quote:
8 because they relate only “ to remedies or modes of procedure , which do not 
create new or take away vested rights, but only operate in furtherance of the 
remedy or confirmation of rights already existing [.]” Smiley , 966 So. 2d at 
334 (quoting City of Lakeland v. Catinella , 129 So. 2d 133, 136 (Fla. 1961)).  
At no point, does the Legislature characterize the amendment as remedial 
or as a clarification of existing law. Instead, a s mentioned above, the 2021 
amendment substantively impacts the rights of owners, heirs, and creditors 
in terms of forced sale and the rights of owners, spouses, and minor children 
of owners  in terms of devise.  
Finally, we recognize authority exists for the “recent controversy rule” 
of interpretation: “When . . . an amendment to a statute is enacted soon after 
controversies as to the interpretation of the original act arise, a court may 
consider that amendment as a legislative interpretation of the original law 
and not as a substantive change  thereof .” Lowry v. Parole & Prob . Comm ’n, 
473 So. 2d 1248 , 1250  (Fla. 1985) . The sequence of events involving the 
issuance of our prior opinion  that recogniz es this area of the law  might be in 
flux, our certification to the Supreme Court, the Supreme Court taking 
jurisdiction, the Legislature enacting the 2021 amendment directly 
addressing the issue, and the Supreme Court discharging  its jurisdiction, 
admittedly move this case towards the ambit of this rule. However, the

citations.label: flcourts-media.flcourts.gov · PDF page 9
citations.quote:
9 validity of this rule of interpretation has been called into question by the 
Supreme Court and has been rejected by the Second District.  See Ham v. 
Portfolio Recovery Assoc s., LLC , 308 So. 3d 942, 946 -47 (Fla. 2020) ; 
Conage v. United States , 346 So. 3d 594, 598 -99 (Fla. 2022) ; State v. Crose , 
378 So. 3d 1217, 1244 -45 (Fla. 2d DCA 2024) (en banc). In any event, its 
application to these facts do es not change the result given the substantive 
nature of the rights at issue, the Legislature’s directive that the amendment 
have a future effective date, and the absence of any indication the 
Legislature viewed the amendment  as remedial or serving only as a 
clarification.  
Affirmed.

items.summary:
Holding: The 2021 amendment defining a cooperative-unit interest as real property did not apply retroactively to the decedent’s 2017 death. The amendment affected substantive rights of owners, heirs and creditors, carried a future effective date, and supplied no retroactive or remedial instruction. The ruling does not deny the amendment’s prospective effect.
Disposition: Order denying the claimed homestead protection under retroactive application affirmed.
Author: Judge Logue. Panel: Logue, Lindsey and Gooden.
Official opinion retrieved October 12, 2026; issuance date stated in document and index. Any printed rehearing or revision qualification is preserved; subsequent docket finality and treatment not independently verified.

curiae and its interest in the case is included in the word count.

items.summary:
The Court amends rule 9.370 to include the amicus identity and interest statement in the word count. Its opinion states that rule 9.900 forms gain service certificates, including a certificate for service on the Attorney General with the notice of constitutional question. Amendments take effect January 1, 2027 at 12:01 a.m. Review covered the opinion narrative, amicus rule and first amended form; the remaining forms are collected, not individually reviewed.
